unit that f reads is on only on its own region, so g_f = 1 - 1/(kappa m) > 0. On another compact X that holds the
vertex points the units of different blocks may overlap, but g_f > 0 still holds: for each layer-1 unit d, at a vertex
point of another unit, that unit is on and every other unit is off with margin (Lemma T43a part 6), so near it f is on
and d is off, on a set of positive measure. So mu_f({h_d = 0}) > 0 for every d.
So the hardness of Theorem T43 holds for networks that are perfectly clean under D42 at one hidden layer, on every X:
Shonu's conjecture (Remark B.K.1) is still refuted at L = 1 by these networks and mixes. At L >= 2 the detector
networks fail G, as they failed Q4.

## A.6 Clean means interpretable: the definition that exploration gives (proposed; node R-cleannet, PENDING)

Shonu (2026-10-26, evening): "when we say clean, we really mean interpretable. And when we say interpretable, we're
actually pointing to a sort of engineering-ish method where we're exploring the neurons themselves. And so actually
the foundation, rather than building from first principles, is the first principle is actually exploration." So this
section starts from what an interpreter does. The exploration is lab work, recorded in
`research/clean/explore/EXPLORE-LOG.md`. It is the record of where the definitions came from, not a source of proof,
and what it observed is stated here as observation of the log, not as fact. It followed the essay's moves on three
units of InceptionV1: 4e:55 (the unit the essay says "looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars" but is "a
V-shape neuron"), the curve unit 3b:379 and the car unit 4c:447. Its table of operations has twelve moves. Four
observations of the log shape the definitions below.
1. The move that separated jobs was the line-up. The essay: "You look upstream at how it's built and downstream at
   what it does, and both line up." In the log, splitting 4e:55's inputs by what builds them and asking what uses them
   on each part separated a face job from a vehicle job, when its images alone did not.
2. The split can be the network's own. In the log, the unit below that casts the largest vote split 4e:55's inputs
   into pointed animal faces and vehicle bodies with no class labels. The essay: "if I couldn't use groups of nouns at
   all, how would I describe this neuron to someone else?"
3. Use was more informative at the readers than at the output. In the log, single output effects mostly recorded which
   class an input is. The essay: "If you don't understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects
   to". At the classes themselves there is no layer beyond; there D44 uses the change of the class probabilities.
4. One job was not enough. In the log, units of a randomly initialised InceptionV1 had routes feeding readers whose
   gates did not respond to the unit, so their routes looked like one job. The essay's definition of clean has two
   halves: parts "built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers". So the definition asks that a unit be
   READ and have ONE JOB.
Definitions D41 and D42 (votes on targets) stay in the paper as an earlier candidate. This section replaces them as
the definition of clean.

**Definition D43 (canonical form, base law, target) (proposed; nodes R-cleannet and R-explaw, PENDING).** N is a
plain ReLU network or a convolutional ReLU network with stride-1 convolutions, zero padding and max pools (a unit of a
convolutional layer is a channel; its row is its kernel and bias). Pos_l is the set of positions of layer l (one
position for a dense layer).
1. The **canonical form** of N is the result of the following loop, run until nothing changes: (i) from the first
   hidden layer up, rescale every unit with (w, b) != 0 to |(w, b)| = 1 and multiply its outgoing weights by the old
   norm (the function does not change, Fact F1); (ii) merge the units of one layer whose rescaled rows are equal,
   adding their outgoing weights; (iii) delete every unit whose outgoing weights are all 0. Each pass removes a unit
   or changes nothing, so the loop stops.
2. The **base law** nu is a probability law on the inputs X with a finite first moment. Which law belongs to N's kind
   is node R-explaw: (i) the data law of N's kind, or (ii) a law built from N alone. (The node R-cleannet records
   Shonu's earlier requirement that clean be judged without the training inputs; option (i) departs from it, and the
   choice is his.) Write nu_l for nu times the uniform law on Pos_l.
3. A unit u of layer l is **live** when E_{nu_l}[h_u] > 0. Its **target** mu_u is the law on X x Pos_l with density
   h_u / E_{nu_l}[h_u] with respect to nu_l.
Everything below is computed on the canonical form.

**Definition D44 (votes, route, readers, use) (proposed; node R-cleannet, PENDING).** A unit u of layer l reads the
units j of layer l - 1 (for l = 1, the input coordinates) through weights W_u[j, o] at offsets o in its window Omega
(Omega = {0} for a dense or 1 x 1 layer).
1. The **vote** of j at (x, p) is c_uj(x, p) = sum over o of W_u[j, o] h_j(x, p + o), with h_j = 0 outside Pos_{l-1}.
   The **route** rho_u(x, p) is the set of j whose vote is largest. (If every vote is 0, the route is the whole set of
   builders.)
2. A **read** of u by a unit r of layer l + 1 is a pair (r, o) with W_r[u, o] != 0. A read at an offset that leaves
   Pos_{l+1} is 0. When a max pool sits between layers l and l + 1, the reader at p' reads the pooled value; u at p is
   counted as read at p' when p is the position of the pool window at p' whose value is selected, with ties resolved by
   the smallest position (Fact F1: on each set of inputs with a fixed selection pattern the pool is a selection).
3. The **use** of u at (x, p) is the vector g_u(x, p) with one entry per read. For a unit reader,
   g_(r, o)(x, p) = W_r[u, o] 1[z_r(x, p') > 0], with p' the position that reads p through o. For u in the last hidden
   layer, the readers are the classes, with one entry per class: g_c(x) = dq_c / dh_u (x)
   = q_c(x) (W_out[c, u] - sum_c' q_c'(x) W_out[c', u]) (the change of the class probabilities per unit of u; for a
   convolutional network, h_u is the averaged position that the readout reads).
4. The **signed active read** is S_u(x, p) = the sum of the entries of g_u(x, p) for a unit reader, and
   S_u(x) = sum_c W~_cu q_c(x) for the classes, with W~ = P_perp W_out (the centred readout, Fact F11). The **read
   weight** T_u is the sum over reads of |W_r[u, o]|, and, for the classes, the sum of |W~_cu|.
Comment. Why the classes read through the probability change: it is the function-level use. A shift of the readout
(adding one vector to every row of W_out) keeps every probability and every derivative dq / dh_u, so the use does not
depend on how the readout is written (Theorem T46(d)). A unit of a two-class network has
g_u = q_1 q_2 (W_out[1, u] - W_out[2, u]) (1, -1), one ray. The limit of this choice (comment (h) of D45): at the
last hidden layer, which class wins is part of the use.

**Definition D45 (packing index, read index, a clean network) (proposed; node R-cleannet, PENDING).** For a live unit u,
write w_g = mu_u(rho_u = g) and m_g = E_{mu_u}[g_u | rho_u = g] for its routes g. A weighted mean whose total weight is
0 is 0.
1. **Packing index:** pi(u) = 1 - |sum_g w_g m_g|^2 / (sum_g w_g |m_g|)^2, and pi(u) = 0 when the denominator is 0.
   So pi(u) = 0 when every route by which u is built feeds the same readers, up to strength.
2. **Read index:** lambda(u) = (E_{mu_u}[S_u] - E_{nu_l}[S_u]) / T_u, and 0 when T_u = 0: the extra signed read
   that u's readers give where u is on, against anywhere.
2'. **Excess read (agreement read)**, for a unit whose reads are 1 x 1 or dense (one read per reader). Write each
   reader's pre-activation as z_r = W_ru h_u + R_r (R_r, the rest, is what r receives from everything but u), and, for
   the classes, y = W_out[., u] h_u + R (the logits minus u's part). Let S(t, R) be the signed active read of D44 with
   h_u = t and rest R. The independent read index lambda_ind(u) is computed like lambda(u) with the rest taken at an
   independent input: lambda_ind(u) = (E[S(h_u(x, p), R(x', p))] over (x, p) ~ mu_u, x' ~ nu
   - E[S(h_u(x, p), R(x', p))] over (x, p) ~ nu_l, x' ~ nu) / T_u, with x' independent of (x, p) and the rest read at
   the same position p. Reads through a max pool are left out of this item (across a pool the reader sees the pooled
   value, so the split z_r = W_ru h_u + R_r is not defined there); Part C states how H-agree approximates them. The excess read is xi(u) = lambda(u) - lambda_ind(u): how much the
   readers' other votes agree with u where u is on, beyond what u's own vote does.
3. **Use weight:** omega_u = E_{nu_l}[h_u |g_u|].
4. The **cleanliness list** is eps(N) = (eps_pack, eps_unread): eps_pack = the omega-weighted mean of pi(u), and
   eps_unread = the omega-weighted share of live units with lambda(u) <= 0.
5. N is **perfectly clean (weak form)** when every live unit u has pi(u) = 0 and lambda(u) > 0: every unit is READ
   (its readers turn on with it, in the direction of its votes) and has ONE JOB (every route by which it is built
   feeds the same readers, up to strength). N is **perfectly clean (agreement form)** when every live unit has
   pi(u) = 0 and xi(u) > 0: in addition, the other votes its readers receive agree with it. Which form is the
   definition is Shonu's choice (card 3-7). The weak form's read part holds whenever readers' other inputs are
   independent of the unit (Lemma T46b). Whether the agreement form separates trained from untrained networks is
   Hypothesis H-agree. The agreement form excludes the detector networks of T43 (Proposition T50), and, by Lemma
   T46d, every bias-free positive reader that ORs units which are never on together. That includes a family of
   members that are apart (Q2 of D39) read by one coarse positive reader (Q5): the family-and-coarse-reader structure
   this track started from, which Remark B.K.1 (d) asked a new principle not to exclude. A unit read only by readers
   that read it alone has xi = 0 (Lemma T46c), so it is never clean in the agreement form.
6. The agreement list is eps_agree = the omega-weighted share of live units with xi(u) <= 0.
Sources in the essay. Read: "a network's parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers"; "each
input weight votes for its positive side or its negative side". One job: "You look upstream at how it's built and
downstream at what it does, and both line up"; the failure the essay names is "neurons learning unrelated things
together because they rarely interfere". No class name enters (Theorem T46(c)): whether 4e:55's inputs are "cats and
cars" is a question about our labels; whether its routes feed different readers is a question about the network.
Comment (what D45 settles and what it leaves open).
(a) The ambulance. The essay's ambulance unit reads a car-body unit (+) and a taxi-sign unit (-). D42's V counted this
as cancellation. Under D45 the car-body unit has pi = 0 and lambda > 0 when, under its target, its route does not
depend on whether the input is a taxi or an ambulance (Proposition T47 part 3 builds such a law).
(b) The V case. A unit built by one route on one kind of input and by another route on another kind, and read by one
reader, has pi = 0 and can have lambda > 0 (Proposition T47 part 2): an offshoot used like its core is the essay's
"recursive generalization", and D45 calls it clean. With a 1 x 1 or dense reader, "one reader" means one read.
(c) Locality. The use is one layer up (or the classes). A unit whose routes feed the same readers can still have
different effects further down; D45 charges packing to the unit at which routes stop sharing readers. Whether a
deeper use is needed is open.
(d) The route is the coarsest split that the network names: splitting routes further can only raise pi (Lemma T46a
part 3), and the finest split (one route per input) measures the raw spread of use.
(e) Zero padding is part of the architecture, so routes that exist only near borders count.
(f) The read condition lambda(u) > 0 is weak: by Lemma T46b it holds whenever readers' other inputs are independent
of u, and the Part C measurement of H-route found most units of a random initialisation with lambda > 0. The excess
read xi (item 2') removes the part due to u's own vote; Lemma T46c gives xi = 0 under independence, and xi = 0 for a
unit that its readers read alone. Whether xi separates trained from untrained networks is Hypothesis H-agree. Its
cost is Lemma T46d.
(g) In the weak form, the hardness of Theorem T43 stands: the detector networks of D40 at one hidden layer are
perfectly clean in the weak form with the uniform base law on their domain (Proposition T49), and T43's hard mixes
are invariant under their block permutations. So no definition of clean that these networks satisfy removes T43's
hardness for every mix. In the agreement form they are not clean (Proposition T50), and the question is Conjecture
D47.
(h) At the last hidden layer the use includes which class wins. A unit read by two classes whose routes follow the
winning class gets pi > 0 even if one would call it a shared feature (Proposition T47 part 1 is such a circuit, with
the two classes also cancelling the other route). D45 cannot tell packing from reuse there.
(i) D44 is written for plain and convolutional chains. A network with parallel branches and concatenation (such as
InceptionV1) is covered when "layer l + 1" means every convolution that reads the concatenated output; local response
normalisation is not covered. Part C states the approximations it uses.

**Definition D46 (the pair index: the packing index of a planted two-job unit) (proposed; node R-cleannet, PENDING).**
For two live units u_1, u_2 of one layer, let the planted unit be the law that is mu_{u_1} with route 1 and use
g_{u_1} with probability 1/2, and mu_{u_2} with route 2 and use g_{u_2} with probability 1/2. Its pair index
pi(u_1, u_2) is the packing index of item 1 of D45 for this law. It is the packing index a unit would have if it did
u_1's job on u_1's target and u_2's job on u_2's target. It is a reference scale for pi, not a unit of N.

**Definition D49 (two candidate read tests) (proposed; nodes R-cleannet and R-listen, PENDING).** Let u be a live unit
of a dense hidden layer l < L (dense layers only; D45 item 2' also allows 1 x 1 convolutions, which D49 leaves out),
with readers r (the units of layer l + 1 with W_ru != 0). Write z_r = W_ru h_u + R_r as in D45 item 2', b_r for the
bias of r, and R'_r = R_r - b_r for the part of the rest that the other units of layer l send. In the canonical form
(D43) every unit of a hidden layer below L has a reader, so T_u > 0; as in D45, an index is 0 when T_u = 0.
1. The **deciding read** is dec(u) = E_{mu_u}[sum over r of W_ru (1[z_r > 0] - 1[R_r > 0])] / T_u: how often, on
   u's target, u's own vote switches a reader (on for a positive read, off for a negative one), weighted by the read.
2. The **co-active read**, for a base law nu with a finite second moment (so that E_nu[h_u h_k] is finite), is
   coact(u) = E_{mu_u}[sum over r of sign(W_ru) R'_r]: the votes that u's readers receive from the other units at the
   inputs where u is on, signed by u's own read. A unit that is off votes 0, so only the units that are on together
   with u enter. It is not normalised; only its sign is used.
Both are candidates for the read part of D45 that would credit a coarse reader of alternatives (Lemma T46d), which the
excess read xi does not. Lemma T52 states what each one does.

**Remark A.6.1 (the networks of Part B under D45).** The two-class networks of Theorems T20, T32, T33, T34, the
teacher of T22, and the detector networks of D40 at one hidden layer have every unit in the last hidden layer, read by
two classes; by the comment of D44 every use lies on one ray, so pi = 0 for every unit and every base law (Lemma T46a
part 4). Their read indices depend on the base law; Proposition T49 settles the detector networks. The networks of
Part B do not test the packing index; Proposition T47 builds circuits that do.

## A.7 Maps of a network (Trunk T5, added 2026-10-28)

Trunk T5 gives the rule a map M of N on P. This section makes "map" a mathematical object. How a map is found (by
people, agents or a program) is outside the trunk. Checking a map is inside it: every claim has an error that anyone
can compute from N and P. Source (Shonu, 2026-10-28): "assume that we're given a network which is already mapped";
"we can't just ... say, hey, this is mapped and not have a mathematical theory attached to that all the way to the
fundamentals".

**Definition DM1 (claim, map).** A **claim** is a type together with finite objects: lists of N's units, of points of
P, of rational numbers, and of permutations. Each type gives an error eps(N, P, claim) >= 0 that can be computed in
time polynomial in the bit length of (N, P, claim), with eps = 0 exactly when the claim holds. No claim's objects or
error refer to a build, a target size or a zoom. A **map** M of N on P is a finite list of claims. A concept (for
example "car") enters a map only through its extension: a set of points of P. Throughout, every point of P has weight
p_x > 0, so an error that is a p-weighted sum of non-negative terms is 0 exactly when every term is 0. The rules of
DM2 on how districts and their sets sit together are syntactic conditions on M, checked in polynomial time; they are not
claims.

**Definition DM2 (district claim, districts, regions).** A **district claim** (D, Omega) names a set D of units of one
hidden layer and a set Omega of points of P. Its error is
   eps_dist(D, Omega) = max over u in D with A_u > 0 of eps_u,   eps_u = (sum over x in P outside Omega of p_x h_u(x)) / A_u,
   A_u = sum over x in P of p_x h_u(x)
(the largest member's share of its own activity that lies outside Omega; eps_u is **u's term**; a member that is off on
all of P has no term, and a district with no term has error 0). It is 0
exactly when every member of D is off at every point of P outside Omega. (Changed 2026-10-28: the first form summed the
members' terms. That sum grows by (n - 1) eps_u when u is replaced by n copies of itself, which changes nothing in N
(Proposition TN1). Both forms are 0 for the same claims and agree for a district of one member.) It does not change when a unit is rescaled as
in Fact F1 (in-weights and bias times c > 0, out-weights divided by c), which keeps N's function. The **districts** of a map are the
sets D of its district claims. In a map they are pairwise disjoint, and two district claims of the same layer have
sets Omega that are equal or disjoint. A **region** of a layer is a set that is the Omega of some district of that
layer. A map **covers** a layer when its districts of that layer contain every unit of the layer (a unit that is off
at every point of P can be a district with Omega empty).

**Definition DM3 (shelter claim).** A **shelter claim** for a district (D, Omega) of a hidden layer says that the
vector z_D(x) of the members' pre-activations is the same at every point of P outside Omega. Its error is
   eps_shel(D) = max over u in D with B_u > 0 of e_u,   e_u = (sum over x, x' in P outside Omega of p_x p_x' (z_u(x) - z_u(x'))^2) / B_u,
   B_u = sum over x in P of p_x (z_u(x) - zbar_u)^2,   zbar_u = sum over x in P of p_x z_u(x)
(the variance of z_u over P, so a large constant in z_u does not shrink the error; rational for rational data, and
unchanged by the rescaling of Fact F1; e_u is **u's term**; a member with B_u = 0 has z_u constant on P and has no
term). (Changed 2026-10-28 from the sum of the members' terms, for the reason given in DM2.)
Source: the essay's gate sentence ("a neuron in front of them acts as a gate ... its negative side keeps the dogs out.
The dogs go on to their own area, which doesn't have to worry about cars") supports "off outside its area", which is
DM2. DM3 asks more: outside its region the district's in-votes, also those below 0, do not change. This is what class
(b) builds need, since their new units read pre-activations that relu would erase (Theorem TU10 of `UNIT-BRANCH.md`);
a gate in front that switches off all of the district's inputs gives it.

**Definition DM4 (judgment claim).** A **judgment claim** (R, K, a) names a region R of the last hidden layer, a set K
of units that lie in districts with region R, and rational weights (a_k) over K. Its error is
   eps_judg(R, K, a) = sum over x in R of p_x (1 - sum over k in K of a_k h_k(x))^2.
It is 0 exactly when the weighted sum of the units of K is 1 at every point of R. (The units of K are 0 outside R when
their district claims hold.) Syntactic rules, like those of DM2: a map holds at most one judgment claim per region, and
its weight vector a is not 0. Source: the essay's car neuron, "a reusable judgment and a sheltered place for taxis,
ambulances, and other specialists".

**Definition DM5 (family claim).** A **family claim** (c, Gamma_0, rho_0, (pi_l), sigma) lists positive rational scales
c_u, one per hidden unit, generators Gamma_0 of a finite group and, for each generator, the matrices of Definition D20
(an input matrix rho_0(gamma) that is a signed permutation matrix, one permutation per hidden layer, one permutation of
the classes; signed permutation matrices are orthogonal and generate a finite group, a syntactic condition). This is
narrower than D20, whose input matrices may be any orthogonal matrices (for example rational rotations). Let N^c be N
with each unit's in-weights and bias multiplied by c_u and its out-weights divided by c_u (the same function, since
relu is positively homogeneous). The error is the sum over the generators of the squared Frobenius norms of the defects
of the identities of D20 parts 1 and 2 computed on N^c (for example |W^c_l rho_{l-1}(gamma) - pi_l(gamma) W^c_l|^2),
plus the defect of the mix, sum over x in P of (p_x - p(rho_0(gamma) x))^2 (p is 0 outside P). All terms are rational.
The error is 0 exactly when the identities hold at every generator and P is invariant under every generator; then they
hold for every product of generators, with the products of the listed permutations (W rho(g1 g2) = W rho(g1) rho(g2) =
pi(g1) W rho(g2) = pi(g1) pi(g2) W). This is a rational form of the equivariance part of D20: D20's reduced form uses
scales 1 / |(w, b)|, which can be irrational, and its other conditions (faithful action, merged equal units) are not part
of this claim. Without faithfulness the claim with every permutation the identity always holds; like M_1 of Theorem TM3,
such a claim says nothing.

**Definition DM7 (blend claim) (two logits).** Let N have two logits, and let S be a set of units of the last hidden
layer with gap weights alpha_u = W_out[1, u] - W_out[2, u]. Write t_S(x) = sum over u in S of alpha_u h_u(x) (what S
sends to the gap). A point x_0 of P is a **blend** of S when there are points x_1, ..., x_q of P with z_S(x_0) in the
convex hull of z_S(x_1), ..., z_S(x_q) and t_S(x_0) outside the interval [min_k t_S(x_k), max_k t_S(x_k)]: a mix of
the group's inputs at which the group sends less than at all of them, or more than at all of them (both cases of
Proposition T59 part 2, which rules out a monotone output in either direction). A **blend claim** (S) says that P holds
no blend of S. Its error is
   eps_blend(S) = sum over the blends x_0 of S of p_x0.
It is rational, and computable in polynomial time: for each x_0 it is two linear programs, membership of z_S(x_0) in the
convex hull of the vectors z_S(x) with t_S(x) > t_S(x_0), and in the hull of those with t_S(x) < t_S(x_0). It does not
depend on which logit is called class 1 (swapping the two rows changes the sign of t_S and exchanges the two cases). It does not change under the rescaling of Fact F1 (a
positive scale of one coordinate of z_S keeps convex combinations, and t_S does not change). The form for three or more
logits is open.
Source: Hypothesis H-freefam's paraphrase of the essay (the blend of two curves is another curve, so some member fires
on it), read the other way: one unit with a monotone output cannot be quieter, or louder, at a mix of its members'
inputs than at all of them (Proposition T59 part 2), so a group folds into one unit only if P holds no such mix.

**Definition DM8 (flat claim).** A **flat claim** (F) for a set F of units of the last hidden layer that lie in no
district says that each unit u of F is constant on every non-empty region of the map in that layer. Its error is the
largest over u in F of **u's term**
   eps_flat(u) = (sum over regions R of sum over x, x' in R of p_x p_x' (h_u(x) - h_u(x'))^2) / V_u,
   V_u = sum over x in P of p_x (h_u(x) - hbar_u)^2,   hbar_u = sum over x in P of p_x h_u(x)
(the variance of h_u over P, as in DM3, so a large constant in h_u does not shrink the error; 0 if V_u = 0). It is
rational and unchanged by the rescaling of Fact F1. A unit u "has a flat claim" when it lies in the set F of one; a
map holds each unit in at most one flat claim. (Changed 2026-10-28: the first form named one unit per claim, so the list
of errors got one more entry for every copy of a unit, Proposition TN1. With F = {u} the forms agree.) (The first form divided by the sum of p_x h_u(x)^2; referee
REFEREE-BE-2026-10-28.md finding 20. Error 0 means the same under both forms.)

**Definition DM9 (quiet claim).** A **quiet claim** for a district (D, Omega) of the last hidden layer says that, at the
points outside Omega, N's logits receive from D the same amount for every class. Its error is
   eps_quiet(D, Omega) = sum over x in P outside Omega of p_x osc(sum over u in D of W_N[., u] h_u(x)),
where osc(v) = max_i v_i - min_i v_i. It is 0 when eps_dist(D, Omega) = 0, and also when the members' writes outside
Omega add one amount to every logit. It is unchanged by the rescaling of Fact F1 (each product W_N[., u] h_u(x) is) and
can be computed in polynomial time. It is in output units: it weighs each leak by what N's own readers do with it.
Source: the essay's "a representation matters only through what reads it" (node R-edgetether), and Proposition TE5,
which shows that the errors DM2 to DM4 and DM8 alone cannot bound the robust optimum of Definition DE2.

**Definition DM10 (proportional claim) (added 2026-10-28, Part B.Y).** Let layer L be the last hidden layer, with positions read as
follows (Definition DY1 of Part B.Y uses the same reading): a channel u has pre-activations z_u(x, s) at positions s = 1, ..., T, and the logits read its pooled
value p_u(x) = (1/T) sum over s of relu(z_u(x, s)); with T = 1 this is a unit of a dense layer. For functions f, g of
(x, s) write <f, g> = sum over x in P of p_x (1/T) sum over s of f(x, s) g(x, s) and |f| = <f, f>^(1/2). For a channel u
let s_u = |z_u|, c_u = s_u |P_perp W_N[., u]| (P_perp as in Fact F11), and, when s_u > 0, zhat_u = z_u / s_u. The
**read members** of a set Q of channels are the u in Q with c_u > 0 and p_u not 0 on P. A **proportional claim** (Q)
says that the read members of Q have positively proportional pre-activations on P: zhat_u is the same function for
every read member. Let z_Q = sum over read members u of omega_u zhat_u with omega_u = c_u / (sum over read members v of
c_v) (z_Q = 0 if Q has no read member). Its error is
   eps_prop(Q) = (sum over read members u of Q of c_u |zhat_u - z_Q|)^2.
It is 0 exactly when the claim holds (if every read member has zhat_u = z_Q they are all equal; if they are all equal,
z_Q is that common function). Computation (bit model): with rational data the error is algebraic (the square of a sum
of products of square roots of rationals). It can be computed to b bits in time polynomial in the size of (N, P, Q) and
b, and whether it is 0 is decided exactly in polynomial time by rational checks (c_u > 0, p_u not 0 on P, and positive
proportionality of the z_u on P x positions, by cross-products and signs). Whether this meets DM1's "computed in
polynomial time" is a reading, recorded with node R-propcomplete (card 3-22); a rational surrogate error is possible
if it does not. It does not change under the rescaling of Fact F1
(z_u and s_u scale by the same c > 0 and W_N[., u] by 1 / c, so zhat_u and c_u do not change), nor under a copy of a
member, read for a layer with positions as channels with z = lam_i z_u at every position and u's logit weights (for a
channel with an identity skip this is an identity of the algebra on (z_u, W_N[., u]), not a re-writing of N's layers,
since scaling the skip needs a 1 x 1 projection): copy i has u's zhat and c_i = lam_i c_u, and the copies together
carry u's share of every sum. A proportional claim that holds u is read as holding every copy (Definition DN1). A set with one read member always has error 0. A member counts by
the size of its pre-activation times its centred read norm |P_perp W_N[., u]| (not by the size of its pooled output:
a channel whose pre-activation is mostly far below 0 counts by that size).
Source: the essay's families of units that do the same job, read in their strongest form (one job, one direction of
pre-activation, so the units are copies of one another up to scale), and DM6 item 5: each class of c(S) has a proportional claim with
error 0 (an error-0 set may also hold unread members of other classes).

**Definition DM11 (an area map of the stream; block-read and write claims) (added 2026-10-29, Part B.V; node
R-streamregion, decided 2026-10-29; laminar for now, node S-laminar).** Let N be a network of Definition DV1 with stream
width d. An **area family** is a finite set
of nonzero subspaces of R^d (the **areas**) in which any two areas are nested or meet only in 0, and, for each area
and at the top, the sum of the maximal areas inside it is direct (widened 2026-10-29, Part B.V.5; node S-laminar,
decided by delegation: Shonu allows areas at an angle, "I'm going to be fine with some like subspace crossing"). The
**laminar** case: any two areas nested or orthogonal. The **children**
of an area A are the maximal areas strictly inside A; their sum is direct (in the laminar case they are pairwise
orthogonal, since two maximal ones are not nested).
The **own part** of A is a complement O_A of the sum of its children inside A, and the **outside part** a complement of
the sum of the top areas in R^d. In the laminar case both are the orthogonal complements, and that is the default. At
an angle they are part of the map, given by rational spanning vectors. The own parts and the outside part (the
**members**) then form a direct decomposition of R^d, with projections Q_A (onto member A along the others; the
orthogonal P_A in the laminar case). At an angle, the bounds that project onto the members (Theorem TV6, Definitions DM12 and DM14, with V and S in DM12
sums of members) use the substitution
of Lemma TV16 part 5: Q_A on the stream side (|Q_A Pi w|, |P_perp U' Q_A|, and U Q_S, L Q_V in DM12) and the
transpose on the read side (|Q_F^T r'| in place of |P_F r'|). The block-read and write claims below use the
orthogonal P_A onto A alone: it is canonical, and their zero sets do not depend on the complements. The energy claim
of DM13 keeps the orthogonal P_D (Proposition TV17).
Claims about an area A:
1. **Block-read claim** "no block reads A": error eps_br(A) = sum over l = 1, ..., L of |R_l P_A|_F^2 (P_A the orthogonal
   projection onto A, |.|_F the Frobenius norm). It is 0 exactly when every read vector of every block is orthogonal
   to A. This error changes under two exact symmetries of DV1: the rescaling of Fact F1 (read vector a r, write
   vector w / a, a > 0, for sigma positively homogeneous) and **stream scaling** (e, W_l and c_l times c > 0 and every
   eps_l times c^2, which keeps every n_(eps_l)(h) and so the function). For Lipschitz sigma_l, with constant Lip_l,
   the **output-weighted** form changes under neither:
   eps_br^w(A) = sum over l and over neurons i of block l of
                 Lip_l^2 (|w_(l,i)|^2 / E_P |h_l(x)|^2) |P_A r_(l,i)|^2 E_P |n_(eps_l)(h_(l-1)(x))|^2.
   It is 0 exactly when, for every neuron, P_A r = 0, or w = 0, or Lip_l = 0, or n_(eps_l)(h_(l-1)) = 0 on P. The two
   forms are two errors of the same claim.
2. **Write claim** "writer a writes inside A", for a neuron a of block l with write vector w_a and inside value g_a:
   eps_w(a, A) = |P_(A perp) w_a|^2 E_P g_a(x)^2; for the first write, E_P |P_(A perp) e(x)|^2; for a block bias c_l,
   |P_(A perp) c_l|^2. It is 0 exactly when what a writes on P lies in A.
A subspace is given by a list of rational spanning vectors B, so P_A = B (B^T B)^(-1) B^T is rational and computed in
polynomial time (DM1 lists units, points, rationals and permutations as claim objects; subspaces are added under node
R-streamregion). eps_br is rational in N's weights. The write error, and the errors of DM12 and DM13, need N's forward
pass (sigma_l, and square roots in n_eps). They are computed to b bits in time polynomial in the size and b, in a model
where sigma_l and the square root are computed to b bits, and whether such an error is exactly 0 is then not decided
exactly (as for DM10). For sigma = relu in the no-norm form they are rational. Every error of DM11 to DM13 is unchanged
by the rotation of Fact F13 part 3 when the areas rotate with it (for example |R_l Q^T P_(QA)|_F = |R_l P_A|_F).
Write claims give an area its meaning: the space that a family of
writers writes into. No theorem of Part B.V uses them (Comment after Theorem TV2).
Source: the essay: "the directions neurons write to and read from are a good place to start"; subspace methods "find
sensible subspaces, and we can follow them across layers"; and the stream "has no privileged basis". A district of
T5 is a set of units inside one hidden layer; an area is a subspace that crosses every block. Node R-streamregion.

**Definition DM12 (readout claim) (added 2026-10-29, Part B.V).** Let N be as in DM11, with C logits, and let
P_perp = I - (1/C) 1 1^T as in Fact F11. For a subspace S of R^d and a subspace V of S, the **readout claim** (S, V)
says that the logits read S through V on P. Its error is
   eps_ro(S, V) = min over C x d matrices L of E_P |P_perp (U P_S n(x) - L P_V n(x))|^2,   n(x) = n_(eps_(L+1))(h_L(x)).
The minimum is a linear least-squares problem, so it is attained and computed in polynomial time (normal equations).
It is 0 exactly when some L makes P_perp U P_S n(x) = P_perp L P_V n(x) at every point of P. Write L*(S, V) for the
least-norm minimiser. The claim names V; it names no size and no build. In a map, V is an area of the map (DM14). In substance, a readout claim (S, V) together with the energy claims
of DM13 on S minus V fixes a cut of S, and dim V is a size: a map that serves a zoom holds one such V per group and
level, as merge partitions do for DY2.

**Definition DM13 (energy claim) (added 2026-10-29, Part B.V).** For a subspace D of R^d and a norm l in
{1, ..., L + 1} (block l, or the logits for l = L + 1), the **energy claim** (D, l) says that the stream's energy in D
before norm l is the same at every point of P. Its error is the weighted variance
   eps_en(D, l) = E_P (|P_D h_(l-1)(x)|^2 - c_l(D))^2,   c_l(D) = E_P |P_D h_(l-1)(x)|^2,
which is 0 exactly when |P_D h_(l-1)(x)|^2 is the same at every point of P. It has the units of |h|^4 and is not normalised. In the no-norm form of Definition DV1 no energy claim is needed.
At an angle (DM11), for a cut that keeps a complement K of D with projection Q onto K along D (Lemma TV16), the
**oblique energy claim** (D, K, l) says that e_Q(h_(l-1)(x)) = |h_(l-1)(x)|^2 - |Q h_(l-1)(x)|^2 is the same at every
point of P; its error is E_P (e_Q(h_(l-1)(x)) - c^Q_l(D))^2 with c^Q_l(D) the mean. For K = D perp it is the claim
above. In a map, D and K are sums of members (added 2026-10-29, Part B.V.6).

**Definition DM14 (carried leak claim) (added 2026-10-29, Part B.V; rewritten 2026-10-29, B.V.3).** Let N be as in
Definition DV1 with Lipschitz sigma_l and every eps_l > 0 in the norm form, D a subspace and A_1, ..., A_m a direct decomposition of
R^d (orthogonal, or at an angle with the substitution of Lemma TV16 part 5; both given by rational spanning vectors, as in DM11). With Pi = P_(D perp), c_l(D) as in DM13 and
eps'_l = eps_l + c_l(D), define from N, P and D alone, as in Theorem TV6 with the reads Pi r_(l,i), N's biases and the
logit matrix U Pi:
   leak_(l,i)(x) = (r_(l,i) . Pi h_(l-1)(x)) (1 / nu'_l(x) - 1 / nu_l(x)) - r_(l,i) . P_D h_(l-1)(x) / nu_l(x),
   nu_l = (|h_(l-1)|^2 + eps_l)^(1/2), nu'_l = (|Pi h_(l-1)|^2 + eps'_l)^(1/2) (both 1 in the no-norm form),
and lambda_l, T_l, M_l, u and omega as in TV6, with Lip_l the Lipschitz constant of N's sigma_l. The **carried leak
claim** (D, A_1, ..., A_m, l) for a block l = 1, ..., L (it names the decomposition, on which its error depends) says: for every area A with (u^T M_l)_A > 0, lambda_l[A] = 0 on P (the leak
of D at block l reaches the logits along no route of TV6). Its error is eps_cl(D, l) = (u^T M_l ||lambda_l||)^2, which
is 0 exactly when the claim holds, since every term is >= 0. For l = L + 1 the claim says omega = 0 on P (the logits
lose nothing directly), with error eps_cl(D, L + 1) = ||omega||^2. Each error needs N's forward pass, so it is computed
in the bit-model reading of DM11. The errors carry N's gains (Lipschitz constants, write norms, 1 / rho_l), as the quiet
claim DM9 carries what readers receive. In a map, A_1, ..., A_m are the **members** of the map's decomposition (the
own parts of its areas and the part of R^d outside every area), and D is a sum of members. Then the claim names map
objects only, as a district claim names a district: it says that dropping those members loses nothing on P, a property
of N and P. It names no build and no target size. Which claims a map holds does depend on the zoom it serves (one D per
level); as for districts, T5 puts that dependence in completeness, a relation between map and zoom (Definition DM15).
(So node R-cutclaim, which asked whether a claim may name a cut, is dropped. The readout and energy claims of DM12 and
DM13 are read the same way, with V and S minus V sums of members.)

**Definition DM6 (a map complete for a zoom) (decided by Shonu, card 3-19: "the exactness promise applies only to
complete maps").** A map M is **complete** for a zoom G_0, ..., G_m when, for every level j and every group S of G_j:
1. S lies in the last hidden layer and is a union of districts of M (district claims of DM2);
2. M has a shelter claim (DM3) for every district inside S;
3. every non-empty region that meets S (is the region of a district of S) meets no other group of G_j, and, unless the
   region is all of P, M has a judgment claim (DM4) for it whose units are kept at level j;
4. every unit of the last hidden layer lies in a district of M or has a flat claim (DM8);
5. if k_S < c(S): either N has two logits and M has a blend claim (DM7) for the set S, or (added 2026-11-01, node
   R-poleclaim, revised after REFEREE-BQ10) M has a pole claim (Definition DQ13) with K = C, whose sets D_g are the groups
   of G_j with |J_g| = k_g, covering every group of G_j, in which case items 2, 3 and 4 are not required at this level (Corollary TQ17.1 uses none of them). Here c(S) is the number of classes of the members of S under "z_u = c z_v at every point of P
   for some c > 0" (pre-activations positively proportional on P). (Changed 2026-10-28 from |S|: a copy of a member,
   Definition DN1, adds members but no class.)
Completeness is a relation between a map and a zoom, not a claim, so the rule of DM1 that no claim names the zoom
stands. It is checkable in polynomial time (it reads the list of claims and the zoom). Items 1 to 4 are what Theorem TM1
needs (for any number of logits). Its first branch is not needed by any proved positive result except on T43's instances
(Theorem TM5), where its role is to exclude groups that hold a blend, the hard ones there. Its second branch is what Corollary TQ17.1 needs. A group with
k_S >= c(S) needs no blend claim (copying one member of each class is exact: on P every member is relu of a positive
multiple of its class's pre-activation, so h_u = c h_v). Because every blend claim can be added to a map in
polynomial time and its error is a function of (N, P, S), "a complete error-0 map exists" is in effect a condition on
(N, P, zoom): a restriction of the inputs, option (d) of card 3-19 in another form. Scope, said plainly: T5's exactness
promise now covers only groups in the last hidden layer, and (for k_S < c(S)) two logits, or C logits with total written
rank C/2 (Corollary TQ17.1); for deeper layers, and for other totals at three or more logits, a zoom has no complete map
yet, so T5 promises exactness nowhere there. Under the pole branch, item 1 is met trivially: with items 2 and 3 gone, a district claim (S, P) has error 0, so the districts carry no content, and the pole claim carries all of it. This is the degenerate map of card 3-19, and here it is harmless only because the pole claim itself is the condition. Theorem TQ18 reaches other sizes through the
one-time computation, not through a claim. With every error 0,
completeness is proved to give exactness only on the inputs of Corollary TM5.1 (and, for the split alone, Theorem
TM1), and of Corollary TQ17.1; for general networks it is Conjecture CM2. ("Region" in item 3 is DM2's; the regions A_c
of a pole claim are DQ10's.)

**Hypothesis H-map (a real network has a map with small errors) (proposed; node R-mapreal, PENDING).** For a trained
image network and a mix (its training mix, or a developer's mix of a few concepts), there is a map of one of its hidden
layers whose regions are the label classes of a fixed labelling of P with at least two classes (each region the set of
images with one label), and whose district, shelter and judgment claims have small errors (the normalised errors of DM2
to DM4). (A map with one region, every image, would satisfy any such statement and is excluded.) Part C measures the
errors of candidate maps. Revised reading (2026-11-01): the regions need not be label classes, and the claims need not be of these types. A map is found by agents who read the network (Part C, map agents pilot), and label regions are the wrong start.

**Hypothesis H-weak (N's own readers send little through weak activations) (proposed; node R-weak, PENDING).** For a
trained image network and a mix of its kind of inputs, set to 0 every activation of the last hidden layer that is
below a fraction theta of its unit's largest value on the mix, and keep N's readers. Then the change of the output,
D_P(N_theta) with N as the teacher, is small next to the share of activity that was removed, for theta up to a
fraction that Part C measures. This is the quantity of term (c) of Theorem TE4 for the map whose errors are the weak
entries (Lemma TE0 bounds the change by the sum over x of p_x osc of what N sent through them). Source: the essay, "you
can ablate almost all the weak activations of the network for almost no cost. The places where removing them costs
the most are some of the easiest to understand" (it names the last layer among those places).

**Hypothesis H-scale (larger networks of one family are cleaner) (proposed; node R-scale, PENDING).** In a family of
networks of one architecture trained the same way at several sizes, a fixed map of the last hidden layer (regions:
the photos of two concepts; districts: each unit in the region that holds most of its activity) has output-unit errors
that fall as the size grows. The output-unit district error is
   Lambda(N) = (sum over x of p_x osc(sum over u of W_N[., u] leak_u(x))) / (sum over x of p_x osc(y_N(x) - c_N)),
where leak_u(x) = h_u(x) at the points outside u's region and 0 inside: what N itself sends through the values the map
calls errors, as a share of what N sends in all. Its numerator is at most the sum of the map's quiet errors (Definition
DM9). Source: Shonu's reading of the essay (2026-10-28): "larger networks are actually way cleaner".
In the terms of Definition DN2 below, Lambda(N) is the output deviation Lambda_M(N) of the map's district claims.
H-scale has two forms, which B.N keeps apart: the **quiet form** (Lambda_M(N) falls with size) and the **fair form**
(the fair deviation phi(N, M) falls with size). Both are about the map rule of H-scale. Corollary TN4 needs a third form,
the **map form**, for maps that meet the premises of Theorem TE4: Lambda_M(N), the largest relative deviation r_j of a
kept unit and the largest sigma_u of a group member (Definition DN2) do not grow with size. All three forms are about N
and its map alone.
(Added 2026-10-28, B.N.) The activity-weighted share of earlier drafts is not one of them: it changes when one unit is
rescaled as in Fact F1, so it is not a property of N's function.

**Definition DN1 (a split of a unit; a copy) (added 2026-10-28).** Let u be a unit of the last hidden layer L of N and
n >= 1. A **split** of u is a network N' with N's layers 1 to L - 1 and N's units of layer L other than u, plus n new
units u_1, ..., u_n of layer L (each relu of an affine function of layer L - 1), such that
   h_u1(x) + ... + h_un(x) = h_u(x) at every point x of P,
with logit weights W_N'[., u_i] = W_N[., u] for every i, and N's other logit weights and bias. Then y_N' = y_N on P. A
**copy** is the split in which u_i has u's in-weights and bias times lam_i, with lam_i > 0 and lam_1 + ... + lam_n = 1.
Then h_ui = lam_i h_u and z_ui = lam_i z_u on every input, and y_N' = y_N on every input (relu is positively
homogeneous). By Fact F1 a copy is the same network as n units that all have u's in-weights and bias, with logit
weights lam_i W_N[., u]. The **split map** M' names u_1, ..., u_n wherever M names u: they replace u in u's district
(with the same Omega) and in its shelter claim, each u_i has the weight a_u in a judgment claim that holds u, each u_i
gets u's flat claim, and a blend claim, a quiet claim or a group that holds u holds every u_i (a group keeps its target
size). Family claims (DM5) are not carried over (B.E and B.N do not use them). For a copy, Definition DM6 reads which
units sit in which claims and the class count c(S) of item 5, and a copy does not change c(S) (each u_i is positively
proportional to u on P). So the split map of a copy is complete for the split zoom when M is complete for the zoom.
For a split that is not a copy, c(S) can grow, and M' may need a blend claim that M did not.
Source: the essay, "bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize" and "With more room, that neuron
differentiates into many specific cars". A split is the simplest form of this: one unit's activity shared out among
narrower units that add up to it. A copy is the case with nothing new: the most a network can grow without changing.

**Definition DN2 (write mass, fair deviation, output spread, output deviation) (added 2026-10-28).** Let M be a map of
N in the setting of Definition DE2, with clean table (h^0, z^0). For a unit u of layer L write
d_u = sum over x of p_x |h_u(x) - h^0_u(x)| and A_u = sum over x of p_x h_u(x).
1. The **relative deviation** of u is r_u = d_u / A_u when A_u > 0. (For a unit of a district with no judgment or flat
   entry, r_u is u's term in eps_dist.) A unit with A_u = 0 and d_u > 0 can occur only in a judgment claim whose units
   K' are all 0 on its region (the case omega_k = 1 / |K'| of DE2 item 4); call such a unit **dead-moved**.
2. N's **write mass** of u is mu_u = osc(W_N[., u]) A_u, and M(N) = sum over u of mu_u.
3. The **fair deviation** is phi(N, M) = (sum over u with A_u > 0 of mu_u r_u) / M(N) (0 when M(N) = 0): a mean of the
   relative deviations with weights mu_u / M(N), which add to 1.
4. The **output spread** is O(N) = sum over x of p_x osc(sum over u of W_N[., u] h_u(x)): what layer L sends to the
   logits, without the bias. The **cancellation ratio** is rho(N) = M(N) / O(N) when O(N) > 0.
5. The **deviation sent** is D_M(N) = sum over x of p_x osc(sum over u of W_N[., u] (h_u(x) - h^0_u(x))), and the
   **output deviation** is Lambda_M(N) = D_M(N) / O(N) when O(N) > 0: the share of what layer L sends that rides on the
   entries the map calls errors. D°_M(N) and Lambda°_M(N) are the same sums over the points of P that lie in a region
   that meets no group, or in no region.
6. For a class (b) build B with swings sw_B: its **kept mass** M_K(B) = sum over kept units j of layer L with A_j > 0 of
   sw_B(j) A_j, and phi_K(B) = (sum of sw_B(j) A_j r_j) / M_K(B); its **box mass** M_S(B) = sum over the group members u
   with B_u > 0 of nu_u, with nu_u = (sum over B's box units i of sw_B(i) |m_iu|) sqrt(B_u) (B_u the variance of z_u
   over P, as in DM3), and sigma(B) = (sum of nu_u sigma_u) / M_S(B), with
   sigma_u = (sum over x of p_x |z_u(x) - z^0_u(x)|) / sqrt(B_u). Its **dead term** E_dead(B) is the sum over the
   dead-moved kept units j of sw_B(j) d_j, and N's **dead term** D_dead(N) is the sum over the dead-moved units u of
   osc(W_N[., u]) d_u. Both are 0 when no unit is dead-moved, a property of N and M alone.
7. A mean over an empty set or with total weight 0 is 0 (phi when M(N) = 0, phi_K when M_K(B) = 0, sigma when
   M_S(B) = 0).
Each of r_u, mu_u, mu_u r_u, phi, O, rho, D_M, Lambda_M, D_dead, sw_B(j) A_j, nu_u, sigma_u and E_dead is unchanged by
the rescaling of Fact F1 (values, pre-activations, A_u, d_u and sqrt(B_u) scale by c; logit weights, swings and read
weights by 1/c).
Source: the essay, "a representation matters only through what reads it" (node R-edgetether): each unit is weighed by
what its readers receive from it.

**Hypothesis H-mass (growth does not inflate the write) (proposed; node R-mass, PENDING).** In a family as in H-scale,
with the same map rule and a zoom of the same shape at each size: (1) the output spread O(N) does not grow with the
size; (2) there is a number c such that at every size some e-near clean assembly B^0 of Theorem TE4 has kept and box
masses M_K(B^0) and M_S(B^0) at most c O(N). (Not every e-near assembly need: their masses can be unbounded.) Part (1) is about N alone. Part (2) is about the rule's output and is measured once B^0 is built. A
build fails (2) when the clean split needs large logit weights of both signs that cancel. Source: Shonu (2026-10-28):
"since the larger networks are hopefully more well-trained, if we choose the right larger networks, then we're going
to see some really nice results". The essay says nothing direct about write mass, so this hypothesis is Shonu's, not
the essay's.

**Hypothesis H-active (a trained network's areas favour their own classes) (proposed; node R-active, PENDING).**
For a map of N that splits P into the areas of sibling nodes, there are pairwise disjoint class sets K_w such that
the active-class summaries of Part B.Q (Definition DQ1) are small against the areas' information: the ratio
(sum over w of eps_act(A_w, K_w)) / (sum over w of I_w) (Definition DI1) is below 1/10. Below 1 is the least for
TQ1's packed build to beat dropping the detail. "Trained" means the network as released (here torchvision's
IMAGENET1K_V1 weights); the threshold is mine. Source: the essay ("well trained networks are already clean") and
Shonu (2026-10-31): "this is absolutely genuinely possible given our new understanding that networks are already
clean". H-active is about the bound of TQ1, not about the least itself.

Comment. Each claim type is a principle of clean read as a checkable statement: DM2 is "a district stays in its own
area", DM3 is the gate in front, DM4 is the district's judgment, DM5 is Q1 (moved copies). The list of errors of the
claims is the list eps of Shonu's "multiple metrics" (node R-cleannet). "N is clean when it has a map with small
errors" would be empty: every N has the map with one district per layer and Omega = P, whose errors are all 0 (the sums
are empty). A definition of clean through maps must ask for maps that are fine enough for the zoom (card 3-19).

# Part B: theorems

## B.T The trunk itself: does a least build exist, can the least builds nest, can a fast rule find them

This section works at the trunk T\* (Part 0), with no hypothesis about the network. It asks the three questions that
the trunk's own words raise. Does a least build exist? Can the least builds of different sizes nest? Can a fast rule
find them for every network? Plan: `~/.claude/plans/okay-i-think-last-fancy-cosmos.md`.

**Reading of the trunk's words.** The trunk text is a draft (`DECISIONS.md` section 1). The results of this section
use the readings below. Each one makes a word precise. Two kinds of reading matter differently. For the positive
results (T19, T21) the first reading narrows the question: a law with a density is not covered, and node S-finite
marks this. For the counterexamples and hardness results (T20, T22, T23) the question is whether a reading is broader
than T\* means: they refute T\* only if their networks count as "trained" and their point lists count as "image
mixes". Node N-anynet marks the first (it is the option "every network" in each decision of `DECISIONS.md` section
3). For the second, an affine change of input coordinates puts any finite point list inside the image cube [0, 1]^d
(compose the first layer of every network with the inverse map), so the point lists may be taken inside [0, 1]^d;
they are still not natural images.

| Word in T\* | Reading used in B.T |
|---|---|
| an image mix P | a finite list of points x_1, ..., x_n in R^d with weights pi_i > 0 that sum to 1. The rule reads P, so P is a finite object (a training set, or a developer's list) |
| a trained network N | any network of the kind. A narrower reading (networks that some training run on images produces) needs a named training set and method; whether it avoids the counterexamples of T20, T22 and T23 is open (node N-anynet) |
| does not train | the rule is an algorithm with a proved guarantee about its output (the least value, or within a stated eps of it). Gradient descent run until it stops has no such guarantee. Theorem T21's rule is exact global optimisation, which counts as "not training" in this sense |
| of the same kind as N | a plain ReLU network (Definition D15) with as many hidden layers as N |
| k units in each layer | width k in every hidden layer |
| D_P | E_P KL(softmax(y_N(x)) \|\| softmax(y_B(x))), as in Definition D7, over whole-network builds |
| a rule (fast) | an algorithm. "Fast" means a running time bounded by a polynomial in the bit length of (N, P) |

**Definition D15 (plain ReLU network; build of width k; data vector).** A plain ReLU network with one hidden layer of
width k, input dimension d and n_y logits is y(x) = sum_{j=1}^{k} a_j relu(w_j^T x + b_j) + c, with w_j in R^d,
b_j in R and a_j, c in R^{n_y}. Its hidden units are the maps x -> relu(w_j^T x + b_j). A deeper plain ReLU network
composes such affine maps with relu after each hidden layer and an affine head. For a teacher N with one hidden
layer, a **build of width k** is a plain ReLU network with one hidden layer of width k and the same d and n_y. For a
finite mix P, the **data vector** of a unit is (relu(w^T x_i + b))_{i = 1..n}. Two units are **equal on P up to
scale** when their data vectors are positive multiples of each other, or both zero.

**Two logits.** When n_y = 2, write Delta(x) = y_1(x) - y_2(x) for the logit gap and sigma(t) = 1 / (1 + e^{-t}).
Softmax depends only on the gap, so D_P(B) = E_P l(Delta_B(x); Delta_N(x)) with
l(f; t) = KL(Bern(sigma(t)) || Bern(sigma(f))) = log(1 + e^f) - sigma(t) f - H(sigma(t)),
where H(s) = -s log s - (1 - s) log(1 - s) (natural logarithms). Also D2_P(B) = 1/4 E_P (Delta_B - Delta_N)^2, since
for two logits |P_perp v|^2 = (v_1 - v_2)^2 / 2. A build of width k has the gap
Delta_B(x) = sum_j alpha_j relu(w_j^T x + b_j) + gamma, with alpha_j = a_{j,1} - a_{j,2} and gamma = c_1 - c_2, and
every real alpha_j and gamma occurs. Four properties of l are used below.
(l1) l(f; t) >= 0, with equality only at f = t.
(l2) l(.; t) is convex, decreasing for f <= t, increasing for f >= t, and tends to infinity as f -> +infinity or
f -> -infinity.
(l3) |d/df l(f; t)| = |sigma(f) - sigma(t)| < 1.
(l4) l(f; 0) = log cosh(f / 2).
Proof. d/df l = e^f / (1 + e^f) - sigma(t) = sigma(f) - sigma(t). This is increasing in f, so l is convex, and it is
zero only at f = t, where l = 0 (the KL of a law to itself). This gives (l1), (l3) and the monotone parts of (l2). As
f -> +infinity the derivative tends to 1 - sigma(t) > 0, and as f -> -infinity it tends to -sigma(t) < 0, so l tends to
infinity at both ends. For (l4): sigma(f) (1 - sigma(f)) = 1 / (4 cosh^2(f / 2)), and
l(f; 0) = KL(Bern(1/2) || Bern(sigma(f))) = -1/2 log(4 sigma(f) (1 - sigma(f))). QED.

**Definition D16 (nesting).** Builds B_1 and B_2 of widths 1 and 2 are **weakly nested** on P when the hidden unit of
B_1 is equal on P up to scale to a hidden unit of B_2. They are **strongly nested** when B_1 is B_2 with one hidden unit
and its output weights removed, all other weights unchanged. Strong nesting implies weak nesting. The trunk's "the
B_k nest" asks at least for weak nesting of least builds. Shonu's reading of an instant switch (a prefix of one stored
build) asks for strong nesting.

**Theorem T19 (a least build exists, for two logits and one hidden layer) (under: two logits, one hidden layer, a
finite mix).** Let N be any network with n_y = 2 logits (N enters only through the values Delta_N(x_i)), P a finite
mix and k >= 1. Among the builds of width k (Definition D15),
D_P has a minimum: some build reaches the infimum. The same holds for D2_P, and for every objective
E_P l'(Delta_B(x); Delta_N(x)) with l'(.; t) continuous and tending to infinity at both ends.
Proof. Write X~ for the n x (d + 1) matrix with rows (x_i^T, 1) and theta = (w, b). For a subset A of {1, ..., n} let
Theta_A = {theta : X~_i theta >= 0 for i in A, X~_i theta <= 0 for i not in A}, a closed polyhedral cone, and
E_A = diag(1_A) X~. For theta in Theta_A the data vector of the unit is E_A theta (at a point with X~_i theta = 0 both
are zero). Every theta lies in Theta_A for A = {i : X~_i theta > 0}. Since relu is positively homogeneous,
alpha relu(theta^T x~) = s relu(|alpha| theta^T x~) with s = 1 for alpha >= 0 and s = -1 otherwise, and |alpha| theta
lies in the same Theta_A. So the set of gap vectors (Delta_B(x_i))_i over all builds of width k is the union, over the
finitely many choices of signs s in {-1, 1}^k and subsets A_1, ..., A_k, of
R(s, A) = {sum_j s_j E_{A_j} theta_j + gamma 1 : theta_j in Theta_{A_j}, gamma in R}.
Each R(s, A) is the image of a polyhedral cone under a linear map. A polyhedral cone is finitely generated
(Minkowski and Weyl), so its image is finitely generated, hence a closed polyhedral cone. The union of finitely many
closed sets is closed. The objective F(v) = sum_i pi_i l(v_i; Delta_N(x_i)) is continuous, and coercive by (l2),
because every pi_i > 0. Pick any v_0 in the union. The set of v in the union with F(v) <= F(v_0) is closed and bounded,
so F has a minimiser v* on it, and v* is the gap vector of some build. For D2_P the objective is
1/4 sum_i pi_i (v_i - Delta_N(x_i))^2, which is also continuous and coercive. QED.
Lean: none, by hand. The finite-union step is standard; that finitely generated cones are closed is not in the Lean library in
the form needed here. The argument is by hand.

**Remark B.T.1 (more logits, more layers).** With n_y >= 3 the output weights a_j are vectors and the sign step of
T19 does not apply. The set of logit matrices is then {Y : every column of Y lies in span(u_1, ..., u_k, 1)}, with
u_j data vectors. Sets of this kind need not be closed for a general finite union of closed cones. In R^3 with the
non-negative orthant, k = 2 and no vector 1, the plane {v : v_1 + v_2 = 0} is the limit of the planes
{v : v_1 + v_2 = e v_3} (e > 0), each spanned by the non-negative vectors (e, 0, 1) and (0, e, 1), but it meets the
orthant in one ray only, so no two non-negative vectors span it. The orthant is itself a set of relu data vectors
(three points in R^2 in general position), but with the vector 1 added this example disappears. Theorem T23 gives an
example that survives the vector 1, with three logits. Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender 2021 show that sets of
network functions of a fixed size are not closed in L^p for laws with a density (literature table). For finite P,
T19 shows closedness in the two-logit, one-hidden-layer case.

**Theorem T23 (the least need not exist) (under: none).** Let d = 2, n_y = 3 and k = 2. Let P be uniform on the six
points s_i = (i - 3, 0) for i = 1, ..., 5 and s_6 = (1, 1). Let c1 = (2, 1, 0, -2, -4, 0) and c2 = (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1),
and let N be a plain ReLU network with one hidden layer (width 5, from Lemma T22a) and logits
y_N(s_i) = (c1_i, c2_i, 0). Then the infimum of D_P over builds of width 2 is 0, and no build of width 2 reaches it.
The same holds for D2_P.
Proof. Write G(y) = (y_1 - y_3, y_2 - y_3). Two logit vectors give the same softmax exactly when their images under G
are equal, so D_P(B) = 0 and D2_P(B) = 0 each hold exactly when G(y_B(s_i)) = (c1_i, c2_i) at all six points. For a
build of width 2, G(y_B(x)) = A relu(W x + b) + c with A = G applied to the two output-weight columns and c = G(c'),
and every 2 x 2 matrix A and every c occur. So the set of vectors (G(y_B(s_i)))_i is the set of outputs of all
two-output networks with one hidden layer of width 2 on the six points.
Infimum 0 (the example of Lim, Michalek and Qi; literature table). For m = 1, 2, ... take W = [[-1, 2m + 1], [1, m - 1]],
b = 0, A = [[1, -2], [0, 1/m]], c = 0. Then W s_i = (i - 3)(-1, 1) for i <= 5 and W s_6 = (2m, m). With x = i - 3, the
outputs are (relu(-x) - 2 relu(x), relu(x) / m) = (c1_i, relu(x) / m) for i <= 5 and (2m - 2m, m / m) = (0, 1) at s_6.
As m grows they tend to (c1, c2). The objective is continuous in the logits, so its infimum is 0.
Not reached. Suppose some build reaches 0. Then c1, c2 and the vector 1 lie in span(1, u_1, u_2), with u_j the data
vectors of the two units. They are linearly independent (c2 is the only one that is non-zero at s_6 alone, and c1 is
not constant on the first five points), so span(1, u_1, u_2) = U = span(1, c1, c2), and u_1, u_2 lie in U. Take any relu data vector u in U, u = alpha 1 + beta c1 + gamma c2. On the first five points (all on one line,
at x = -2, ..., 2) u is relu(a x + b0) for some a, b0 (the second input coordinate is 0 there). If a = 0, u is
constant on the five points, and beta = 0 at once, since c1 is not constant there. Take the second
difference D at the interior points x = -1, 0, 1, as in the proof of T20. D c1 = -e_0 and D1 = D c2 = 0 there, so
D u = -beta e_0. By the identity of T20, D relu(a x + b0) = |a| h_t >= 0 with support at most two adjacent points, so
beta <= 0, and if beta < 0 then the support is {0}, which forces t = 0 and b0 = 0, so u restricted to the five points
is |a| relu(x) or |a| relu(-x). Compare with alpha + beta c1 on the five points: at x = 0 it gives alpha = 0, and then
at x = -2 (for relu(x)) or at x = 2 (for relu(-x)) it gives beta = 0, a contradiction. So beta = 0 for every relu
data vector in U, and u_1, u_2 lie in span(1, c2). Then span(1, u_1, u_2) has dimension at most 2, not 3. So no build
reaches 0.
Every minimising sequence of builds has unbounded weights: if a subsequence had bounded weights, a further
subsequence would converge, and by continuity its limit would be a build with value 0. The same example works for
every n_y >= 3 (extra logits equal to 0 in N; the argument uses only the first two components of G) and every d >= 2
(the six points placed in a plane). QED.
Lean: `t23_core` (if relu(a x + b) equals alpha + beta c1 at x = -2, ..., 2, then beta = 0), `relu_second_diff`. The
span argument is by hand.

**Theorem T20 (the least builds of widths 1 and 2 need not nest) (under: none).** Let d = 1, let P be uniform on the
seven points {-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3}, and let N be the plain ReLU network with one hidden layer of width 2 and logits
y_N(x) = (T(x), 0), T(x) = relu(x - 1) + relu(-x - 1). Builds have widths 1 and 2 (Definition D15). Then, for D_P and
for D2_P:
1. The least value at width 2 is 0. Every build of width 2 with value 0 has its two hidden units equal on P up to
   scale to relu(x - 1) and relu(-x - 1), or to relu(x + 1) and relu(1 - x). For each of these two pairs some build
   with those units has value 0.
2. No least build of width 1 has a hidden unit that is equal on P up to scale to any of relu(x - 1), relu(-x - 1),
   relu(x + 1), relu(1 - x).
3. So no least build of width 1 and least build of width 2 are weakly nested, and none are strongly nested. For this N
   and this P there is no list of least builds B_1, B_2 that nest.
4. The same holds in every input dimension d: place the seven points on a line, at x e_1. A unit's data vector then
   depends on (w, b) only through w_1 and b, so the sets of data vectors, and with them all values, are those of d = 1.
Proof. (1) By (l1), and since a squared error is zero only at a match, a build has value 0 exactly when Delta_B = T at
all seven points. N itself is such a build, so the least value is 0. Let D be the second difference on the interior
points m in I = {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2}: (D v)_m = v_{m-1} - 2 v_m + v_{m+1}. D is zero on constant and affine vectors, and
D T = e_{-1} + e_1. A unit relu(w x + b) with w = 0 has a constant data vector. With w != 0 and t = -b / w its data
vector is |w| relu(x - t) (w > 0) or |w| relu(t - x) (w < 0). Since relu(t - x) = relu(x - t) - (x - t), both have
second difference |w| h_t, with h_t(m) = relu(m - 1 - t) - 2 relu(m - t) + relu(m + 1 - t) = max(0, 1 - |m - t|).
So h_t >= 0, and its support in I is the set of m in I with |m - t| < 1: at most two adjacent integers.
Suppose Delta_B = T. Then beta_1 h_{t_1} + beta_2 h_{t_2} = e_{-1} + e_1 on I, with beta_j = alpha_j |w_j| (beta_j = 0
for a unit with w_j = 0). The points -1 and 1 are not adjacent, so one support holds -1 and the other holds 1; say
-1 in supp h_{t_1} and 1 in supp h_{t_2}, and then beta_1, beta_2 > 0. If 0 were in supp h_{t_1}, then at m = 0 the
sum would need beta_1 h_{t_1}(0) + beta_2 h_{t_2}(0) = 0 with the first term positive and the second non-negative,
which is false. If -2 were in supp h_{t_1}, then supp h_{t_2} (two adjacent integers at most, holding 1, not 0) misses
-2, and the sum is positive at -2, which is false. So supp h_{t_1} = {-1}. That forces |t_1 + 2| >= 1, |t_1| >= 1 and
|t_1 + 1| < 1, so t_1 = -1, and beta_1 = 1. In the same way t_2 = 1 and beta_2 = 1. Then D(Delta_B - T) = 0, so
Delta_B - T is affine on the seven points. Write the units, up to their positive scale, as relu(sigma_1 (x + 1)) and
relu(sigma_2 (x - 1)) with signs sigma_j. Using relu(x + 1) = relu(-x - 1) + (x + 1) and
relu(1 - x) = relu(x - 1) + (1 - x): for (sigma_1, sigma_2) = (-1, +1), Delta_B - T = gamma, so gamma = 0; for
(+1, -1), Delta_B - T = gamma + 2, so gamma = -2; for (+1, +1) and (-1, -1) the difference is gamma + x + 1 or
gamma + 1 - x, never zero at all seven points. The two remaining cases do give Delta_B = T.
(2) Let u be one of the four units and V(u) the infimum of the objective over width-1 builds alpha u + gamma. The map
x -> -x fixes P and T and exchanges relu(x - 1) with relu(-x - 1) and relu(x + 1) with relu(1 - x), so it suffices to
treat u_a = relu(x - 1) and u_b = relu(x + 1). For D2_P, V(u) is 1/28 times the least-squares residual of T on
span(u, 1), from the normal equations: V(u_a) = 1/28 * 85/26 (at alpha = 17/26, gamma = 15/26) and
V(u_b) = 1/28 * 493/110 (at alpha = 17/110, gamma = 7/11). The width-1 build B_c with gap relu(x - 8/5) + 3/5 has
D2_P(B_c) = 1/28 * 16/5, and 16/5 < 85/26 < 493/110. For D_P, a lower bound comes from duality: for every s in
(0, 1)^7 with sum_i (s_i - q_i) u(x_i) = 0 and sum_i (s_i - q_i) = 0, where q_i = sigma(T(x_i)),
V(u) >= 1/7 sum_i (H(s_i) - H(q_i)).
Indeed log(1 + e^f) >= s f + H(s) for all f and all s in (0, 1) (the right side is maximised at s = sigma(f), where it
equals the left side), so for f_i = alpha u(x_i) + gamma,
D_P >= 1/7 sum_i [(s_i - q_i) f_i + H(s_i) - H(q_i)] = 1/7 sum_i (H(s_i) - H(q_i)).
The check `model/t20_nesting.py` takes s = s_0 + A z, with s_0 rational (the sigmoid of a numerical minimiser,
rounded), A the 7 x 2 matrix with columns u and 1, and z the exact solution of the 2 x 2 system that makes the two
constraints hold. That z is irrational (q is), so it is enclosed with interval arithmetic (mpmath, 60 digits), and every
logarithm is bounded the same way. The enclosure of each s_i lies inside (0, 1). The vectors s_0 are written to the
check's output file. The certified bounds are V(relu(x - 1)) = V(relu(-x - 1)) > 416449 / 10^7 and
V(relu(x + 1)) = V(relu(1 - x)) > 583137 / 10^7. The competitor B_c' has gap alpha relu(x - 3/2) + gamma with
alpha = 969140 / 968833 and gamma = 219763 / 439837, and D_P(B_c') < 410684 / 10^7. This step is a computer-assisted
inequality. In both cases a build whose unit is one of the four has a value at least V(u), which is
larger than the value of B_c (or B_c'), so it is not least. Least builds of width 1 exist by Theorem T19.
(3) By (1) every least build of width 2 has its units among the four, and by (2) no least build of width 1 has its
unit among them. QED.
Lean: `relu_second_diff` (the identity for h_t), `t20_d2_gap_a`, `t20_d2_gap_b` (for every alpha and gamma the
residual for u_a is at least 85/26 and for u_b at least 493/110), `t20_d2_competitor` (the competitor's residual is
16/5, and 16/5 < 85/26 < 493/110). The interval-arithmetic bounds for
D_P are not in Lean (logarithms on intervals); they are in the check script.

**Remark B.T.2 (where nesting came from before).** In the gated class with one shared gate (H-gate) and the objective
D2, the least builds are the top principal directions of one covariance (Theorems T9 and T6). With a strict gap
between the eigenvalues at each width (the premise of T6), they nest, because the optimum at width k + 1 adds one
eigenvector to the optimum at width k. Theorem T20 shows that per-unit relu gates remove this already for a teacher of
width 2. The least builds of width 2 put their kinks at x = -1 and x = 1. No least build of width 1 does (part 2).

**Lemma T22a (a network that outputs any labels) (under: none).** Let n >= 2 distinct points x_1, ..., x_n in Q^d and
labels t_1, ..., t_n in Q be given. There is a plain ReLU network N with one hidden layer of width n - 1, n_y = 2 and
rational weights with Delta_N(x_i) = t_i for every i. It can be computed in time polynomial in the bit length of the
input. More generally, for logit vectors y_1, ..., y_n in Q^{n_y} the same n - 1 hidden units with one broken line per
logit give y_N(x_i) = y_i.
Proof. For i != j the polynomial p_ij(tau) = sum_{l=1}^{d} (x_i - x_j)_l tau^{l-1} is not zero and has at most d - 1
roots. So some integer tau in {1, ..., (d - 1) n^2 + 1} is a root of none of them, and v = (1, tau, ..., tau^{d-1})
gives distinct numbers v^T x_i. Sort them: s_(1) < ... < s_(n), with labels t_(1), ..., t_(n). Put
mu_0 = 0, mu_j = (t_(j+1) - t_(j)) / (s_(j+1) - s_(j)) for j = 1, ..., n - 1, and
g(s) = t_(1) + sum_{j=1}^{n-1} (mu_j - mu_{j-1}) relu(s - s_(j)).
On [s_(j), s_(j+1)] the slope of g is the sum of mu_i - mu_{i-1} over i <= j, which is mu_j, and g(s_(1)) = t_(1). So g
is the broken line through the points (s_(i), t_(i)), and g(s_(i)) = t_(i). Take hidden unit j to be
relu(v^T x - s_(j)), first logit g(v^T x) and second logit 0. All numbers are rational, of size polynomial in the
input. For logit vectors, use the same kinks and one set of coefficients mu per logit. QED.
Lean: `broken_line_interp` (g(s_(i)) = t_(i), by induction on i).

**Theorem T21 (the least splits into finitely many convex pieces; an exact rule for D2) (under: two logits, one
hidden layer, a finite mix).** Let n_y = 2, P a finite mix on n points of R^d, and k >= 1.
1. The least value of D_P (and of D2_P) over builds of width k equals the minimum, over at most (2 R)^k choices
   (s, A), of the minimum of a convex function over a polyhedron. Here R is the number of regions of the arrangement of
   the n hyperplanes {theta : X~_i theta = 0} in R^{d+1}, and R <= 2 sum_{i=0}^{d} C(n - 1, i) (C the binomial
   coefficient).
2. The regions can be listed with at most 2 n R linear programs, each of polynomial size.
3. For D2_P with rational points, weights and teacher values, each piece is a convex quadratic program with rational
   data, and a least build with rational weights exists. So an exact rule that does not train exists for D2_P. With a
   polynomial-time method for convex quadratic programs, its cost is polynomial in n and the bit length for fixed d and
   k, and the number of pieces grows like n^{d k}.
4. For D_P the pieces have a transcendental objective. Part 1 gives a reduction to finitely many smooth convex
   problems; no claim is made here about their cost in the bit model.
Proof. By the proof of T19, the set of gap vectors is the union of the sets R(s, A). On each, the gap vector is a
linear function of (theta_1, ..., theta_k, gamma) with the linear constraints theta_j in Theta_{A_j}. The objective is
convex in the gap vector by (l2), so it is convex in these variables. Only subsets A that come from regions are
needed: every theta lies in the closure of some region, and Theta_A for that region's A is closed and contains it, with
the right data vector (at the boundary the data vector is zero on both sides). The theta with all X~_i theta = 0
gives A empty. The bound on R is the count of regions of a central arrangement of n hyperplanes in R^{d+1} (Cover 1965;
Zaslavsky 1975; literature table). Each piece reaches its minimum (coercive, as in T19). For D2_P a piece minimises a
convex quadratic with rational coefficients over a rational polyhedron. A minimiser solves the KKT conditions, which
for one fixed set of active constraints are linear equations with rational coefficients, so a rational minimiser
exists. (2) Add the hyperplanes one at a time. A region of the first m - 1 hyperplanes is a sign vector. For each
such region test with two linear programs whether hyperplane m cuts it (feasibility of the strict sign vector with
sign + and with sign - for row m, written with margins 1 since the cones are homogeneous). Each step at most doubles
a region, and every region of the first m hyperplanes arises this way, so at most 2 R tests per step and 2 n R in
all. (3) A piece reaches its minimum (coercive, as in T19). Take a minimiser x* and its set J of active constraints. The
set K of pairs (x, lambda) that satisfy the KKT conditions for J (stationarity, the constraints in J as equalities,
the others as inequalities, lambda >= 0) is a polyhedron given by rational data. It is not empty (x* with its
multipliers is in it), and for a convex program every x in its projection is a minimiser. A non-empty rational
polyhedron has a rational point, so a rational minimiser exists. Convex quadratic programs with rational data, and linear programs, are solved exactly in polynomial
time (Kozlov, Tarasov and Khachiyan 1979; recalled, not re-checked here). QED.
Lean: none, by hand. Counting and listing regions of an arrangement and the KKT step are standard and not in the Lean
library in the form needed. Arora, Basu, Mianjy and Mukherjee 2018 (Theorem 4.1) give the same reduction, for one
output and any convex loss, with running time O(2^k n^{d k} poly(n, d, k)) in a real-number model of computation.

**Theorem T22 (no fast exact rule for every network) (under: none).** Let TRUNK-1 be the problem: given a plain ReLU
network N with one hidden layer, n_y = 2 and rational weights, a finite mix P with rational points and weights, and a
rational eps > 0, return a build B of width 1 with rational weights and D_P(B) <= inf D_P + eps (the infimum over
builds of width 1).
1. If TRUNK-1 has an algorithm whose running time is bounded by a polynomial in the bit length of its input, then
   P = NP.
2. If TRUNK-1 has an algorithm with running time rho(d) S^{o(d)}, for a computable rho, with d the input dimension of P
   and S the bit length of the input, then the Exponential Time Hypothesis fails.
3. Parts 1 and 2 also hold with D2_P in place of D_P.
4. Parts 1 to 3 also hold for the relative version: return a build B of width 1 with
   D_P(B) <= (1 + 1 / (16 n)) inf D_P, where n is the number of points of P. Looser factors (for example a constant,
   or 1 + 1/sqrt(S)) are left open; they would need a padding argument that is not given here.
Any rule that takes eps as part of its input and returns, for every network and every mix, a build of width 1 within
eps of the infimum solves TRUNK-1.
So even the part of the trunk that asks for one size, and allows a stated eps, has no polynomial-time rule unless
P = NP. (The full trunk asks for more. By Theorems T20 and T23 it has no solution at all for some networks.)
Proof. We reduce from Multicolored Clique: given a graph G = (V, E) whose vertices carry kappa colors, decide whether
G has a clique of kappa vertices, one of each color. This problem is NP-hard and has no algorithm with running time
rho(kappa) |V|^{o(kappa)} unless the Exponential Time Hypothesis fails (Cygan et al. 2015, as quoted by Froese,
Hertrich and Niedermeier 2022; literature table). The point set is the one of Froese, Hertrich and Niedermeier 2022
(proof of their Theorem 1). We add the teacher, replace their copies by weights, and redo the error bounds for KL and
for builds with a free sign and a free output bias.
Points. Let N_V = |V| and let x~_1, x~_2, ... be the rational points ((1 - i^2) / (1 + i^2), 2 i / (1 + i^2)) of the
unit circle (i = 1, 2, ...). They are distinct, and none is minus another (all have a positive second coordinate). For
the i-th vertex of color j let x_v in Q^{2 kappa} be x~_i placed in coordinates 2j - 1 and 2j, zero elsewhere. Call a
pair of distinct vertices bad when they have the same color or are not adjacent, and let m_uv = (x_u + x_v) / 2 for
each bad pair. All these points are distinct: a vertex point has one non-zero block, of norm 1. The midpoint of a
same-color pair has one non-zero block, of norm below 1 and not zero, and a chord of a circle is fixed by its midpoint
when that midpoint is not the center. The midpoint of a pair of different colors has two non-zero blocks, which give
back both vertices.
Labels and weights. Label 2 at every vertex point and 0 at every midpoint. Put
delta = 1 / (16 (N_V - kappa + 1)) and M = ceil(12 (N_V + 1) / delta^2). Give weight 1 to each vertex point and M to
each midpoint, and divide by the total Z. The teacher N is the network of Lemma T22a for these points and labels.
All sizes are polynomial in |V|, and d = 2 kappa.
Constants. Let l_0 = l(0; 2), the loss of gap 0 at a vertex. From (l3), l_0 = integral from 0 to 2 of
(sigma(2) - sigma(f)) df >= integral from 0 to 1 of (sigma(2) - sigma(1)) df >= 7/8 - 3/4 = 1/8, using e^2 >= 7 and
e <= 3. Also l_0 <= log 2 < 1. Let Gamma = (N_V - kappa) l_0. For a build B write L(B) = Z D_P(B) (the weighted sum
before division).
Midpoint step. For every build of width 1, Delta_B = phi(w^T x + b) with phi(t) = alpha relu(t) + gamma monotone. On
the segment from x_u to x_v the argument w^T x + b is affine, so Delta_B is monotone along the segment, and
Delta_B(m_uv) >= min(Delta_B(x_u), Delta_B(x_v)).
If G has a colorful clique. Choose its vertices v_1, ..., v_kappa, with v_j the i_j-th vertex of color j. Let
eta = 1 - max over i != i' of <x~_i, x~_i'>, which is rational and positive. Put w = (2 / eta)(x~_{i_1}, ..., x~_{i_kappa})
and b = 1 - 2 / eta, and let B* have gap 2 relu(w^T x + b). Then w^T x + b = 1 at the clique's vertex points and
