3. (in the paper's notion of error, for D2) with eta = 0, D2_P(B'; N) - D2*_k(N) <= 2 dist(N, N') delta_k(N)
   + 2 dist(N, N')^2 <= 2 dist(N, N') ||Yhat_N||_P + 2 dist(N, N')^2.
Proof. ||.||_P is a norm on the centred matrices (every pi_i > 0), so the distance to a fixed non-empty set is
1-Lipschitz: for any point Y of O_k(P), ||Y - Yhat_N|| <= ||Y - Yhat_N'|| + dist(N, N'); taking the infimum over Y
gives delta_k(N) <= delta_k(N') + dist(N, N'), and the same with N and N' exchanged gives 1. For 2,
||Yhat_B' - Yhat_N|| <= ||Yhat_B' - Yhat_N'|| + dist(N, N') <= delta_k(N') + eta + dist(N, N')
<= delta_k(N) + 2 dist(N, N') + eta, the last step by 1. For 3, D2_P(B'; N) = (1/2) ||Yhat_B' - Yhat_N||^2
<= (1/2) (delta_k(N) + 2 dist)^2 = D2*_k(N) + 2 dist delta_k(N) + 2 dist^2, and delta_k(N) <= ||Yhat_N||_P because 0
is in O_k(P). QED.
Lean: `infDist_lipschitz` (part 1) and `transfer_bound` (part 2) in `lean/coarse/Coarse/Shape.lean` (any metric space
and any set; uses Mathlib's `Metric.infDist_le_infDist_add_dist`). Part 3 by hand (one square).
Comment: a reading for the trunk, not a result at it. Suppose eps(N) were defined as the output distance on the mix
from N to a perfectly clean network N' with the same L and the same widths as N (a proposal under node R-cleannet,
PENDING; a second proposal beside D21's weight-based eps, with no relation between the two proved). A rule that
returns a least build for an N' within eps(N) + eta of N then has error at most 2 (eps + eta) delta_k(N) +
2 (eps + eta)^2 (part 3). That is 0 at eps = 0, but it depends on delta_k(N) (at most ||Yhat_N||_P) as well as on
eps, so it is not yet a bound that depends only on eps. The class of N' must be fixed: if N' may have any width, a
sketch in referee report 19 (not proved here) suggests eps would be 0 for every N on mixes whose points lie in distinct
orbits with trivial stabilisers, and the bound would say nothing. The nearest clean N' need not exist (the set of clean
networks need not be closed), hence "within eps + eta". The result is under R-obj (D2), a RETRO node, so it is a side
branch (D.1's rule). For D_P, KL is not a distance, and no D_P form of T42 is claimed here.

**Remark B.S.1 (the optimum is a set, and symmetry permutes it).** Least builds need not be unique: on instance I3 of
B.G two builds with different patterns both equal N on the mix (Remark B.G.1). Under the premises of Lemma T36 (an
invariant mix, and N equivariant on its support), and with T36's action extended to any depth (turn the first layer's
weights by rho_0(gamma), and permute the head's outputs by sigma(gamma)), gamma . B has the pattern of B with the
points moved by gamma (the unit indices stay), so the group permutes the patterns and maps optimal patterns to optimal
patterns. T20's least width-1 builds for D2 are one orbit of two builds (Remark B.Z.1, exact computer-assisted). A rule
returns one member of the set; every member has error 0.

**Table B.S.3 (earlier results in the language of the output set).** Special cases: results about plain ReLU builds
on a finite mix. Analogues: results about another class of builds (gated chains, D11 and D12), where the same
picture holds with "pattern" replaced by the gate configuration.
| Result | Kind | In the language of D35 to D37 |
|---|---|---|
| T19 | special case | two logits, one hidden layer: O_k(P) is a finite union of closed polyhedral cones, so a least build exists |
| T21 | special case | the same: D*_k is the least of finitely many convex problems (an exact rule for D2) |
| T22 | special case | for D2, choosing an optimal pattern at width 1 is NP-hard: given an optimal pattern sigma (its cells are non-empty), the two convex quadratic programs over R(+1, A) and R(-1, A) are solved exactly in polynomial time (T21 part 3), which gives a least build and so solves TRUNK-1 for D2 (T22 part 3). For D_P not shown |
| T23 | special case | three logits: O_k(P) need not be closed, so the infimum need not be reached; an optimal pattern still exists (T41 part 2), and T23's minimising sequence keeps one pattern |
| T20 | special case | the optimal patterns nest: at width 1 (D2) the least unit relu(x - 8/5) fires on {2, 3} (Remark B.Z.1), and the width-2 least pattern is ({2, 3}, {-3, -2}). The least points inside the shared piece do not nest (kink 8/5 against 1). So nested pieces do not give nested builds |
| T36 | special case | the symmetry group permutes the patterns (Remark B.S.1) |
| T38 | special case | the first-order condition at a least build (a local minimum over all builds), which lies in an optimal piece; at a least point interior to a piece it is the normal equation of T41.1 part 3 |
| T39 | special case | the piece fixed by the gate (region G); its least point is one fit when the condition of T39 part 2 holds (under H-flatgate: T39a); otherwise L_G is only a lower bound |
| T40 | special case | the gate's piece is not an optimal piece (I1) |
| T42 | special case | the optimum distance delta_k (not D2*_k itself) is 1-Lipschitz in the network's outputs on the mix |
| T9 | analogue | under H-gate the gates are fixed, so there is one gate configuration; its output set is the image of the matrices of rank at most k plus a free bias (a determinantal cone, not a linear space), and the nearest point is the Eckart-Young truncation |
| T16, T17 | analogues | self-gated chains: the infimum over the gates' effective reads plays the role of the minimum over pieces; for smooth (T16) or affine (T17) gates there are no pieces |

## B.W The developer's zoom: grouped builds, step by step (Trunk T4)

Trunk T4 (`DECISIONS.md` section 1) replaces the size per layer of T\*\*\* by a zoom that the developer chooses. This
Part fixes what a grouped build is (Definition D50), names the kinds of groups by which members are on together
(Definition D51), orders the classes of builds (Theorem T54), counts the cost of one step of the zoom (Theorem T55),
shows that one big group handed over in a single step keeps the hardness of T43 (Proposition T57), and gives an exact
closed form for a group whose members are on together (Theorem T58), tests by one linear program whether a group
merges exactly into one unit (Proposition T59, with the detector networks in T59.1 to T59.3), and says when step by
step can copy a direct merge (Lemma T60, Corollary T60.1). Statements are for one hidden layer unless they
say otherwise. In deeper layers "reads only its group" needs a map from the build's new units below to N's units
(Remark B.W.3).

**Definition D50 (zoom, grouped builds, and the classes (a), (b) and (r)).** Let N have one hidden layer with
pre-activations z_i(x) = w_i^T x + b_i (i = 1, ..., n), units h_i = relu(z_i) and logits A h + c. For a set S of
units, z_S(x) is the vector of the z_i with i in S, W_S the matrix with rows w_i, and b_S the vector of the b_i.
1. A **grouping** G is a set of disjoint non-empty groups S of units, each with a target size k_S >= 0 (k_S = 0
   drops the group). The units in
   no group are **kept**; the set of kept units is K(G). Its width is |K(G)| + sum over S of k_S.
2. A **zoom** is a list of groupings G_0, ..., G_m in which every group of G_(j+1) is a union of groups and kept units
   of G_j, and every group of G_j lies inside a group of G_(j+1) (groups never dissolve). Trunk T4 says "a union of
   groups of G_j"; D50 reads a kept unit as a group of one unit carrying N's own unit, so kept units may join a group.
   A group of G_(j+1) that is a group of G_j with the same size is **unchanged**; the others are **changed**.
   The groups and kept units of G_j inside a changed group are its **children**.
3. **Class (a)** at G: the builds made of N's kept units relu(z_i), i in K(G), and, for each group S, k_S units
   relu(w^T x + b) with any w and b, with any logits.
4. **Class (b)** at G: as (a), but each of the k_S units of a group S is relu(m^T z_S(x) + beta) with m in R^S and
   beta real. Such a unit reads the input only through the pre-activations of its own group.
5. **Class (r)** along a zoom. Let B_0 be a least build of class (b) at G_0 (when G_0 has no groups, take B_0 = N; least
   builds need not be unique, and the sequence depends on the choice). Given B_j, every unit u of B_j has a pre-activation p_u(x), affine in x. A build of the step to
   G_(j+1) copies the units of the unchanged groups and the kept units from B_j; for each changed group S' it has
   k_(S') new units relu(m^T p_(S')(x) + beta), where p_(S') lists the pre-activations of B_j's units in the children
   of S' (a kept child i contributes z_i); its logits are free. B_(j+1) is a least build of this step. An **(r)
   sequence** is any such choice B_0, ..., B_m.
6. V_a(G) and V_b(G) are the infima of D_P over classes (a) and (b) at G.
Comment: under (a) each new unit may compute anything, so a grouping only sets a count (and which units stay as
copies). Class (b) is a reading of T4's "new units that read only that group's units": the new unit reads the group's
pre-activations z_S, not its outputs relu(z_S). Reading the outputs would put a second hidden layer inside the build,
so the build would not be of N's kind. Class (r) is Shonu's step-by-step idea (card 3-11): a coarser unit is built
from the coarse units of the level below, not from N's units directly.

**Definition D51 (the co-firing kind of a group).** Let S be a group of units of one layer of N, with pre-activations
z_S(x), and let P be a finite mix.
1. S is **AND on P** if at every point x of P either z_i(x) >= 0 for every i in S, or z_i(x) <= 0 for every i in S
   (the members are on together, or off together).
2. S is **OR on P** if at every point x of P at most one i in S has z_i(x) > 0 (at most one member is on).
3. Otherwise S is **mixed on P**. The same words are used with a domain X in place of the points of P.
Comment: the kind reads only the signs of N's own pre-activations, so it applies to any group, with or without a
meaning. AND and OR overlap: a point where every member is off satisfies both, and a group of one unit, or a group
that is off at every point, is both. Graded versions (the share of the mix where the condition fails) belong in Part C. The "teams" and
"alternatives" of card 3-9 are graded forms of AND and OR.

**Theorem T54 (the order of the classes, and existence) (under: two logits, one hidden layer, a finite mix).** Let G
be a grouping, G_0, ..., G_m a zoom, and let every point of P have a positive weight.
1. A least (b) build at G exists, and for every B_j a least build of the step to G_(j+1) exists. So (r) sequences
   exist.
2. Every unit of an (r) build B_j that belongs to a group S of G_j has a pre-activation m^T z_S(x) + beta. So B_j is a
   (b) build at G_j, every (b) build is an (a) build, and V_a(G_j) <= V_b(G_j) <= D_P(B_j) for every (r) sequence.
3. If, for every group S of G, the rows w_i (i in S) span R^d, then the (b) builds at G are exactly the (a) builds at
   G, and V_a(G) = V_b(G).
Parts 2 and 3 hold for any number of logits and any mix.
Proof. (2) By induction on j. At level 0 the units of N are z_i, and the units of B_0 are (b) units. Suppose the claim
holds at level j. A copied unit keeps its pre-activation and its group. A kept unit i has z_i. A new unit of a changed
group S' has pre-activation m^T p_(S')(x) + beta; each entry of p_(S') is the pre-activation of a unit of a child of
S', which by the induction is m_c^T z_(S_c)(x) + beta_c with S_c a subset of S'. So m^T p_(S') + beta is an affine
combination of the z_i with i in S', of the form m'^T z_(S')(x) + beta'. A (b) unit relu(m^T z_S(x) + beta) equals
relu((W_S^T m)^T x + b_S^T m + beta), a unit of N's kind, so (b) builds are (a) builds. An infimum over a set is at
most the value of each member, and an infimum over a larger set is at most one over a smaller set.
(3) For any (w, b), the equation W_S^T m = w has a solution because the rows of W_S span R^d (the linear algebra of
Lemma T31, applied to one group). With
beta = b - b_S^T m, relu(w^T x + b) = relu(m^T z_S(x) + beta).
(1) The gap of a build at the n_P points of P is the vector sum over new units u of alpha_u relu(Z theta_u), plus a
combination of the fixed data vectors of the kept and copied units, plus gamma 1. For a (b) unit of S, Z is the matrix
of the vectors (x_j, 1) and theta_u ranges over the linear subspace L_S = {(W_S^T m, b_S^T m + beta)} of R^(d+1). For a
new unit of a step, Z is the matrix of the vectors (p_(S')(x_j), 1) and theta_u ranges over all of R^(s+1). On each
closed cell of the sign arrangement of the rows of Z, intersected with L_S, relu(Z theta) is linear in theta, and
the sign of alpha_u is absorbed as in Theorem T19 (alpha relu(t) = sign(alpha) relu(|alpha| t), and |alpha| theta is
in the same linear space). So the set of gap vectors is a finite union of sets C + V, with C the image of a product of
closed polyhedral cones under a linear map and V the span of the fixed data vectors and 1. Each C + V is a finitely
generated cone, so it is closed, and a finite union of closed sets is closed. Both objectives are continuous in the
gap vector and coercive (as in T19), so each reaches its least value on this closed set. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (parts 2 and 3 are linear algebra; part 1 repeats the proof of T19 on a subspace).

**Theorem T55 (the cost of one step of the zoom) (under: two logits, one hidden layer, a finite mix).** Let a step
from G_j to G_(j+1) change the groups S'_1, ..., S'_q, where S'_t has s_t children units and target size k_t, and let P
have n_P points.
1. The least value of the step is the minimum, over at most the product over t of (2 R_t)^(k_t) choices, of a convex
   problem over a polyhedron, with R_t <= 2 sum_(i=0)^(s'_t) C(n_P - 1, i) and s'_t = min(s_t, d).
2. For D2_P with rational points, weights, teacher values and B_j, each problem is a convex quadratic program with
   rational data, and a least step with rational weights exists. With a polynomial-time method for convex quadratic
   programs (Theorem T21 part 3), the exact cost of a step is polynomial in n_P and in the bit length of its data when
   the sum of the s'_t k_t is fixed.
Proof. As the proof of Theorem T21, with three changes. (i) The new units of S'_t read the vectors
zeta_j = (p_(S'_t)(x_j), 1) in R^(s_t + 1) in place of (x_j, 1). Since p_(S'_t) is affine in x in R^d, these vectors lie
in a linear subspace of dimension at most s'_t + 1, and only the regions of the central arrangement of the n_P
hyperplanes {theta : zeta_j^T theta = 0} restricted to that subspace are needed; there are at most
2 sum_(i=0)^(s'_t) C(n_P - 1, i) of them (Cover 1965; Zaslavsky 1975; literature table). (ii) The copied and kept units
have fixed data vectors with free output weights. They enter each piece as a linear part, so each piece stays a convex
problem over a polyhedron, a convex quadratic program for D2_P. (iii) A sign and a region are chosen for each new unit,
so the count is a product over the changed groups. The regions are listed as in T21 part 2 (at most 2 n_P R_t linear
programs for each changed group). Existence and rationality are as in T21 part 3. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (as T21).
Comment: the data of step j + 1 contain the weights found at step j. Each step is polynomial in its own bit length, but
no bound is proved here on how the bit lengths grow along a zoom. So T55 does not give a polynomial bound for a zoom
of many steps (Remark B.W.2).

**Proposition T57 (one big group handed over in one step keeps the hardness of T43) (under: none).** Let CLEAN-GROUP
be the problem: given a detector network N^1 (Definition D40, one hidden layer), a finite mix P with rational points
and weights, invariant under the block
permutations S_kappa, the grouping with one group S made of all units of layer 1 and k_S = 1, and a rational eps > 0,
return a (b) build at that grouping with rational weights within eps of V_b (and, in the relative version, within
the factor of T22 part 4 of V_b). Then parts 1 to 3 of Theorem T43 hold for CLEAN-GROUP, for D_P and for D2_P (the
D2 version: the same problem with D2_P in place of D_P).
Proof. The weight of the unit d_(j,i) is the vector x~_i placed in block j. Two distinct x~_i are distinct unit vectors,
and neither is minus the other (both have a positive second coordinate; proof of T22), so they are linearly
independent. Since m >= 2, the units of each block span that block's copy of R^2, so the rows of S span R^(2 kappa).
The group holds every unit, so no unit is kept. By Theorem T54 part 3, the (b) builds at this grouping are exactly the
builds of width 1 of N's kind (with free logits, the gap is alpha relu(.) + gamma with every alpha and gamma). A (b)
unit (m, beta) gives the plain unit (W_S^T m, b_S^T m + beta) in polynomial time and back, so rational answers map to
rational answers. So CLEAN-GROUP is the problem CLEAN-TRUNK of T43 with L = 1. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (a reuse of T43 and of T54 part 3).
Comment: handing the group over does not help when the group is big. The rule must still choose which detectors the
one new unit covers, and that choice is the clique puzzle of T43. This corrects a row of card 3-10, which first said
that a given grouping makes T43 easy.

**Theorem T58 (a group whose members are on together collapses exactly) (under: none).** Let N have L hidden layers,
let S be a group of s units of hidden layer l with pre-activations z_S(x) (computed by N), and let Omega_S be the block
of the next layer's weights (of the logit weights if l = L) that reads S. For two logits with l = L, write N's logits
as (Delta_N, 0), which has the same softmax, so that the gap reads S through one row alpha. Let B be N with S replaced
by k units relu(v_t^T z_S(x)), t = 1, ..., k, read by the next layer through a matrix U in place of Omega_S, with every
other weight as in N.
1. If S is AND on P (Definition D51) and Omega_S = U V with V >= 0 entrywise (rows v_t), then B equals N at every point of
   P, in every layer after l and in the logits. So D_P(B) = 0, the least possible value. If S is AND on a domain X,
   then B equals N on X, so D_P(B) = 0 for every mix on X.
2. Such U and V exist with k = rank(Omega_S) + 1; with k = rank(Omega_S) when the row space of Omega_S has a basis of non-negative
   vectors (for example when it contains a vector with every entry positive); and, for two logits with l = L, with k = 1 when alpha >= 0 or alpha <= 0, and with k = 2 always.
Proof. (1) Fix a point x of P. If z_S(x) >= 0, then relu(z_S) = z_S and v_t^T z_S >= 0 (as v_t >= 0), so
relu(V z_S) = V z_S and U relu(V z_S) = U V z_S = Omega_S z_S = Omega_S relu(z_S). If z_S(x) <= 0, then relu(z_S) = 0 and
v_t^T z_S <= 0, so relu(V z_S) = 0, and both sides are 0. So the next layer's pre-activations agree in B and N at x.
Every later layer is the same function of them in B and N, so all later layers and the logits agree. Equal logits give
KL 0 at x. (2) Let r = rank Omega_S and let the rows R_1, ..., R_r of R be a basis of the row space, so Omega_S = U_0 R. Let
c >= 0 be at least minus the least entry of R, and let V have the rows R_t + c 1^T (t = 1, ..., r) and 1^T. Then
V >= 0 and R = E V with E = [I_r, -c 1], so Omega_S = (U_0 E) V with r + 1 rows. If q in the row space has every entry
positive, take a basis with R_1 = q and use the rows q and R_t + c_t q (t >= 2), with c_t large enough that each row is
>= 0. They span the same space, so r rows suffice; any basis of non-negative vectors serves the same way. For two logits with l = L: if alpha is one-signed, V = |alpha| and
U = the sign of alpha; in general alpha = alpha^+ - alpha^- with alpha^+ = max(alpha, 0) and alpha^- = max(-alpha, 0),
both >= 0, so V has the rows alpha^+ and alpha^- and U = (1, -1). QED.
Lean: `and_collapse` (for v >= 0 and z all >= 0 or all <= 0, sum v_i relu(z_i) = relu(sum v_i z_i)) and
`and_collapse_split` (the two-unit form for a row of both signs) in `lean/coarse/Coarse/Zoom.lean`; the
factorisations of part 2 by hand. Check: `model/tr_and.py`.
Comment: this is the AND case of card 3-10. The new units are linear algebra on the members' votes: no search over
pieces, and the mix enters only through where the members are on together. It is Corollary T39.1 without a gate
unit: the AND region is its own gate. T58 gives no lower bound on k: on a finite P fewer units can fit exactly (T28
part 2). In the language of D50 (l = L, one hidden layer), B is a (b) build. When the children of S are N's own units (kept at
the level before), the same replacement inside B_j keeps B_j's function on P, so that step costs no more than
D_P(B_j); it is not shown to be a least step. When the children are new units, the step reads their pre-activations
p, and T58 applies with p in place of z_S and the AND property taken for p.

**Proposition T59 (when a group merges exactly into one unit: a linear program, and the blend obstruction) (under:
none).** Let S be a group of units of one layer of N, with pre-activations z_S(x), read downstream through one row of
weights alpha (as for two logits with S in the top hidden layer, or a group with one reader), and let
t(x) = sum over i in S of alpha_i relu(z_i(x)). Call a unit relu(l(x)) with l(x) = m^T z_S(x) + beta, together with an
output weight a and an offset gamma, an **exact merge** of S on P if a relu(l(x)) + gamma = t(x) at every point x of
P, and a **strict exact merge** if moreover a > 0 and gamma = 0.
1. If t >= 0 on P, a strict exact merge exists if and only if the linear program "l(x) = t(x) at the points where
   t(x) > 0, and l(x) <= 0 at the points where t(x) = 0" in the unknowns (m, beta) is feasible.
2. If P contains points x_1, ..., x_q and a point x_0 with t(x_0) < min_k t(x_k) whose pre-activation vector z_S(x_0)
   is a convex combination of the z_S(x_k), then no exact merge exists.
3. If S is AND on P (Definition D51) and alpha >= 0, then m = alpha and beta = 0 give a strict exact merge.
Proof. (1) The scale a > 0 can be moved into (m, beta), since a relu(u) = relu(a u), so take a = 1. At a point with
t(x) > 0, relu(l) = t(x) > 0 holds exactly when l = t(x). At a point with t(x) = 0, relu(l) = 0 holds exactly when
l <= 0. (2) The map phi(u) = a relu(u) + gamma is non-decreasing if a >= 0 and non-increasing if a <= 0. The map l is
affine in z, so l(x_0) is a convex combination of the l(x_k), and min_k l(x_k) <= l(x_0) <= max_k l(x_k). If phi is
non-decreasing, phi(l(x_0)) >= phi(min_k l(x_k)) >= min_k t(x_k); if it is non-increasing, phi(l(x_0)) >=
phi(max_k l(x_k)) >= min_k t(x_k). Either way phi(l(x_0)) > t(x_0). (3) With m = alpha and beta = 0 the value is
l = sum alpha_i z_i(x). If t(x) > 0, some z_i(x) > 0, so by AND every z_i(x) >= 0 and l = t(x). If t(x) = 0, either
every z_i(x) <= 0, so l <= 0, or every z_i(x) >= 0, so l = t(x) = 0. QED.
Lean: `and_collapse` covers part 3; parts 1 and 2 by hand.
Comment: this is the classifier of card 3-10 as a test. An AND group with alpha >= 0 merges exactly (part 3). An OR
group fails when the mix holds a blend of members' firing points at which the group is quieter (part 2): one ReLU
composed with a monotone output cannot dip between two inputs in pre-activation space. Part 2 needs no symmetry and no
clean property.

**Corollary T59.1 (a group with a bad pair does not merge exactly) (under: none).** In the instance of Theorem T43
with L = 1 (the network N^1 of Definition D40 and T22's points), let S be a set of layer-1 units that contains two
units u and v whose vertex points form a bad pair (two units of one block, or two units of different blocks that are
not adjacent in the coloured graph), and let G be the grouping with the one group S of target size 1 (every other
unit kept). Then no (b) build at G has D_P = 0 (nor D2_P = 0).
Proof. A (b) build at G has gap a relu(l(x)) + sum over kept units of a_i h_i(x) + gamma, with l = m^T z_S + beta. At
the vertex points of u and of v only that unit is on (Lemma T43a part 2), and at the midpoint of a bad pair every unit
is off (Lemma T43a parts 5 and 6: the gap is c times the sum of the units, all >= 0, and it is 0 there). So at these three points every kept unit is
off, and the gap is a relu(l) + gamma. D_P = 0 needs the gap to equal N's gap (2, 2, 0) at them (as in T20, by (l1)).
The pre-activations of layer 1 are affine in x, so z_S at the midpoint is the average of its values at the two vertex
points, and the proof of Proposition T59 part 2 (with x_1, x_2 the vertex points, x_0 the midpoint) rules this out.
QED.
Lean: none, by hand.

**Corollary T59.2 (a group with no bad pair merges exactly) (under: none).** In the same instance, let S be a set of
layer-1 units with no bad pair: S = {d_(j, i_j) : j in J} for a set J of blocks, with any two members adjacent in the
coloured graph. Let c' >= 4 / eta and l(x) = c' (sum over u in S of z_u(x) + |J| r - 1) + 2. Then
relu(l) = c (sum over u in S of h_u) at every point of P. So the build at G (group S, target size 1) with this unit
(output weight 1) and every other unit kept with N's weight c equals N on P.
Proof. Write sigma(x) = sum over j in J of <x~_(i_j), x_(j)>. Then the sum of the z_u over S is sigma(x) - |J| r, so
l(x) = c' (sigma(x) - 1) + 2, and sigma is linear in x. Every vertex point x_p has sigma(x_p) <= 1 (inner products of
unit vectors), with equality exactly at the vertex points of members. At a member's vertex point, l = 2 = c (1 - r),
the value of c times the sum of the members' outputs there (only that member is on). Every other point of P needs
l <= 0, that is sigma <= 1 - 2 / c', because the members are off there (other vertex points: Lemma T43a part 2;
midpoints of bad pairs: part 6). Since c' >= 4 / eta it suffices that sigma <= 1 - eta / 2. At a vertex point that is
not a member's: sigma = <x~_(i_j), x~_a> <= 1 - eta if its block j is in J (a != i_j), and sigma = 0 otherwise. At the
midpoint of a bad pair (p, q): sigma = (sigma(x_p) + sigma(x_q)) / 2 by linearity. If both were 1, p and q would be
members, and two members are not a bad pair; so one of them is a non-member vertex point, with sigma <= 1 - eta or
sigma = 0, and then sigma(mid) <= (1 + (1 - eta)) / 2 = 1 - eta / 2 (as 0 <= 1 - eta). Finally eta <= 1/5
(x~_1 = (0, 1) and x~_2 = (-3/5, 4/5) have inner product 4/5), so 1 - eta >= 0. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (the inequalities of Lemma T43a and linearity of sigma).

**Corollary T59.3 (the groups that one unit replaces with no loss are the cliques) (under: none).** In the same
instance, a set S of layer-1 units has a (b) build at the grouping {S, target size 1} with D_P = 0 if and only if S
has no bad pair, that is, if and only if S is a colourful clique of the coloured graph on the colours it meets. So the
largest group that one new unit replaces with no loss is a largest colourful clique, and it has kappa units exactly
when H has a clique of kappa vertices.
Proof. Corollaries T59.1 and T59.2, and the definition of the coloured graph in the proof of T43 (colourful cliques
of kappa colours are the cliques of H). QED.
Lean: none, by hand.
Comment: this is the classifier of card 3-10 at work on the detector networks. A merge is free exactly when the mix
holds no silent blend inside the group, and the hard part of T43 is to find a large free group.

**Lemma T60 (when step by step can copy a direct merge) (under: one hidden layer).** Let a step of an (r) sequence
change a group S' whose children are S_1, ..., S_q (groups or kept units of G_j). Let child c have k_c units in B_j,
with pre-activations M_c z_(S_c)(x) + beta_c (rows of M_c; Theorem T54 part 2; for a kept unit i, M_c = e_i^T and
beta_c = 0). Let relu(m^T z_(S')(x) + beta) be any (b) unit of S', and write m_c for the part of m on S_c.
1. If every m_c is in the row space of M_c (m_c = M_c^T mu_c), then the (r) unit relu(sum over c of mu_c^T p_c(x) +
   beta - sum over c of mu_c^T beta_c) equals the (b) unit at every input. So a step can reach every (b) build at
   G_(j+1) whose units in changed groups have this property and whose units in unchanged groups, and kept units, are
   those of B_j.
2. Conversely, if the vectors (z_(S')(x), 1), x in P, span R^(|S'| + 1) and some (r) pre-activation equals
   m^T z_(S')(x) + beta at every point x of P, then every m_c is in the row space of M_c. (The spanning premise needs
   |P| >= |S'| + 1 and rows of W_(S') that are linearly independent; part 2 says nothing about groups with dependent
   rows.)
3. Let a child S_c of this step have units with rows M_c. At every later level of the same (r) sequence, every unit of
   the group that contains S_c has a pre-activation whose part on S_c is in the row space of M_c.
Proof. (1) sum mu_c^T p_c = sum mu_c^T M_c z_(S_c) + sum mu_c^T beta_c = m^T z_(S') + sum mu_c^T beta_c. (2) An (r)
pre-activation is sum mu_c^T M_c z_(S_c) + beta'', an affine function of z_(S'); two affine functions that agree on
points that affinely span R^(|S'|) have the same coefficients, so m_c = M_c^T mu_c. (3) By induction on the level. At
this step the claim holds for the new units of S' (part (1)'s computation: their part on S_c is M_c^T mu_c). At a later
step, a unit of an unchanged group is copied, and a new unit of a changed group reads the pre-activations of its
children; the child that contains S_c has, by the induction, units whose parts on S_c are in the row space of M_c, the
other children do not meet S_c, and a combination of vectors of a space stays in it. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (linear algebra).
Comment: step by step reaches a direct merge when each child's coarse units already point, on that child's members,
in the direction the parent needs (parts 1 and 2), and a direction on S_c that the child's units lack never comes
back at a later level (part 3). This does not say that such a step must lose: a different build may reach the same
D_P.

**Corollary T60.1 (step by step is exact on the detector networks when the target groups are cliques) (under:
none).** In the instance of Theorem T43 with L = 1, let G\* be a grouping in which every group has no bad pair and
target size 1. For every zoom from the grouping with no groups to G\* in which every group of every level has target
size 1 and lies inside a group of G\*, there is an (r) sequence with D_P(B_j) = 0 = V_b(G_j) at every level j. So Hypothesis H-recur holds
for these networks and targets, along every zoom.
Proof. Every group S of every level lies in a group of G\*, so it has no bad pair. Let B_j use, for each group S with
k_S = 1, the unit of Corollary T59.2 for S, and keep every other unit; then B_j equals N on P (T59.2 for each group;
the groups are disjoint and the replaced contributions add), so D_P(B_j) = 0, the least possible value, and
V_b(G_j) = 0. Fix one c' (for example c' = 4 / eta) for the whole zoom, so that a group's unit is the same at every level where
the group is unchanged. It remains to see that B_(j+1) is reached by a step from B_j. The unit of T59.2 for S' has
pre-activation c' (sum over u in S' of z_u) + a constant, so its part on a child S_c is c' 1, and the child's unit has
part c' 1 on S_c (a group, by T59.2) or is z_i itself (a kept unit). Both are in the child's row space, so Lemma T60
part 1 gives an (r) unit equal to it. Unchanged groups are copied. A step reaching D_P = 0 is a least step. Zooms of
this form exist: inside each group of G\*, merge two units, then the group and one more unit, and so on. QED.
Lean: none, by hand.
Comment: for these mixes, when every merge in the tree is free, every tree works. The question of D52 is left for
target groups that must pay (that contain a bad pair): there a merge must choose which members to keep, and Lemma T60
part 3 says that a direction the merged unit drops does not come back at a later level. The statement needs T43's
mixes: on other mixes on X a group with no bad pair can fail (at the midpoint of two members in different blocks,
sigma = 1 and the unit is on while both members are off).

**Proposition T61 (two lossy groups can be exact together) (under: none).** In the instance of Theorem T43 with
kappa = 2, m = 2 and H one edge (units A = d_(1,1), B = d_(1,2), C = d_(2,1), D = d_(2,2); bad pairs A-B, C-D, A-C,
B-D), let G be the grouping with the groups {A, C} and {B, D}, each of target size 1. Then the (b) build
   relu(-20 z_A - 40 z_C - 45/2) + relu(-40 z_B - 20 z_D - 45/2) - 18
equals N's gap at every point of P, so V_b(G) = 0. Each group alone (the other two units kept) has V_b > 0
(Corollary T59.1).
Proof. Write tau = (<x~_1, x_(1)>, <x~_1, x_(2)>) and s = (<x~_2, x_(1)>, <x~_2, x_(2)>). With r = 39/40 the two
pre-activations are 36 - 20 tau_1 - 40 tau_2 and 36 - 40 s_1 - 20 s_2. Here x~_1 = (0, 1), x~_2 = (-3/5, 4/5) and
<x~_1, x~_2> = 4/5. At the eight points of P, (tau; s) is: A (1, 0; 4/5, 0), B (4/5, 0; 1, 0), C (0, 1; 0, 4/5),
D (0, 4/5; 0, 1), mid AB (9/10, 0; 9/10, 0), mid CD (0, 9/10; 0, 9/10), mid AC (1/2, 1/2; 2/5, 2/5), mid BD (2/5, 2/5;
1/2, 1/2). The two pre-activations are then A (16, 4), B (20, -4), C (-4, 20), D (4, 16), mid AB (18, 0), mid CD
(0, 18), mid AC (6, 12), mid BD (12, 6), so the build's gap is 2 at the four vertex points and 0 at the four midpoints,
which is N's gap (Lemma T43a part 6). QED.
Lean: none, by hand (eight evaluations). Check: `model/tr_acbd.py` (exact fractions).
Comment: the two new units are not detectors. Each is on at most points and turns off towards its own members, and
only their sum, less a constant, gives N. Neither is a good summary of its group alone: a least build for {A, C} with
B and D kept pays (T59.1). So a step-by-step build that first merges {A, C} alone, then {B, D}, and copies the first
unit, starts from a unit chosen for the wrong situation. In the numeric check (Part C, H-recur row) that zoom ends at a
positive value at level 2 on every branch. The best builds of a level need not extend the best builds of the level
before (compare T20). A variant of (r) that refits every group from its children at each level would avoid the
copy; its cost is a product over all groups (T55), and whether it makes D52 true is open.

### B.W.2 The units that a conflicting group needs: presence units, split units, and the dip identity

Proposition T61 found a zero-loss build whose units are not detectors of their groups. This subsection names the
kinds of unit (Definition D54), names the blends that must be paid for (Definition D55), proves the identity that
says who pays (Lemma T62a and Corollary T62b), and proves that the family grouping of T61's instance forbids units
that fire only where their members fire (Theorem T62).

**Definition D54 (presence units, split units, dials, switches).** Let u = a relu(l(x)) be a new unit of a group S in
a (b) build (Definition D50), with l = m^T z_S + beta, and let P be a finite mix. For a member i of S, the **points of
i** are P_i = {x in P : z_i(x) > 0}.
1. u is a **presence unit** of S if l(x) > 0 only at points of the union of the P_i (it fires only where a member
   fires).
2. u is **split** if it fires at some point of some P_i and l <= 0 at every point of some non-empty P_j with j != i. Members i
   and j sit at its two ends: the essay's "on each other's negative poles" (essay idea I1).
3. u is a **dial** or a **detector** as in Definition D31 (by the weight of P on which it fires).
4. u **switches** across two points x, x' if l(x) > 0 > l(x') or l(x) < 0 < l(x').

**Definition D55 (conflicting segments and groups).** Let N have two logits, and let t be the target gap on P (N's
gap). Two points x, x' of P
whose midpoint x\\_bar is also in P form a **conflicting segment** if t(x\\_bar) < (t(x) + t(x')) / 2. A group S is
**conflicting** on P if some conflicting segment has both ends in the union of the P_i (i in S), and **free**
otherwise.
Comment: on the detector networks with T43's mixes, P_u is the vertex point of u alone (Lemma T43a parts 2, 5 and 6),
every bad pair gives a conflicting segment (gap 2, 0, 2), and the midpoint of a good pair is not in P (proof of T22).
So the conflicting groups are exactly the groups with a bad pair.

**Lemma T62a (the dip identity) (under: one hidden layer).** Let f(x) = sum over k of a_k relu(l_k(x)) + c(x), with
every l_k and c affine in x (for example the gap of a build of N's kind with one hidden layer). For points x, x' with
midpoint x\\_bar,
   f(x\\_bar) - (f(x) + f(x')) / 2 = sum over k of a_k delta_k,
where delta_k = 0 if l_k(x) and l_k(x') have the same weak sign, and delta_k = -min(|l_k(x)|, |l_k(x')|) / 2 if unit k
switches across x, x'. In particular every delta_k <= 0.
Proof. Each l_k and c is affine, so its value at x\\_bar is the average of its values at x and x', and c contributes 0.
If l_k(x) and l_k(x') are both >= 0 or both <= 0, relu is affine on the interval between them, so relu(l_k(x\\_bar)) is
the average of the end values. Otherwise write l_k(x) = p > 0 > -q = l_k(x') (or the reverse). Then
relu((p - q) / 2) - p / 2 = -q / 2 if p >= q, and = -p / 2 if p < q, which is -min(p, q) / 2. QED.
Lean: `dip_switch` and `dip_same_sign` in `lean/coarse/Coarse/Zoom.lean` (the identity for one unit, with
l(x) >= 0 >= l(x')); the swapped direction, the sum over k and the affine part by hand.

**Corollary T62b (every conflicting segment is paid by a switching unit) (under: one hidden layer).** Let a build of N's
kind with one hidden layer have gap f = t at every point of P. Then for every conflicting segment [x, x'] some unit
with a positive output weight switches across it, and the sum of a_k min(|l_k(x)|, |l_k(x')|) / 2 over the switching
units with a_k > 0 is at least (t(x) + t(x')) / 2 - t(x\\_bar).
Proof. By Lemma T62a with f = t, the left side is t(x\\_bar) - (t(x) + t(x')) / 2 < 0. Terms with a_k <= 0 are >= 0, so
the terms with a_k > 0 sum to at most the left side, and they are non-zero only for switching units. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (from Lemma T62a).
Comment: this is the general form of Proposition T59 part 2. A unit that fires at both ends of a segment never pays
for it. A presence unit of a group pays only across segments with one end among its members' points and the other end
where it is off.

**Theorem T62 (in the zero-loss builds of the family grouping of T61's instance every unit is split) (under:
none).** In the instance of
Proposition T61 (units A, B, C, D; bad pairs A-B, C-D, A-C, B-D), let G = {{A, C}, {B, D}}, each group of target size 1
({A, C} and {B, D} are the families of the block swap, Definition D38). In every (b) build at G with D_P = 0 (or
D2_P = 0), with units a_1 relu(l_1) for {A, C} and a_2 relu(l_2) for {B, D}:
1. a_1 > 0 and a_2 > 0;
2. each unit switches across exactly two of the four segments A-B, B-D, D-C, C-A between vertex points, the two units
   across complementary pairs, and on each of its segments [x, x'] the switching unit has
   a_k min(|l_k(x)|, |l_k(x')|) / 2 = 2;
3. neither unit is a presence unit of its group: each fires at a point of P where neither of its members is on;
4. each unit fires at exactly one of the vertex points of its two members, so it is split (Definition D54).
Together with Proposition T61, such builds exist; T61's two units are split dials.
Proof. Every point of P has a positive weight (1 or M), so D_P = 0 holds exactly when the build's gap equals N's gap
at every point of P (as in T20, by (l1); for D2_P directly): 2 at the
four vertex points, 0 at the four midpoints. Each of the four segments joins the two vertex points of a bad pair, and
its midpoint is in P, so it is conflicting with t-values (2, 0, 2).
(2) and (1). By Corollary T62b each segment has a switching unit. Look at one unit's signs at the four vertex points
around the cycle A-B-D-C-A. Unit 1 has l_1 = p tau_1 + q tau_2 + b with the tau of T61's proof, so
l_1(B) = (4/5) l_1(A) + b / 5 and l_1(D) = (4/5) l_1(C) + b / 5. A switch across A-B forces b to have the strict sign
of l_1(B) (if l_1(A) > 0 > l_1(B) then b / 5 < -(4/5) l_1(A) < 0, and the reverse case gives b > 0), and a switch
across C-D forces b to have the strict sign of l_1(D). Switching across all four segments makes the signs alternate
around the cycle, so l_1(B) and l_1(D) have opposite signs, and b would have both. For unit 2, with the s of T61's
proof, l_2(A) = (4/5) l_2(B) + b' / 5 and l_2(C) = (4/5) l_2(D) + b' / 5, so the same argument applies with l_2(A) and
l_2(C), which alternate in sign too. If a unit switches strictly across three segments of the cycle, the signs at the
four corners force a strict switch across the fourth, so no unit switches across three. Two units must cover four
segments, each at most two, so each switches across exactly two and the pairs are complementary. On each segment only
one unit switches, so its term a_k delta_k equals -2 by Lemma T62a; then a_k > 0 and a_k min(|l_k|) / 2 = 2.
(3). Suppose unit 1 is a presence unit of {A, C}: it fires on P only at A or C (P_A = {A}, P_C = {C}, since at the
other points of P the units A and C are off, Lemma T43a parts 2, 5 and 6). By (2) it switches somewhere, so it fires at
A or at C. It cannot fire at both: l_1 is affine, so l_1(mid AC) would be the average of two positive numbers, and the
unit would fire at mid AC, where no member is on. By the block swap (which maps A to C, B to D, P to itself and the
grouping to itself) we may take it to fire at A only. Then l_1 <= 0 at B, C, D, and its two switching segments are
the ones at A, A-B and A-C (strict, so l_1(B) < 0 and l_1(C) < 0). By (2) unit 2 switches across B-D and D-C and not
across A-B or A-C, so l_2(D) is strictly opposite in sign to l_2(B) and l_2(C). If l_2(D) > 0 > l_2(B), then at B both
units are off, so gamma = 2, and at D unit 1 is off and gap = a_2 l_2(D) + 2 > 2, a contradiction. If
l_2(D) < 0 < l_2(B), then at D both units are off, so gamma = 2, and at B the gap is a_2 l_2(B) + 2 > 2, a
contradiction. So unit 1 is not a presence unit. For unit 2 use the reflection rho of R^2 that swaps x~_1 and x~_2,
applied in each block: it is orthogonal, so it maps X to itself and each d_(j,i) to d_(j,i'), with A <-> B and C <-> D;
it maps the vertex points and the four bad-pair midpoints onto themselves, keeps N's gap, and maps G to itself with
the groups exchanged.
(4). Both output weights are positive, so the gap is at least gamma, with equality only where both units are off. If
both units were off at some vertex point, then gamma = 2 and any vertex point where a unit fires would have gap > 2;
since each unit switches somewhere it fires at some vertex point, a contradiction. So at every vertex point at least
one unit fires. Suppose unit 1 fires at both A and C. Then it does not switch across C-A, so its two segments are A-B
and B-D (it is off only at B), or B-D and D-C (off only at D), or A-B and D-C (off at B and D). In the last case unit 2
fires at B and D (unit 1 is off there) and must switch across B-D, a contradiction. The second case is the block-swap
image of the first, so take the first: unit 1 has signs (A +, B -, C +, D +) and unit 2 switches across C-A and D-C,
not across A-B or B-D, and fires at B (unit 1 is off there), so unit 2 has signs (A +, B +, C -, D +). Write
L_k = a_k l_k and e = 2 - gamma. The gaps at the vertex points give L_1(C) = e, L_2(B) = e, L_1(A) + L_2(A) = e and
L_1(D) + L_2(D) = e. The relations of (2) give L_1(B) - L_1(D) = (4/5)(L_1(A) - L_1(C)) and
L_2(A) - L_2(C) = (4/5)(L_2(B) - L_2(D)), so L_1(B) = L_1(D) - (4/5) L_2(A) and L_2(C) = L_2(A) - (4/5) L_1(D). Then
L_1(B) < 0 needs L_2(A) > (5/4) L_1(D), and L_2(C) < 0 needs L_2(A) < (4/5) L_1(D), which cannot both hold since
L_1(D) > 0. So unit 1 fires at most at one of A, C. Suppose it fires at neither: then unit 2 fires at A and C, unit 1
fires at B or D, and its two switching segments are among A-B, B-D and D-C. If unit 1 fires at both B and D it switches
across A-B and D-C, so unit 2 switches across B-D and C-A, which contradicts unit 2 firing at both A and C. If it fires
at B only, it switches across A-B and B-D, so unit 2 switches across C-A and D-C; but unit 2 fires at A, C and D (unit 1
is off at D), so it does not switch across D-C, a contradiction; firing at D only is the block-swap image. So unit 1
fires at exactly one of A, C. Unit 2 follows by rho. Each P_u is non-empty, so each unit is split.
T61's units: unit 1 fires at A, B, D and at mid AB, mid AC, mid BD, which carry the weight (3 + 3M) / (4 + 4M) = 3/4 of
P, so it is a dial (Definition D31); unit 2 follows by rho. QED.
Lean: `dip_switch`, `dip_same_sign` (the identity); the sign cases by hand.
Comment: in words. The developer's family grouping puts two units that never fire together, and whose blend the mix
marks "nothing", into one group. In a zero-loss build the group's neuron fires at exactly one of its members (part 4).
So each new neuron pays for the blends around one of its members by turning off there, and stays on elsewhere: in T61
the {A, C} neuron is on at A, off at C, highest at B (a member of the other group), and on at three of the four blend
photos. The
coarse neuron is a contrast inside its family ("A, not C"), not a coarse detector of the family. Step by step cannot
find it by merging {A, C} alone, because with B and D still present a contrast unit is not least (T61's comment).

**Remark B.W.4 (what the least builds use on the smallest instance).** An exploration of every grouping with target
sizes 1 on T61's instance (`model/tr_poles.py`; zero-loss pieces by linear programs, least builds by a convex solver
on every piece) shows four kinds of answer. Free groups (the clique grouping {A, D}, {B, C}): presence units suffice
(Corollary T59.2), among many other zero-loss builds. One conflicting group with the other units kept: the least unit
is a presence unit that fires on a clique of the group's members and drops the others (it pays, Corollary T59.1). The
two family groups together ({A, C}, {B, D}): every zero-loss build found has two split dials (Theorem T62 proves that
none has a presence unit). The same-block pairing ({A, B}, {C, D}): no zero-loss build, and its least build also uses
split dials. On T20 the least unit is a presence detector; on T33 it is a dial that fires where no member fires. The
numbers are in the H-freefam row of Part C.

**Remark B.W.1 (an OR group pays).** In Theorem T20 the two units relu(x - 1) and relu(-x - 1) are never on together
on P, so they form an OR group (Definition D51). Every build of width 1 has D_P > 0 and D2_P > 0 (the proof of T25 part
3). So an OR group need not collapse exactly to one unit, unlike an AND group read with a one-signed row (T58 part 2).
A closed form for the least cost of an OR step is open (Conjecture D53).

**Remark B.W.2 (what T43 says about step by step).** Take the objective D2_P. On a detector network, (r) along a zoom
from G_0 = no groups, in which every step changes one group with at least two and at most s_0 children and target size 1 (s_0 a fixed
constant), needs
at most n - 1 steps, and each step is polynomial in its own bit length (T55 part 2). If the bit lengths also grew at
most polynomially along the zoom, a rule that chose such a zoom in polynomial time and always reached V_b at the top
would solve CLEAN-GROUP (Proposition T57, D2 version) in polynomial time, and then P = NP (Theorem T43 part 3). The
growth of the bit lengths is not bounded here, so this is a remark, not a theorem. For D_P, T55 says nothing about the
cost in the bit model (as T21 part 4), and errors of approximate steps would also add up.

**Remark B.W.3 (deeper layers).** In a layer l >= 2 of a build, the units below may themselves be new, so "reads only
its group" needs a map from the build's units of layer l - 1 to N's. When only the top hidden layer l = L changes and
the layers below are kept as N's, D50 applies with x replaced by N's layer L - 1. For l < L the layers above are
nonlinear, so a build is not of D50's form (one hidden layer, then free logits), and T54 and T55 do not apply; Theorem
T58 is stated with the layers above kept as N's. The general case needs a reading of T4's phrase in deeper layers;
the three readings and the choice are card 3-12 of `DECISIONS.md` (node R-deep, PENDING).

## B.X Circuits, kinks along lines, and coarse circuits

Parts B.W and B.W.2 found four kinds of coarse unit (AND collapse, free-group detector, clique detector, split dial).
This Part looks one level up. A network's gap, restricted to the line between two inputs, is a piecewise-linear
function of the position on the line; its bends (kinks) sit where some unit, in any layer, crosses zero. Theorem T63
writes the dip at any point of the line as a sum over these kinks, at every depth. Proposition T64 says what one unit
of one hidden layer can do on a line (one monotone kink), and from it Lemma T62a, Corollary T62b and the two-point case
of Proposition T59 part 2 follow. Theorem T65 turns this into a lower bound on the size of any exact build with one
hidden layer: a covering number of the mix's strict dip lines, which depends only on N's gap on P and on P. Corollary
T65.1 shows that T20's impossibility is such a bound. Proposition T66 is a depth separation between plain networks:
k layers of two units do what one hidden layer needs 2^(k-1) - 1 units for. These results are elementary; none of them
yet says what a least coarse circuit is (that is Conjecture D61). Definitions D58 to D60 fix the words.

**Definition D58 (circuit as a set of units).** Let N be a plain ReLU network with two logits. Here a **circuit** of N
is a set S of N's hidden units, in any layers, taken with every edge among them and to their readers; the chains of
edges of Definition D5 are its paths. The definition only marks which units a coarse circuit may replace; the function
to keep is N's gap on P.

**Definition D59 (lines, kinks, dips, dip lines).** For points x, x' and t in [0, 1] write x(t) = (1 - t) x + t x'. For
a continuous piecewise-linear f, the function g(t) = f(x(t)) is piecewise linear; its **kinks** are the t in (0, 1)
where its slope changes, and the **jump** at a kink is the right slope minus the left slope. For lambda in (0, 1), the
**lambda-dip** of f on [x, x'] is f(x(lambda)) - (1 - lambda) f(x) - lambda f(x'). A **dip line** of f on a finite mix
P is a triple (x, x', lambda) with x, x' and x(lambda) in P; it is **strict** if its lambda-dip is negative. The **dip
profile** of f on P is the list of its dip lines with their dips; it depends only on f's values on P. (The kinks of f
on a line depend on f off P; Theorem T65 does not use them.)

**Definition D60 (coarse circuit).** Let S be a circuit of N. A **coarse circuit** for S is a plain layered ReLU network
obtained from N by removing the units of S and adding new units in any hidden layers, such that every unit of hidden
layer l (new or kept) reads only units of layer l - 1 (the input for l = 1), and the units and logits that read S's
units read new units instead. A value that must pass through a layer is carried by a relay pair relu(s), relu(-s),
whose two units count as new units. It is **exact on P** if its gap equals N's gap at every point of P. (The classes
(a) and (b) of Definition D50 are coarse circuits whose new units all sit in the one hidden layer.)

**Theorem T63 (the kink formula) (under: none).** Let f be the gap of a plain ReLU network of any depth, x, x' points
and lambda in (0, 1). Then g(t) = f(x(t)) is continuous and piecewise linear on [0, 1] with finitely many kinks
t_1, ..., t_r in (0, 1), each kink is a zero of some hidden unit's pre-activation along the line, and
   f(x(lambda)) - (1 - lambda) f(x) - lambda f(x') = - sum over j of jump_j K_lambda(t_j),
   K_lambda(t) = min(t (1 - lambda), lambda (1 - t)) >= 0.
Proof. Along the line, every input coordinate is affine in t. By induction over the layers, each unit's pre-activation
p(t) is continuous and piecewise linear with finitely many pieces: an affine combination of such functions is one, and
relu(p) is one (on a piece where p is not identically 0, p has at most one zero; where p is identically 0, relu(p) is
0). For the kinks: let t0 be a kink of g, and take a lowest hidden unit whose output has a kink at t0 (one exists,
since the logits are affine in the last layer). Every unit below it has no kink at t0, so its pre-activation is affine
near t0, and relu of an affine function has a kink at t0 only if it changes sign strictly there. So every kink of g is
a strict sign change of some hidden unit's pre-activation. Write
g(t) = g(0) + b t + sum_j jump_j relu(t - t_j) on [0, 1], with b the slope on the first piece (the sum adds each slope
change after its kink). Then g(lambda) - (1 - lambda) g(0) - lambda g(1) = sum_j jump_j (relu(lambda - t_j) -
lambda relu(1 - t_j)), since the affine part cancels. For t_j <= lambda the bracket is (lambda - t_j) - lambda (1 - t_j)
= -t_j (1 - lambda); for t_j >= lambda it is -lambda (1 - t_j). Both are -K_lambda(t_j). QED.
Lean: `kink_green` (the bracket for one kink) in `lean/coarse/Coarse/Zoom.lean`; the representation of g and the sum
by hand. Check: `model/tr_kinks.py` (random rational networks with two and three hidden layers, exact fractions).
Comment: a dip is made by kinks with positive jumps (where the line bends upward) and spoiled by kinks with negative
jumps. The formula itself holds for any continuous piecewise-linear g; the network enters only in where the kinks
are.

**Proposition T64 (one unit of one hidden layer on a line) (under: one hidden layer).** Let u(x) = a relu(l(x)) with l
affine and a != 0. Along any line, u(x(t)) is monotone and has at most one kink. It has one exactly when l(x) and l(x') have
strictly opposite signs (u switches across the line, Definition D54), at t* = l(x) / (l(x) - l(x')), with jump
a |l(x') - l(x)|. Consequently, for the gap f of a build of N's kind with one hidden layer:
1. the kinks of f on a line are among the switch points of its units, at most one per unit;
2. for lambda = 1/2 the dip is the sum of the terms of Lemma T62a;
3. a single unit plus a constant cannot have f(x(lambda)) < min(f(x), f(x')) (Proposition T59 part 2 for two points);
4. a strict dip line is switched across by some unit with a > 0 (Corollary T62b, for any lambda).
Proof. l(x(t)) = (1 - t) l(x) + t l(x') is affine in t, and relu of an affine function of t is monotone with at most one
kink, at its zero, where its slope changes by |l(x') - l(x)|; multiplying by a gives the jump. (1) is this for each
unit. (2) T63 with t* and the jump: K_(1/2)(t*) |l(x') - l(x)| = min(|l(x)|, |l(x')|) / 2. (3) A monotone function
plus a constant takes, at an inner point of the line, a value between its values at the ends. (4) By T63 a negative
dip needs a kink with a positive jump, that is a switching unit with a > 0. QED.
Lean: `kink_green`, `dip_switch`, `dip_same_sign`; the rest by hand.

**Theorem T65 (a covering bound on the size of an exact build with one hidden layer) (under: two logits, one hidden
layer, a finite mix).** Let a build of N's kind with one hidden layer and k units have its gap equal to N's gap on P,
and let D be the set of strict dip lines of N's gap on P. Then every line in D is switched across by a unit of the
build with a positive output weight. So k is at least tau(D), the least number of affine functions on the input space
such that, for every (x, x', lambda) in D, x and x' get strictly opposite signs under at least one of them. For a (b)
build at a grouping G (Definition D50), let D' be the lines of D that no kept unit switches across; then the sum of the
k_S is at least tau_b(D'), the least number of affine functions, each in the span of (z_S, 1) for some group S of G,
that switch across every line of D'.
Proof. The build's gap equals N's gap at x, x' and x(lambda), so its lambda-dip on each line of D is negative; by
Proposition T64 part 4 some unit with a > 0 switches across it. The units' pre-activations are affine functions with
the stated property, so there are at least tau(D) of them. For a (b) build, a line of D' is not switched across by a
kept unit, so it is switched across by a new unit, whose pre-activation is in the span of (z_S, 1) for its group. QED.
Lean: none, by hand.
Comment: tau(D) depends only on N's gap on P and on P. The bound is not always tight: on T61's instance one plain unit
switches across all four dip lines (an affine function positive at A and D and negative at B and C), so tau = 1 in
class (a), yet no build of width 1 is exact (T64 part 3: one unit plus a constant cannot take the values 2, 0, 2 at A,
mid AB, B). In class (b) at the family grouping, T62's argument shows tau_b = 2, and T61 reaches it.

**Corollary T65.1 (T20's impossibility is a covering bound) (under: one hidden layer).** In Theorem T20 (d = 1, P the
integers -3 to 3, N's gap T(x) = relu(x - 1) + relu(-x - 1)), the lines (0, 2, 1/2) and (-2, 0, 1/2) are strict dip
lines, and no point lies strictly inside both (0, 2) and (-2, 0). So tau(D) >= 2, and no build of width 1 is exact.
Proof. T(1) = 0 < (T(0) + T(2)) / 2 = 1/2 and T(-1) = 0 < (T(-2) + T(0)) / 2 = 1/2. In one dimension an affine function
gives the ends of a segment strictly opposite signs only if its zero lies strictly inside the segment; the two open
segments are disjoint. Theorem T65. QED.
Lean: none, by hand.

**Lemma T65a (parity on a closed polygon) (under: none).** Let v_1, ..., v_q be points with v_(q+1) = v_1, and let l be
affine with l(v_i) != 0 for every i. Then the number of sides [v_i, v_(i+1)] whose ends have strictly opposite signs
under l is even.
Proof. Going once around, the sign of l changes exactly at those sides, and it returns to its starting value. QED.
Lean: none, by hand.
Comment: this is the step "no unit switches across three sides" of Theorem T62: three strict switches already make
all four vertices non-zero, so T65a covers that step.

**Proposition T66 (a depth separation on a finite grid) (under: none).** Let k >= 1, d = 1, P the 2^k + 1 points
j / 2^k (j = 0, ..., 2^k), and t(j / 2^k) = j mod 2.
1. Every plain ReLU network with one hidden layer whose output equals t on P has at least 2^(k-1) - 1 units.
2. The plain ReLU network with k hidden layers of two units each that computes m(m(...m(x))) (k times), with the tent
   map m(s) = 2 relu(s) - 4 relu(s - 1/2), equals t on P.
Proof. (1) For every even j with 0 < j < 2^k, the line ((j - 1) / 2^k, (j + 1) / 2^k, 1/2) is a strict dip line
(t = 1, 0, 1). There are 2^(k-1) - 1 of them, and their open segments are disjoint, so in one dimension no affine
function switches across two of them, and tau(D) >= 2^(k-1) - 1 (the argument of Theorem T65 applies to any one-layer
output: Proposition T64 needs no logits). (2) Layer 1 has the units relu(x) and
relu(x - 1/2); layer i + 1 has relu(s_i) and relu(s_i - 1/2) with s_i = 2 h_1 - 4 h_2 of layer i (an affine function of
layer i, so the network is a plain layered ReLU network); the output is s_k. On [0, 1], m(s) = 2 s for s <= 1/2 and 2 - 2 s for s >= 1/2, so
m maps j / 2^k to j' / 2^(k-1) with j' = j or 2^k - j, and j' has the parity of j. By induction on k, m^k(j / 2^k) =
j mod 2: for k = 1, m(0) = 0, m(1/2) = 1, m(1) = 0. QED.
Lean: none, by hand. Check: `model/tr_kinks.py` (exact fractions, k = 1 to 6).
Comment: this is the finite depth separation of Telgarsky (2015, 2016; literature table). Read as a statement about
coarse circuits (Definition D60): if a circuit's job on the mix is such a zigzag, a coarse circuit that may span layers
can be exponentially smaller than one confined to one hidden layer. No clean network with such a circuit is named
here; whether clean networks need this is open (Conjecture D61).

**Remark B.X.1 (the four kinds of coarse unit, read through dip lines; consequences and analogies).** Consequences:
for a conflicting group alone (T59.1), a strict dip line between two members' firing points cannot be served by a
unit that fires at both ends (T64 part 3, two points); for conflicting groups together (T62), every one of the four
dip lines must be switched across by a unit with a > 0 (T62b), and in class (b) a unit switches across at most two of
them (T62's sign argument with Lemma T65a). Analogies only: for AND groups (T58), AND is a condition on the points of P,
and on a line between two of them the members may cross zero at different places, so T58's proof uses no kinks; for
free groups (T59.2), a free group has no strict dip line among its members' points, so T65 says nothing there, and
T59.2 is an explicit construction. Which units N happens to use does not by itself decide the kind of coarse unit: the
comment after T65 is a case where one cut crosses every dip line and still no one-unit build is exact.

## B.Q How common clean networks are: exact symmetry is rare, perfect cleanliness under D42 is not

Shonu (2026-10-26): the essay says most trained networks are clean, so a definition under which clean networks are
rare is the wrong definition. This section makes two facts exact. Theorem T44: networks with an exact symmetry that
moves a unit (D39's Q1, and D20 for any non-trivial group) form a set of measure zero. Theorem T45: the networks that
are perfectly clean under D42 contain a non-empty open set, so they have positive Lebesgue measure. Neither theorem
says where trained networks land; that is Hypothesis H-typical.

**Theorem T44 (exact symmetry is rare) (under: none).** Fix an architecture (input dimension d, hidden widths
n_1, ..., n_L, n_y classes). Identify a network with its weight vector theta in R^D (all W_l, b_l, W_out, c). The set
of theta for which some tuple (A, pi_1, ..., pi_L, sigma), with A any orthogonal map of R^d and pi_l, sigma
permutations, satisfies the conditions of Definition D20 with rho_0 = A and has some pi_l other than the identity,
has Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, for every input domain X, the set where Aut_X(N) (Definition D38) moves a
hidden unit is null, and so is the set of networks that are perfectly clean (D20) for a group that moves a unit.
Proof. Step 1: a null set B of degenerate weights. Let B be the set of theta with at least one of: (i) a hidden unit u
with (w_u, b_u) = 0 or with a zero outgoing column; (ii) two units u != u' of one hidden layer with (w_u, b_u)
parallel to (w_u', b_u'); (iii) two units u != u' of layer 1 with q(theta) = |w_u|^2 b_u'^2 - |w_u'|^2 b_u^2 = 0.
Each of these finitely many conditions says that a list of polynomials in theta vanishes (the coordinates of a vector,
the 2 x 2 minors of a matrix with two rows, or q). For each condition, one polynomial of its list is not identically
zero: for (i) a single coordinate; for (ii), at the point with b_u = 1, b_u' = 2, w_u = e_1, w_u' = 0, the minor of the
first coordinate and the bias is 1 * 2 - 0 * 1 = 2; for (iii), q = 1 * 4 - 0 * 1 = 4 at the same point. The zero set
of a polynomial that is not identically zero has Lebesgue measure zero, so B is a finite union of null sets, and null.
Step 2: off B, no unit is moved. Take theta not in B. In reduced form (Definition D20) no unit is deleted (no zero
column) and none is merged (by (ii) no two rows are positive multiples of each other); each unit is only rescaled by a
positive factor. Let (A, pi_1, ..., pi_L, sigma) satisfy the conditions. Write the rescaled rows as (w~_u, b~_u).
Layer 1: W~_1 A = pi_1 W~_1 and pi_1 b~_1 = b~_1 say that the rescaled row of the unit u' that pi_1 assigns to u
equals (A^T w~_u, b~_u). If u' != u, then (A^T w_u, b_u) = lambda (w_u', b_u') for some lambda > 0, so
|w_u| = |A^T w_u| = lambda |w_u'| and b_u = lambda b_u', and q(theta) = lambda^2 |w_u'|^2 b_u'^2 - |w_u'|^2 lambda^2
b_u'^2 = 0, which (iii) excludes. So pi_1 is the identity. Layer l >= 2, when pi_{l-1} is the identity:
W~_l = pi_l W~_l and pi_l b~_l = b~_l say that the rescaled rows of u and of its image u' are equal. The rescaled row
of u is (w_u D, b_u) / n_u, with D the positive diagonal of the scales of layer l - 1 and n_u > 0. So if u' != u,
(w_u D, b_u) and (w_u' D, b_u') are positive multiples of each other, hence so are (w_u, b_u) and (w_u', b_u')
(multiply the first block by D^-1), which (ii) excludes. So pi_l is the identity. By induction every pi_l is the
identity. QED.
Lean: none, by hand. Step 2 is a short induction; the fact that a non-zero polynomial vanishes only on a null set is
standard (by induction on the number of variables and Fubini's theorem) and is not re-proved here.
Comment. So a definition of clean that requires a unit to be moved by an exact symmetry of the network (Q1 of D39, or
D20 with a group that moves a unit) holds only on a null set of weights, for every domain and every orthogonal action
on inputs. The theorem says nothing about any law on weights, and nothing about where training ends: a null set can
attract the networks that training finds. The graded distance D21 is not affected: it is a number, not a set. Nor
does the theorem say how close trained networks come to a symmetric one (that is Part C's eps for H-clean).

**Lemma T45a (the cancelled share of a reader's votes) (under: none).** For a reader r and an input x (Definition
D41): (1) 0 <= kappa_r(x) <= 1; (2) kappa_r(x) = 0 exactly when the non-zero votes a_{r,v}(x) all have one sign.
Proof. (1) With S = sum_v |a_{r,v}(x)| > 0, the triangle inequality gives |sum_v a_{r,v}(x)| <= S, so the numerator
lies in [0, S]. (2) If the sum is >= 0 and equals S in absolute value, then sum_v (|a_v| - a_v) = 0 with every term
>= 0, so every term is 0 and every a_v >= 0. If the sum is < 0, then sum_v (|a_v| + a_v) = 0 in the same way and
every a_v <= 0. Conversely, votes of one sign give |sum| = S. QED.
Lean: `vote_cancel_bounds`, `vote_cancel_zero_iff` (`Coarse/Votes.lean`), in the form before the division by S;
the division, and the convention kappa_r = 0 when S = 0, by hand.

**Theorem T45 (the perfectly clean networks under D42 contain an open set) (under: none).** Fix an architecture with
n_y >= 2 and a compact convex input domain X with non-empty interior. Call a network **non-degenerate** when every hidden unit has a non-zero
outgoing column and no two rows (w_u, b_u) of one hidden layer are parallel. Its reduced form (Definition D20) then
only rescales each unit by a positive factor. Call a network **margin-clean** when:
(a) for every reader r and any two units u, v of the layer that r reads, with W_{ru} W_{rv} < 0, no x in X has
z_u(x) >= 0 and z_v(x) >= 0;
(b) every unit u of a layer l >= 2 has a unit v of layer l - 1 with W_{uv} > 0 and z_v(x) > 0 at every x in X with
z_u(x) >= 0;
(c) every unit u of a layer l <= L - 1 has a unit r of layer l + 1 with W_{ru} > 0 and z_r(x) > 0 at every x in X
with z_u(x) >= 0.
Then: (1) a non-degenerate margin-clean network is perfectly clean under D42; (2) the set of non-degenerate
margin-clean networks whose weights W_l (l >= 2) and reads W_{ru} of every reader (for logit differences,
W_out[c, u] - W_out[c', u]) are all non-zero is open in weight space; (3) this set is not empty. So the networks that are perfectly clean under D42 contain a
non-empty open set, which has positive Lebesgue measure.
Proof. (1) A positive rescaling of a unit multiplies its z_u by a positive factor and its outgoing weights by a
positive factor, so it keeps every sign in (a) to (c) and every set {z_u >= 0}. So the reduced form is margin-clean,
and it is enough to compute eps on it. V: fix a live unit u and a reader r of u. The target mu_u gives mass 1 to {h_u > 0}. If at some x with
h_u(x) > 0 the reader heard non-zero votes of both signs, two units v, v' with W_{rv} W_{rv'} < 0 would both be on
at x, against (a). So kappa_r = 0 on {h_u > 0} (Lemma T45a part 2), and E_{mu_u}[kappa_r] = 0. G: for a live unit u
of a layer l >= 2, the unit v of (b) is on wherever z_u >= 0, in particular wherever h_u > 0, so
mu_u({h_v = 0}) = 0 and g_u = 0. B: the same, with the unit r of (c). So eps(N) = (0, 0, 0).
(2) Let theta be in the set. Non-degeneracy is the complement of conditions (i) and (ii) of the proof of Theorem
T44, which are closed, so it holds near theta. The signs of the weights named in (2) do not change in a neighbourhood
of theta, so the
pairs of (a) and the units chosen in (b) and (c) stay the same there. Each z_u(theta', x) is continuous in
(theta', x) (affine maps and relu, composed). Suppose (a) failed at points theta_n -> theta, at inputs x_n in X with
z_u(theta_n, x_n) >= 0 and z_v(theta_n, x_n) >= 0. X is compact, so a subsequence of x_n converges to some x in X,
and continuity gives z_u(theta, x) >= 0 and z_v(theta, x) >= 0, against (a) at theta. For (b), suppose
z_u(theta_n, x_n) >= 0 and z_v(theta_n, x_n) <= 0; the limit gives z_u(theta, x) >= 0 and z_v(theta, x) <= 0,
against (b) at theta. (c) is the same. There are finitely many conditions, so a neighbourhood of theta satisfies all
of them.
(3) Let s = the largest value of |x_1 + ... + x_d| over X (finite, X compact) and t = 1 / (2 s + 2). Number the units
of each layer 1, 2, .... Layer 1: unit u has w_u = (t / u) (1, ..., 1) and b_u = 1, so z_u >= 1 - t s > 0 on X, and
two rows (t/u, ..., t/u, 1) with different u are not parallel. Layers l >= 2: W_l[u, v] = u + v and b_u = 1, so
z_u >= 1 > 0, and two rows (u + 1, u + 2, ..., 1) with different u are not parallel (their bias entries are equal and
the rows differ). Readout: W_out[c, u] = c for every class c = 1, ..., n_y and every unit u, and the readout bias is 0. Every unit is on everywhere on X, so (b) and (c)
hold; every reader reads all its units with weights of one sign (1 for units, c - c' != 0 for logit differences), so
(a) has no pairs; every named weight is non-zero; and every column is non-zero. A non-empty open set has positive Lebesgue measure. QED.
Lean: `vote_cancel_zero_iff` (`Coarse/Votes.lean`) for the step from (a) to kappa_r = 0. The compactness step and
the example by hand.
Comment. The example of (3) is a network whose units are always on, so it is linear on X. It shows only that the
open set is not empty. The perfectly clean set itself is not open (comment (e) of D42): T45 gives stability only for
non-degenerate margin-clean networks. Less trivial members: the network of Theorem T20 on X = [-3, 3] with the reader
relu(x - 1) - relu(-x - 1) (it votes against an alternative: the two units are never on together) satisfies (a), and
(b), (c) are empty at L = 1. The detector networks of D40 at L = 1 satisfy (a) with no pairs. Theorem T45 is not
Hypothesis H-typical: an open set of positive measure need not hold the networks that training finds.

## B.R Routes, uses and reads: the theorems of the definition of A.6

**Lemma T46a (bounds and refinement) (under: none).** For a live unit u (Definitions D43 to D45):
1. 0 <= pi(u) <= 1;
2. pi(u) = 0 exactly when the non-zero route means m_g are positive multiples of one vector;
3. if a route is split into sub-routes (a finer partition of the target), pi(u) does not go down;
4. if every use vector g_u(x, p) lies on one ray (for example, when u has a single read, or when u is in the last
   hidden layer of a two-class network), then pi(u) = 0;
5. -1 <= lambda(u) <= 1.
Proof. (1) The weights w_g are >= 0 and sum to 1, so |sum_g w_g m_g| <= sum_g w_g |m_g| by the triangle inequality;
so the subtracted ratio lies in [0, 1]. (2) Equality in the triangle inequality of a Euclidean space holds exactly
when the non-zero terms are positive multiples of one vector. (3) The numerator |sum_g w_g m_g| is the norm of the
target's mean use, the same for every partition. If route g splits into sub-routes h, then w_g m_g = sum_h w_h m_h,
so w_g |m_g| <= sum_h w_h |m_h|: the denominator does not go down. (4) Every route mean is then a non-negative multiple
of one vector; apply (2). For two classes, see the comment of D44. (5) For a unit reader, S_u lies between minus the
sum of the negative read weights and the sum of the positive ones; for the classes, S_u = sum_c W~_cu q_c lies
between the least and the largest W~_cu, which lie in [-T_u, T_u] with a gap of at most T_u because the W~_cu sum to
0. So the difference of two means of S_u lies in [-T_u, T_u]. QED.
Lean: `route_mean_norm_le` (`Coarse/Routes.lean`) is the key inequality of parts 1 and 3; the rest by hand.

**Lemma T46b (the sign of the read index under independence) (under: none).** Let u be a live unit of a dense layer
(nu with a finite first moment, so h_u is integrable). (1) For a unit reader r with read W_ru != 0, write
z_r = W_ru h_u + R_r. If, under nu_l, R_r is independent of h_u, then W_ru Cov(h_u, 1[z_r > 0]) >= 0. (2) For u in the
last hidden layer, if the rest R of the logits is independent of h_u, then Cov(h_u, S_u) >= 0. So if (1) holds for
every reader of u (pairwise independence is enough), or (2) holds, lambda(u) >= 0.
Proof. Given h_u = t, the gate is on with probability F(t) = P(R_r > -W_ru t), by independence. F is non-decreasing in
t when W_ru > 0 and non-increasing when W_ru < 0, so W_ru F is non-decreasing. Then W_ru Cov(h_u, 1[z_r > 0])
= Cov(h_u, W_ru F(h_u)) >= 0 by Chebyshev's inequality (two non-decreasing functions of one variable). Summing over
the readers, lambda(u) = (sum_r W_ru Cov(h_u, 1[z_r > 0])) / (E[h_u] T_u) >= 0. (2) With w = W~_{., u} (the centred
read), S(t, R) = sum_c w_c softmax(W_out[., u] t + R)_c, and d S / d t = sum_c w_c q_c (W_out[c, u] - sum q W_out[., u])
= Var_q(w) >= 0, because the centring does not change a variance. So E[S(t, R)] over the independent R is
non-decreasing in t, and Chebyshev's inequality gives Cov(h_u, S_u) >= 0. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (a one-variable Chebyshev step and a derivative).
Comment: a reader responds to u at least through u's own vote, so lambda > 0 does not separate a network whose
readers' other inputs co-vary with u from one where they are independent of it. Only the size of lambda can, or the
excess read xi of D45 item 2'. This is why
the condition lambda(u) > 0 of D45 is too weak (comment (f) of D45; Part C, H-route).

**Lemma T46c (the excess read is 0 when the rest ignores the unit) (under: none).** If, under nu_l, the rest of every
reader's input (the vector of all R_r, or R for the classes) is independent of h_u, then xi(u) = 0. In general
lambda_ind(u) >= 0 (Lemma T46b applied to the independent pair, for unit and class readers), so xi(u) <= lambda(u).
A unit whose readers each read it alone (their rest is a constant bias) has xi(u) = 0.
Proof. Under independence the joint law of (h_u(x), R(x)) under nu_l equals the law of (h_u(x), R(x')) with x'
independent, and the target mu_u reweights only by h_u, so the same holds under mu_u. So every expectation in lambda
equals the matching one in lambda_ind, and xi = 0. The second claim is Lemma T46b applied to the independent pair. QED.
Lean: none, by hand.

**Lemma T46d (the excess read of an OR reader) (under: none).** Let u be a live unit of a dense layer whose only reader
is r = relu(W_ru h_u + R) with W_ru > 0, no bias, and R >= 0 (r reads the other units with weights >= 0). Then
lambda(u) = P(h_u = 0, R = 0), lambda_ind(u) = P(h_u = 0) P(R = 0) and xi(u) = Cov(1[h_u = 0], 1[R = 0]) under nu_l.
In particular, if u and the rest are never on together, xi(u) = -P(h_u > 0) P(R > 0) < 0 whenever both have positive
probability.
Proof. The gate is 1[W_ru h_u + R > 0] = 1 - 1[h_u = 0] 1[R = 0], and T_u = W_ru. Under mu_u, h_u > 0, so the gate's
mean is 1 there; under nu_l it is 1 - P(h_u = 0, R = 0). So lambda = P(h_u = 0, R = 0). With R at an independent
input, the same computation gives 1 - P(h_u = 0) P(R = 0) under nu_l and 1 under mu_u, so lambda_ind =
P(h_u = 0) P(R = 0), and xi is the covariance. If the two are never on together, P(h_u = 0, R = 0) =
1 - P(h_u > 0) - P(R > 0), and the covariance is -P(h_u > 0) P(R > 0). QED.
Lean: none, by hand (two lines of probability).
Comment: so the agreement read of an OR reader is the co-occurrence of the unit with the reader's other inputs. A
coarse reader of alternatives that are never on together gives each of them xi < 0; with a threshold (a negative
bias) the sign can change. This is the cost of the agreement form stated in D45 item 5.

**Proposition T50 (the detector networks fail the agreement form) (under: none).** Let N be the detector network N^1 of
Definition D40, u one of its detectors, and nu any base law under which u is live and some other detector is on with
positive probability (for example the uniform law on its domain X). Then xi(u) < 0. So, under the uniform law, N is
perfectly clean in the weak form (Proposition T49) but not in the agreement form. (The proof uses only that the caps
are disjoint, that u is live and that another cap has positive mass.)
Proof. N has two classes; for a detector u, S(t, R) = c (q_1 - 1/2) with q_1 = sigma(c t + R), where R = c times the sum
of the other detectors, and T_u = c. Write phi(a, b) = sigma(a + b) - 1/2 and Delta(a, b) = phi(a, b) - phi(a, 0) >= 0
for b >= 0, with Delta > 0 when b > 0. The caps are disjoint (Lemma T43a part 2), so R = 0 on u's cap and h_u = 0 off
it. Let a(x) = c h_u(x), R' = R(x') with x' independent, and V = nu(cap of u). Then
xi(u) = (E_mu[phi(a, 0)] - E_mu E'[phi(a, R')]) - (E_nu[phi(a(x), R(x))] - E_nu E'[phi(a(x), R')]).
The first bracket is -E_mu E'[Delta(a, R')]. In the second, split x by u's cap: on the cap, R(x) = 0 and the term is
-E'[Delta(a, R')]; off the cap, a = 0 and the term integrates to nu(off) (E_off[phi(0, R)] - E'[phi(0, R')]); since
phi(0, R) = 0 on the cap, E_off[phi(0, R)] nu(off) = E'[phi(0, R')], so the off part is V E'[phi(0, R')]. So
xi(u) = -E_mu E'[Delta(a, R')] - V (E'[phi(0, R')] - E_{cap} E'[Delta(a, R')]).
sigma is concave on [0, infinity), so Delta(a, b) = sigma(a + b) - sigma(a) <= sigma(b) - sigma(0) = phi(0, b) for
a, b >= 0; so the bracket multiplying V is >= 0. The other caps have positive volume, so R' > 0 with positive
probability, and E_mu E'[Delta(a, R')] > 0. So xi(u) < 0. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (concavity of the logistic function on [0, infinity)).
Comment (what T50 shows and what it does not). It shows that the networks T43 uses at one hidden layer are outside the
class of networks perfectly clean in the agreement form, so T43 says nothing about that class. It does not show that
networks in that class avoid the hardness, nor that the class is non-empty. Whether the hardness holds there is
Conjecture D47.

**Theorem T46 (the indices use no labels and no scales) (under: none).** pi(u), lambda(u), xi(u), omega_u and the
entries of eps(N) do not
change when (a) the units of any layer are permuted, (b) a unit's incoming weights and bias are multiplied by c > 0
and its outgoing weights by 1/c, (c) the classes are permuted, or (d) one vector is added to every row of W_out (a
shift of the readout).
Proof. (b) Let N' be N with unit j of layer l rescaled by c. Step (i) of the canonical form rescales j's row c r_j to
norm 1, which gives the same row as for N, and multiplies j's outgoing column, which is (1 / c) times N's, by the norm
c |r_j|: the result is N's column times |r_j|, as for N. The rows of the readers of j are therefore the same as for N
before they are normalised, and the loop runs the same way for N and N' from there on. So N and N' have the same
canonical form, and every object of D43 to D45 is computed on it. (a) The canonical form of a permuted network is the
permuted canonical form (each step of the loop treats units by their rows only, and merges equal rows). A permutation
of the units below relabels the builders, so it maps each route (a set of builders) to its image and keeps the
partition of the target; a permutation of the readers permutes the entries of g_u. Norms and sums do not change. (c) A
permutation of the classes permutes the class entries of g_u, the probabilities, and the centred reads together. (d)
A shift adds sum_k v_k h_k to every logit, which keeps every probability; so q and dq / dh_u do not change, and the
centred readout P_perp W_out does not change because P_perp removes the added constant from each column. For xi: a
