first example. Laminar case: if the dropped parts are pairwise orthogonal, |P_D h|^2 is the sum of
|P_(S_i) h|^2. QED.
Lean: none needed (part 1's read step is two substitutions, R_l Q h = R_l h and |Q h|^2 + c^en_l = |h|^2
inside the root; part 2 is a direct computation); checked in
`model/tv_norm.py` (check G: part 1 on random networks with an unread D and a constructed oblique energy; part 2's
examples, oblique and orthogonal per-area energies, with the least D_P of a constant logit vector by a
one-dimensional search).
Comment. The energy claim of Definition DM13 takes any subspace D, so at an angle a map makes it on the whole dropped
part (a sum of members), as DM14 already does for leaks. Then Theorem TV1 part 2 (orthogonal cut) and part 1 here
(oblique cut) give exactness. The oblique cut of part 1 lies in DV2's class (node R-normconst, widened to c_l > -eps_l); with some
c^en_l < 0 Lemma TV12 does not describe it as a battery direction. Which kind of
cut is better is a property of N and P: by Lemma TV16 part 3 they differ only by one scalar per norm and input.

### B.V.6 A map complete for every zoom at once (added 2026-10-29, round 4)

Corollary TV6.2 puts the stream in T5's form, but its map holds one carried leak claim per level: the claims depend on
which part D_j each level drops, so a new zoom needs new claims. This section gives claims that name one member each.
They do not depend on any zoom. What it does:
1. Definition DM16: the member claim (B, l), one per member B and block l: the leak that member B alone causes,
   carried to the logits along N's own area graph, with gains that do not depend on what else is dropped.
2. Theorem TV18: for every part D that is a sum of members, the projection cut that drops D has loss at most a quarter
   of the squared sum of the square roots of the member claims of the members inside D. Without norms this holds for
   any direct decomposition (areas at an angle) with the oblique cut; with norms, for orthogonal members.
3. Corollary TV18.1: the stream branch in T5's form for every zoom of groups made of members, from one map. The rule
   picks, in each group, which members to drop by a small exact knapsack, and stores the cuts.
4. Proposition TV18.2: the norm form with members at an angle. The energy of a sum of members is not the sum of their
   energies (Proposition TV17 part 2), so each member's term also carries its cross terms with every other member;
   the cut's norm constant may then fall below N's (node R-normconst, widened).

**Definition DM16 (member claims) (added 2026-10-29, Part B.V.6).** Let N be as in Definition DV1 with Lipschitz
sigma_l (constant Lip_l) and every eps_l > 0 in the norm form, and M an area map (DM11) with members A_1, ..., A_m. In
the norm form the members are orthogonal (the laminar case of DM11, with P_A = Q_A); in the no-norm form they are any
direct decomposition, with projections Q_A. Write h_l for N's stream, nu_l(x) = (|h_(l-1)(x)|^2 + eps_l)^(1/2) (nu = 1
in the no-norm form), and r_(l,i), w_(l,i) for N's read and write vectors. For a member B define on P:
   c_l(B) = E_P |Q_B h_(l-1)(x)|^2   (l = 1, ..., L + 1; norm form),
   mu^B_(l,i)(x) = |r_(l,i) . Q_B h_(l-1)(x)| / nu_l(x) + |r_(l,i)| | |Q_B h_(l-1)(x)|^2 - c_l(B) | / nu_l(x)^2   (norm form),
   mu^B_(l,i)(x) = |r_(l,i) . Q_B h_(l-1)(x)|   (no-norm form),
   lambda^B_l[A](x) = Lip_l sum over i of |Q_A w_(l,i)| mu^B_(l,i)(x),
   omega^B(x) = |P_perp U Q_B h_L(x)| / nu_(L+1)(x) + |P_perp U| | |Q_B h_L(x)|^2 - c_(L+1)(B) | / nu_(L+1)(x)^2   (norm
   form; the first term alone in the no-norm form),
and N's own gains, the same for every member:
   T*_l[A, F] = (Lip_l / eps_l^(1/2)) sum over i of |Q_A w_(l,i)| (|Q_F^T r_(l,i)| + |r_(l,i)|)   (norm form),
   T*_l[A, F] = Lip_l sum over i of |Q_A w_(l,i)| |Q_F^T r_(l,i)|   (no-norm form),
   u*_A = (|P_perp U Q_A| + |P_perp U|) / eps_(L+1)^(1/2)   (norm form),   u*_A = |P_perp U Q_A|   (no-norm form),
   M*_l = (I + T*_L) (I + T*_(L-1)) ... (I + T*_(l+1))   (M*_L = I).
The **member claim** (B, l; A_1, ..., A_m), written (B, l), for l = 1, ..., L, says that the leak of member B at block l reaches the logits along no
route of N's own area graph: for every area A with (u*^T M*_l)_A > 0, lambda^B_l[A] = 0 on P. Its error is
eps_mc(B, l) = (u*^T M*_l ||lambda^B_l||)^2, with ||lambda^B_l|| the vector of the ||lambda^B_l[A]||. The claim (B, L + 1)
says omega^B = 0 on P, with error eps_mc(B, L + 1) = ||omega^B||^2. Each error is 0 exactly when its claim holds (every
term is >= 0), is computed from N, P and the member decomposition in the bit-model reading of DM11, and names one
member: no part D, no build, no target size and no zoom. A sufficient condition for eps_mc(B, l) = 0 for every l: no reader reads B (every r_(l,i) and every row of U
orthogonal to B) and, in the norm form, |Q_B h_(l-1)|^2 is the same at every point of P for every l. In the norm
form at an angle, the member claim's error is eps^o(B, l) of Proposition TV18.2 (its terms gamma^B and gains T^o,
u^o).

**Theorem TV18 (a map complete for every zoom at once) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts; member claims).** Let N
and the members be as in Definition DM16, and D any sum of members (K the sum of the others, Q the projection onto K
along D). Let B_D be, in the norm form, the projection cut that drops D (Pi = P_(D perp) = Q, reads Pi r_(l,i), N's
biases, norm constants eps_l + c_l(D), logit matrix U Pi, N's logit bias), and in the no-norm form the oblique cut onto
K (Lemma TV16) with reads Q^T r_(l,i), N's biases, logit matrix U Q and N's logit bias. Then c_l(D) is the sum of the
c_l(B) over the members B inside D, and
   D_P(B_D) <= (1/4) (sum over members B inside D of sum over l = 1, ..., L + 1 of eps_mc(B, l)^(1/2))^2.
The bound is a function of the member claims' errors alone, and 0 when the claims of the members inside D are 0.
Proof. Apply Theorem TV6 part 1 (part 2 in the no-norm form), with Lemma TV16 part 5 for a non-orthogonal
decomposition, to B_D with the members as the areas of the bound. Three steps.
(a) N's gains dominate the cut's. A member A lies in K or in D. In the norm form Pi P_A = P_A for A in K and 0 for A in
D, so |P_A Pi w| <= |P_A w|, |P_F Pi r| <= |P_F r| and |Pi r| <= |r|; in the no-norm form Q Q_A = Q_A or 0, so
|Q_A Q w| <= |Q_A w| and |Q_F^T Q^T r| = |(Q Q_F)^T r| <= |Q_F^T r|. In the norm form the cut's
nu'_l = (|Pi h_(l-1)|^2 + eps_l + c_l(D))^(1/2) >= eps_l^(1/2), since c_l(D) >= 0, so 1 / rho_l <= 1 / eps_l^(1/2).
At the logits, |P_perp U Pi P_A| <= |P_perp U P_A| and |P_perp U Pi| <= |P_perp U| (norm form), and
|P_perp U Q Q_A| <= |P_perp U Q_A| (no-norm form), with 1 / rho_(L+1) <= 1 / eps_(L+1)^(1/2). Hence T_l <= T*_l and
u <= u* entry by entry, so M_l <= M*_l entry by entry (all entries are >= 0) and
u^T M_l v <= u*^T M*_l v' for 0 <= v <= v'.
(b) The leak splits over the members inside D. In the no-norm form leak_(l,i) = r . Q h - r . h = -r . (I - Q) h =
-sum over B in D of r . Q_B h, since I - Q is the sum of the Q_B over the members inside D. In the norm form, by
Definition DM14, leak_(l,i) = (r . Pi h)(1 / nu' - 1 / nu) - r . P_D h / nu, with nu' as in (a) and nu = nu_l. The
second term is minus the sum over B in D of r . P_B h / nu. For the first,
|r . Pi h| |1 / nu' - 1 / nu| = |r . Pi h| |nu^2 - nu'^2| / (nu nu' (nu + nu')) <= |r| |nu^2 - nu'^2| / nu^2, since
|r . Pi h| <= |r| |Pi h| <= |r| nu' and nu + nu' >= nu; and nu^2 - nu'^2 = |P_D h|^2 - c_l(D) = sum over B in D of
(|P_B h|^2 - c_l(B)), by Pythagoras for the orthogonal members (and c_l(D) = sum of c_l(B) by the same identity, averaged).
So |leak_(l,i)(x)| <= sum over B in D of mu^B_(l,i)(x), and lambda_l[A](x) <= sum over B in D of lambda^B_l[A](x) for
every member A (using |P_A Pi w| <= |P_A w| from (a)). The same computation at the logits gives
|omega(x)| <= sum over B in D of omega^B(x).
(c) Minkowski's inequality for ||.|| turns the pointwise sums into ||lambda_l[A]|| <= sum over B in D of
||lambda^B_l[A]|| and ||omega|| <= sum over B in D of ||omega^B||. Put (a) and (c) into TV6's bound:
||omega|| + sum over l of u^T M_l ||lambda_l|| <= sum over B in D of (||omega^B|| + sum over l of u*^T M*_l ||lambda^B_l||),
which is the sum over B in D and l of eps_mc(B, l)^(1/2). Square and divide by 4. QED.
Lean: `mulvec_mono` (one step: for matrices with entries >= 0, A <= A' and 0 <= v <= v' entry by entry give
A v <= A' v'; the product M_l <= M*_l is this step iterated, by hand) in
`lean/coarse/Coarse/Stream.lean`; the rest is Theorem TV6 and the triangle inequality (none needed); checked in
`model/tv_member.py` (check A: the bound for every sum of members, both forms; check B: the exact case).
Comment. The price of zoom-free claims is in the gains: T* and u* use N's read and write vectors and, with norms, the
smallest possible norm size eps_l^(1/2) in place of the cut's rho_l. So the bound is looser than Corollary TV6.1's for any one D, and its exact case is strictly smaller: member
claims cannot see a cancellation inside D. Example (norm form): d = 3, members B_1 = span(e_1), B_2 = span(e_2),
K = span(e_3); first write (cos t_x, sin t_x, 1) with two values of t_x on P; one neuron reads and writes e_3; the
logits read e_3. The cut that drops D = B_1 + B_2 is exact (Theorem TV1 part 2: |P_D h|^2 = 1 on P), but
|P_(B_1) h|^2 = cos^2 t_x varies, the neuron's |r| > 0, and every u*_A > 0, so eps_mc(B_1, 1) > 0. This is the
converse face of Proposition TV17 part 2: energies of members can vary while their sum does not. Lambda_N of Theorem TV15 is linear in the leaks, so its member split
(Lambda_N of D = sum over B in D of terms that depend on D through Pi) does not give zoom-free claims in this simple
way; that is open.

**Corollary TV18.1 (the stream branch in T5's form for every zoom) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts; member
claims).** Let N and the members be as in Theorem TV18, and M a map that holds, for some members B, the member claims (B, l)
for every l = 1, ..., L + 1 (call these members **certified**). Let G_0, ..., G_m be any zoom of areas (Definition
DM15); every area is a sum of members (by induction on the area tree), so every group is. M is **complete** for the
zoom (member form; added to Definition DM15) when, for every level j and group S of G_j, the certified members
inside S have total dimension at least dim S - k_S. The rule: (one-time) compute s_B = sum over l of
eps_mc(B, l)^(1/2) for each certified B; for each level j and each group S of G_j, choose a set D_S of certified
members inside S, with dim S - dim D_S <= k_S (dim D_S the sum of the dimensions of its members), that minimises
the sum of s_B over B in D_S; let D_j be the sum of the D_S and B_j the cut
B_(D_j) of Theorem TV18; store B_j. Then:
1. B_j keeps, in each group S, the members of S not in D_S, at most k_S directions, and keeps every direction outside
   the groups; it is a re-fit area cut at G_j (constants re-set in the norm form, node R-normconst; the oblique cut in
   the no-norm form, node R-cutclass).
2. D_P(B_j) <= (1/4) (sum over groups S of G_j of sum over B in D_S of s_B)^2: a function of the claims' errors alone,
   and 0 when they are 0. Among cuts that drop sums of members, the choice of the D_S makes this bound least.
3. If M is complete for the zoom and every claim of M has error 0, D_P(B_j) = 0, so B_j has the least loss, and its
   weights are a closed form in N's weights, P and M. Completeness is checked by adding dimensions of certified
   members: time polynomial in the size of M. The same map M is complete for every zoom whose target sizes it
   covers; it names no zoom. (Every claim of a map that certifies every member being 0 would force P_perp U h_L = 0
   on P; the exact case is meant for the certified members only.)
4. The one-time computation: the member claims of the certified members (one forward pass of N on P), and for each group one knapsack:
   a dynamic programme over the members of S and the dropped dimension 0, ..., dim S, in time
   O(#members(S) x dim S). After it, switching to level j selects stored weights.
5. (Norm form, members at an angle.) Parts 1 to 4 hold with eps^o(B, l) and the cuts of Proposition TV18.2 in
   place of eps_mc(B, l) and the cuts of Theorem TV18.
Proof. (1) B_(D_j) keeps K_j, the sum of the members outside D_j. Inside S it keeps the members not in D_S, of total
dimension dim S - dim D_S <= k_S. (2) Theorem TV18 with D = D_j; the sum over B in D_j splits over the groups. The
least-sum choice is a 0-1 knapsack (minimum cost, dropped dimension at least dim S - k_S) whose weights are integers
at most d, solved exactly by the dynamic programme: best(i, t) = the least cost with the first i members dropping
dimension at least t, best(i, t) = min(best(i - 1, t), s_(B_i) + best(i - 1, max(t - dim B_i, 0))). (3) Completeness makes the knapsack feasible with certified members only; the bound is then a sum of errors that
are 0; D_P >= 0. The weights are projections of N's matrices. (4) Counting. (5) Part 5 is the same argument with
Proposition TV18.2 in place of Theorem TV18. QED.
Lean: none needed (Theorem TV18 and the textbook knapsack recursion); checked in `model/tv_member.py` (check C: the
dynamic programme against all subsets; check D: the rule on random zooms).
Comment. This is the route that Corollary TV6.2's comment named ("one claim per member, carried along N's own area
graph"), now proved for both forms and any direct decomposition (part 5, with Proposition TV18.2, for the norm form at an
angle). T5's map is zoom-free here: the same list of member claims serves every zoom whose target sizes its certified
members cover. The bound is loose wherever TV6's
gains are; the exact case is what it certifies.

**Proposition TV18.2 (member claims with norms at an angle) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts; member claims).**
Let N be as in Definition DV1 in the norm form, with Lipschitz sigma_l and every eps_l > 0, and let the members
A_1, ..., A_m be any direct decomposition, with projections Q_A. For l = 1, ..., L + 1 and members B, F let
   g^l_(BF)(x) = (Q_B h_(l-1)(x)) . (Q_F h_(l-1)(x)),   gbar^l_(BF) = E_P g^l_(BF),
      gamma^B_l(x) = |g^l_(BB)(x) - gbar^l_(BB)| + 2 sum over F != B of (|g^l_(BF)(x) - gbar^l_(BF)|
                  + |min(gbar^l_(BF), 0)|)   (the last terms are 0 for orthogonal members),
and define the member terms as in Definition DM16 with gamma^B_l in place of | |Q_B h|^2 - c_l(B) |, and the gains with
the zoom-free sizes s(r) = sum over members G of |Q_G^T r| and s(U) = sum over G of |P_perp U Q_G|:
   mu^B_(l,i) = |r_(l,i) . Q_B h_(l-1)| / nu_l + |r_(l,i)| gamma^B_l / nu_l^2,
   omega^B = |P_perp U Q_B h_L| / nu_(L+1) + |P_perp U| gamma^B_(L+1) / nu_(L+1)^2,
   T^o_l[A, F] = (Lip_l / eps_l^(1/2)) sum over i of |Q_A w_(l,i)| (|Q_F^T r_(l,i)| + s(r_(l,i))),
   u^o_A = (|P_perp U Q_A| + s(U)) / eps_(L+1)^(1/2),
with lambda^B_l, M^o_l and the errors eps^o(B, l) formed as in DM16. Let D be a sum of members, K the sum of the others, Q the projection onto K along D,
and B_D the oblique cut onto K (Lemma TV16) with reads R_l Q, N's biases, logit matrix U Q, N's logit bias, and norm constants eps_l + c^+_l(D), with c_l(D) = E_P (|h_(l-1)|^2 - |Q h_(l-1)|^2) and c^+_l(D) = max(c_l(D), 0).
Then
   D_P(B_D) <= (1/4) (sum over members B inside D of sum over l = 1, ..., L + 1 of eps^o(B, l)^(1/2))^2,
which is 0 when the claims of the members inside D are 0. For orthogonal members every term is at least the matching
term of DM16 (s(r) >= |r|), so Theorem TV18 is the sharper statement there.
Proof. (i) Energy. h = sum over B of Q_B h and Q h = sum over B in K of Q_B h, so |h|^2 - |Q h|^2 is the sum of
g_(BF) over the ordered pairs (B, F) with B or F inside D. Its mean c_l(D) is the same sum of gbar_(BF); the diagonal terms gbar_(BB) = E |Q_B h|^2 are >= 0, so
min(c_l(D), 0) >= the sum of min(gbar_(BF), 0) over the off-diagonal ordered pairs touching D. (ii) The cut's norm
size: nu'^2 = |Q h|^2 + eps_l + c^+_l(D) >= eps_l, so rho_l >= eps_l^(1/2), and nu' >= |Q h|. (iii) The leak: the cut's read of
neuron i is r . Q n'(Q h) = r . Q h / nu' (Q Q = Q), so leak_i = r . Q h (1 / nu' - 1 / nu) - r . (I - Q) h / nu. As in
the proof of Theorem TV18, the first term is at most |r| |nu^2 - nu'^2| / nu^2, and nu^2 - nu'^2 = (|h|^2 - |Q h|^2) - c_l(D) + min(c_l(D), 0) is the sum over the ordered pairs touching D of
(g_(BF) - gbar_(BF)), plus min(c_l(D), 0), whose size is at most the sum of |min(gbar_(BF), 0)| over the
off-diagonal pairs touching D, by (i). Give each diagonal pair (B, B), B in D,
to B; each off-diagonal pair (B, F) with B in D to B, and one with only F in D to F. A member B in D receives at most
the pairs (B, F) and (F, B), F != B, and g is symmetric, so |nu^2 - nu'^2| <= sum over B in D of gamma^B_l (the min terms are assigned the same way). The second
term is at most the sum over B in D of |r . Q_B h| / nu, since I - Q is the sum of the Q_B over B in D. So
|leak_i| <= sum over B in D of mu^B_(l,i); the logits are the same computation. (iv) The gains: Theorem TV6 with
Lemma TV16 part 5 for the oblique cut and the member decomposition. TV6's proof uses a read only through its action
on vectors of K and through its size, so the read vector Q^T r may stand; |Q_A Q w| <= |Q_A w|,
|Q_F^T Q^T r| = |(Q Q_F)^T r| <= |Q_F^T r|, |Q^T r| <= s(r) (Q^T is the sum of the Q_G^T over G in K), and in the
same way |P_perp U Q Q_A| <= |P_perp U Q_A| and |P_perp U Q| <= s(U). With (ii), T_l <= T^o_l and u <= u^o entry by entry. (v) Steps (a) and (c) of Theorem TV18's proof finish it. QED.
Lean: `mulvec_mono` (step (v)); the rest is Theorem TV6, Lemma TV16 and the triangle inequality (none needed); checked
in `model/tv_member.py` (check E: every sum of members, norm form, members at an angle, against the bound).
Comment. The constant c_l(D) can be negative at an angle (Proposition TV17 part 1). The cut keeps N's constant
then (c^+ = 0) and each member's claim carries the negative mean cross energies it touches; so no premise is
needed and the constants stay within node R-normconst's c_l >= 0. The price: the exact case needs
min(gbar_(BF), 0) = 0 for the cross pairs. The zoom-free sizes s(r) and the cross terms make this
bound looser than TV18's; at an angle they are what a claim that names one member has to carry.

### B.V.7 One budget for units and stream: the written span (added 2026-10-31)

Shonu (2026-10-31): a developer coarsens a capability, not "a neuron" or "the stream"; if the coarse neurons cannot
write a direction, the stream should be able to drop it at no extra loss. This part makes that a statement about least
losses. Optimality labels (CLAUDE.md, "The bar"): Theorem TV19.2 is EQ (two least losses are equal, for any
objective). Lemma TV19 and Proposition TV19.1 are facts about one network, used by it. Proposition TV19.4 is an example
in which two least losses differ; it carries no label.
1. Definition DV5: the written span and the read kernel of a network on P; "fits in width d'".
2. Lemma TV19: every network fits in the width of its written span. No claim, no premise on sigma or the norm.
3. Proposition TV19.1: without a norm, a network also fits in the width of its written span modulo its read kernel
   (the minimal realization of linear systems: reachable modulo unobservable). With a norm, the same holds when the
   energy of the dropped part is constant on P.
4. Definition DV6 and Theorem TV19.2: the narrow unit builds of a zoom, defined from N alone; their least loss equals
   the least loss of the full-width unit builds once the width is at least dim E_N + sum of the k_S, where E_N (the
   first write, the biases and the kept neurons' writes) is computed from N and P.
5. Proposition TV19.4: the term dim E_N cannot be dropped: for narrow builds whose stream need not hold E_N, a full
   first write forces the full stream. It tests only the dim E_N term, not the sum k_S term.
Scope, said plainly: for dim E_N <= d' < dim E_N + sum k_S nothing is proved here; there the least narrow network may
differ from the least wide one. Below dim E_N the narrow class of DV6 is empty. Studying it needs groups that hold units and stream directions together, a change of
the trunk's wording (node R-jointgroup, card 3-29, PENDING).

**Definition DV5 (written span, read kernel, width) (added 2026-10-31).** Let B be a network of Definition DV1 (either
form) with stream width d, streams h^B_l, read matrices R^B_l and logit matrix U^B.
1. The **written span** of B on P is V_P(B) = span{h^B_l(x) : x in P, l = 0, ..., L}, a subspace of R^d.
2. The **read kernel** of B is Z(B) = (intersection over l of ker R^B_l) intersected with ker(P_perp U^B).
3. For d' <= d, B **fits in width** d' if some network B' of Definition DV1 of the same form, with stream width d',
   the same sigma_l, the same number of neurons in each block and norm constants eps_l + gamma_l with gamma_l >= 0
   (gamma_l = 0 unless said otherwise), has at every point of P the same inside values g_l as B (neuron by neuron) and
   the same softmax of its logits.
Comment. V_P(B) is spanned by the first write on P and the writes W^B_l g^B_l(x) + c^B_l on P (h_l - h_(l-1) is the
write of block l). "Fits" is a tool for Lemma TV19 and Proposition TV19.1; the narrow class whose least loss Theorem
TV19.2 compares is Definition DV6, defined from N alone.

**Lemma TV19 (a network fits in the width of its written span) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts).** Let B be a
network of DV1, either form, and K a subspace of R^d with V_P(B) inside K. Let d' = dim K and Q a d x d' matrix whose
columns are an orthonormal basis of K. The network B' with first write Q^T e^B, writes Q^T W^B_l and Q^T c^B_l, read
matrices R^B_l Q, logit matrix U^B Q, and B's sigma_l, b^B_l, c^B_y and norm constants, has at every point of P the
stream Q^T h^B_l, the inside values g^B_l and the logits of B. So B fits in width dim V_P(B).
Proof. B' is the projection cut of B that drops D = K perp, with norm-constant increments 0 (Definition DV2). By Lemma
TV0 its values are read off the sequence ht_0 = Pi e, ht_l = ht_(l-1) + Pi (W_l gt_l + c_l), Pi = P_K. By induction
ht_l(x) = h_l(x) at every x in P. Base: e(x) = h_0(x) lies in K, so Pi e(x) = e(x). Step: if ht_(l-1)(x) = h_(l-1)(x),
the reads and the norm constants are B's, so gt_l(x) = g_l(x), and W_l g_l(x) + c_l = h_l(x) - h_(l-1)(x) lies in K, so
ht_l(x) = h_(l-1)(x) + (h_l(x) - h_(l-1)(x)) = h_l(x). Lemma TV0 then gives the stream Q^T h_l, the inside values g_l
and the logits U n(h_L) + c_y. QED.
Lean: `written_step` (the step: a projection that fixes h and h' sends h + Pi (h' - h) to h') in
`lean/coarse/Coarse/Stream.lean`; `norm_rot` for the read step of Lemma TV0. The induction is by hand.

**Proposition TV19.1 (the read side) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts).** Let B be a network of DV1, V = V_P(B),
Z' = V intersected with Z(B), W the orthogonal complement of Z' inside V, and Q_W a d x d' matrix whose columns are an
orthonormal basis of W, d' = dim V - dim Z'.
1. (No norm.) In the no-norm form, the network B' with first write Q_W^T e^B, writes Q_W^T W^B_l and Q_W^T c^B_l, read
   matrices R^B_l Q_W, logit matrix U^B Q_W and B's sigma_l, b^B_l, c^B_y has at every point of P the inside values of
   B and the softmax of B's logits. So B fits in width dim V - dim(V intersected with Z(B)).
2. (Norm, exact case.) In the norm form, suppose that for each l = 1, ..., L + 1 the energy |P_(Z') h^B_(l-1)(x)|^2 is
   one number gamma_l at every x in P. Then B' of part 1 with norm constants eps_l + gamma_l (node R-normconst) has the
   same property.
Proof. On V write h = w + z with w = P_W h in W and z = P_(Z') h in Z' (W and Z' are orthogonal and sum to V). Every
h_l(x) lies in V. Let z_l(x) = Q_W^T h_l(x) = Q_W^T w_l(x). Then Q_W z_l(x) = w_l(x) and |z_l(x)| = |w_l(x)|.
(1) Induction on l: B''s stream is z_l. Base: B''s first write is Q_W^T e = Q_W^T h_0 = z_0. Step: if B''s stream
before block l is z_(l-1), its read is R_l Q_W z_(l-1) = R_l w_(l-1) = R_l h_(l-1) - R_l z = R_l h_(l-1), because z lies
in Z(B), inside ker R_l. So its inside values are g_l, and its stream after block l is
z_(l-1) + Q_W^T (h_l - h_(l-1)) = z_l. Logits: U Q_W z_L = U h_L - U z with P_perp U z = 0, so the logit change is a
multiple of the all-ones vector and the softmax is B's.
(2) The same induction, with the read R_l Q_W z / (|z|^2 + eps_l + gamma_l)^(1/2) = R_l w / (|w|^2 + |P_(Z') h|^2 + eps_l)^(1/2)
= R_l h / (|h|^2 + eps_l)^(1/2), since |h|^2 = |w|^2 + |P_(Z') h|^2 and R_l P_(Z') h = 0; the logits in the same way.
QED.
Lean: `quotient_read` (the read step of part 1: R (P_W h) = R h when R kills h - P_W h) and `read_unchanged` (part 2's
read step, Theorem TV1) in `lean/coarse/Coarse/Stream.lean`. The induction is by hand.
Comment. The block maps sigma_l do not matter, because the stream itself is linear and every nonlinear step reads it
through R_l. Part 2 is Theorem TV1's exact case for the network B; the energy condition is a condition on B, not a
claim on N, and no graded form of part 2 is stated here. Both parts and their proofs hold with any subspace of Z' in
place of Z' (W then its orthogonal complement in V). No least-loss statement for the read side is made in this Part.

**Definition DV6 (unit builds of a zoom, wide and narrow) (added 2026-10-31).** Let N be a network of DV1 (either
form) and G a grouping of its neurons, each group S inside one block l(S), with sizes k_S. Let
   E_N = span{e(x) : x in P} + span{c_1, ..., c_L} + span{write vectors of the neurons of N in no group}
(e, c_l and the write vectors are N's), computed from N and P alone.
1. A **wide unit build** at G is a network of DV1 of stream width d with N's first write e, N's biases c_l, N's norm
   constants, every neuron in no group with N's read vector, bias and write vector, each group S replaced by at most
   k_S new neurons of block l(S) with sigma_(l(S)) and any read vectors, biases and write vectors in R^d, and N's
   logit matrix and bias (the **fixed-logit** class) or any logit matrix and bias (the **free-logit** class).
   Bc(G) is the class (of either kind).
2. For d' <= d, a **narrow unit build** of width d' is given by a d x d' matrix Q with orthonormal columns whose
   range contains E_N, and is the network of DV1 of stream width d' with first write Q^T e, biases Q^T c_l, N's norm
   constants, every neuron in no group with read vector Q^T r (r N's read vector), N's bias and write vector Q^T w
   (w N's write vector), each group S replaced by at most k_S new neurons of block l(S) with any read vectors, biases
   and write vectors in R^(d'), and logit matrix U_N Q with N's bias (fixed-logit) or any C x d' logit matrix and any
   bias (free-logit). Bc_(d')(G) is the class (of the same kind as Bc(G)); it is empty when d' < dim E_N.
3. The **relaxed narrow class** Bc'_(d')(G) is item 2 with the condition "range contains E_N" dropped: Q is any
   d x d' matrix with orthonormal columns. It contains Bc_(d')(G) and is not empty for any d' >= 1.
These classes are read from N, P, G and d' alone. For an objective J (D_P, D2_P or any function of the softmax of the
logits on P), V^J(Bc) is the infimum of J over a class Bc.

**Theorem TV19.2 (one budget: the stream adds nothing to the least loss) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts).**
Let N, G, E_N, Bc(G) and Bc_(d')(G) be as in Definition DV6 (either kind, either norm form). For every objective J
and every d' with dim E_N + (sum over S of k_S) <= d' <= d:
   V^J(Bc_(d')(G)) = V^J(Bc(G)).
More: every narrow build has the inside values and the softmax of some wide build at every point of P, and every wide
build has those of some narrow build. So a least wide build cut to a subspace (Lemma TV19) is a least narrow build,
and a least narrow build lifted by Q is a least wide build.
Proof. (Lift: narrow to wide.) Let B' in Bc_(d')(G) be given by Q, with new neurons (r'_j, b'_j, w'_j) and logit
matrix U'. Let B be the wide network with N's first write, biases, kept neurons and norm constants, new neurons
(Q r'_j, b'_j, Q w'_j) and logit matrix U' Q^T and B''s logit bias c' (free kind), or N's logit matrix U_N and bias (fixed kind, where U' = U_N Q);
B is in Bc(G). Claim: h^B_l(x) = Q z_l(x) at every x in P, with z_l the stream of B'. Base: e(x) lies in E_N, inside
the range of Q, so e(x) = Q Q^T e(x) = Q z_0(x). Step: if h^B_(l-1) = Q z_(l-1), then n(Q z) = Q n(z) (`norm_rot`,
stated for any linear isometry; Q is an isometry from R^(d') into R^d), so a kept neuron reads r . Q n(z) = (Q^T r) . n(z), B''s read, and a new neuron reads
(Q r') . Q n(z) = r' . n(z), B''s read; so the inside values agree. The writes: a kept write w lies in E_N, so
w = Q Q^T w; the bias c_l = Q Q^T c_l in the same way; a new write is Q w'. So h^B_l = Q z_(l-1) + Q (B''s write) =
Q z_l. Logits: for the fixed kind U_N n(Q z_L) = U_N Q n(z_L), B''s logits; for the free kind U' Q^T Q n(z_L) = U' n(z_L).
So J(B) = J(B'), and V^J(Bc(G)) <= V^J(Bc_(d')(G)).
(Projection: wide to narrow.) Let B in Bc(G). Its stream on P is e plus the biases plus the writes of its neurons, so
V_P(B) lies in K_0 = E_N + span{its new write vectors}, of dimension at most dim E_N + sum k_S <= d'. Pick a subspace
K of dimension d' with K_0 inside K (d' <= d), and Q with orthonormal columns spanning K. By Lemma TV19, the network
with first write Q^T e, writes Q^T W_l, biases Q^T c_l, reads R_l Q and logit matrix U Q has B's inside values and
logits on P. Its kept neurons have read vectors Q^T r and write vectors Q^T w with r, w N's; its new neurons have
some vectors in R^(d'); its logit matrix is U_N Q (fixed kind) or some C x d' matrix (free kind); the range of Q
contains E_N. So it is in Bc_(d')(G), and V^J(Bc_(d')(G)) <= V^J(Bc(G)). QED.
Lean: none needed beyond `norm_rot` (any linear isometry) and `written_step` (Lemma TV19); the two inclusions are
bookkeeping.
Content, said plainly: the theorem allows a narrower stream only when dim E_N + sum k_S < d. E_N holds
span{e(x) : x in P}, so a first write that spans R^d on P (typical when P has at least d points in general position)
gives E_N = R^d, and then only d' = d is allowed.
Comment (what it gives, said plainly). A zoom that coarsens neurons gets the narrower stream at no cost, for the least
loss itself: down to width dim E_N + sum k_S, the narrow and the wide optimum are the same, and each is the other cut
or lifted. The price sits in E_N: the first write on P, the biases and the kept neurons' writes. The stream narrows
only as far as these allow. (A transformer is not a network of DV1, which has one position and no attention, so
nothing here is proved for it.)

**Proposition TV19.4 (the first write cannot be left out of the count) (under: pure-stream networks; area cuts).**
Take the no-norm form, d = 2, L = 0 (no blocks, so G is empty and k = 0), C = 3, P = {e_1, e_2, 0} with equal
weights, first write e(x) = x, and N with logit matrix U_N = [e_1, e_2, 0]^T (rows) and bias 0. Let Bc be the
free-logit class of Definition DV6. Then dim E_N = 2 (so Bc_1 is empty), V^(D_P)(Bc) = 0, and the relaxed free-logit
narrow class of width 1 (DV6 item 3) has V^(D_P)(Bc'_1) > 0.
Proof. N is in Bc with D_P = 0. A member of Bc'_1 is given by a unit vector q in R^2: its first write is
z(x) = q^T x and it has centred logits P_perp (u z(x) + c') with u in R^3, so its
centred logits at the three points have differences P_perp u (z(e_1) - z(0)) and P_perp u (z(e_2) - z(0)) on one line.
N's differences P_perp e_1 and P_perp e_2 (centred, in R^3) are independent. If the infimum were 0, there would be
width-1 builds with D_P -> 0; by Pinsker's inequality (|p - q|_1^2 <= 2 KL(p || q)) their softmaxes at the three points
converge to N's, and since the softmax is a homeomorphism from centred logits onto the open simplex, their centred
logits converge to N's. Pairs of dependent vectors converge to a dependent pair. So the infimum is positive. QED.
Lean: none needed (a 2 x 2 determinant and a limit); checked in `model/tv_written.py` (check D).

## B.G A gate in front of a family: the gated fold

Theorem T38 says what a least unit computes on its region. It does not say which region. The tiny networks of
T32 to T34 have one hidden layer and no unit that plays the role of a gate, so nothing in them can supply a region.
This section adds the structure that the essay's picture needs: a gate in layer 1 in front of a family in layer 2
(Hypothesis H-front). It asks one question: can the region come from the network's gate, and the value from a
formula?

**Setting of B.G.** N is a plain ReLU network with two hidden layers and two logits. Layer 1 gives h(x) in R^m. Layer
2 has units n_i(x) = relu(a_i^T h(x) + b_i), and N's gap is Delta_N(x) = sum_i c_i n_i(x) + c_0, so Delta_N depends on
x only through h(x). A build keeps N's layer 1 unchanged and replaces layer 2 by k new units: its gap is
gap_B(x) = sum_j s_j relu(theta_j^T h~(x)) + gamma, with h~ = (h, 1), signs s_j in {+1, -1} and output sizes absorbed
into theta_j. Write z_x = h(x). The gate of H-front is written q, its value on G (under H-flatgate) q_1.

**Instances of B.G.** Gamma = the rotations by 90 degrees of (x_1, x_2), fixing x_3. Layer 1:
h = (relu(x_1), relu(x_2), relu(-x_1), relu(-x_2), relu(x_3)); the fifth unit is the gate q. Points with x_3 = 1 are in
the gate's region; points with x_3 = 0 are off it.
- I1: layer 2 has four members relu(h_i + 5 q - 6), i = 1 to 4, and N's gap is their sum (c_0 = 0). The mix is uniform
  on 13 points: with x_3 = 1, the orbits of (2, 0), (2, 2) and (1, 1) (N's gap 1, 2 and 0); with x_3 = 0, the origin.
- I2: the members of I1. The mix: with x_3 = 1, the orbits of (2, 0) and (1, 1) and the point (0, 0) (gap 1, 0 and 0);
  with x_3 = 0, the origin. Off-gate weight w_0, the rest uniform.
- I3: the points and weights of I1, and members relu(h_i + 5 q - 5). On G these are h_i, so N's gap is
  S = h_1 + h_2 + h_3 + h_4 there, and 0 at the origin.

**Definition D32 (gate fold).** Under H-front, with gate q and region G, a build of width 1 is a gate fold if its
unit's firing set on the support of P is exactly G: theta^T h~(x) > 0 for x in G, and <= 0 for the other points of
the support. With several gates q_1, ..., q_k and regions G_1, ..., G_k, a build of width k is a gate fold if its
units' firing sets are G_1, ..., G_k.

**Lemma T39 (the least gate fold is the fit on the gate's region, and N's value off it) (under: two logits, a finite
mix, first layer kept, H-front).** Let l(f; t) be the per-point loss: (f - t)^2 / 4 for D2_P, and
KL(sigma(t) || sigma(f)) for D_P (two logits). Let f_G be an affine function of z that minimises
sum over x in G of pi_x l(f(z_x); Delta_N(x)) over all affine f (a pi-weighted least-squares fit of N's gap on G for
D2; a soft-label logistic fit for D_P), and let L_G be the minimum. Then:
0. For builds of this setting, the objective is the one-hidden-layer objective (Definition D15) on the points z_x with
   the weights pi_x and the teacher gap Delta_N.
1. Every gate fold has objective at least L_G.
2. The fitted values F_x = f_G(z_x), x in G, are the same for every minimiser f_G. A gate fold with sign s, unit theta
   and constant gamma has objective L_G if and only if gamma = Delta_0 and s theta^T h~(x) = F_x - Delta_0 for every x
   in G. Such a gate fold exists if and only if there are a sign s and an affine function u of z with
   u(z_x) = F_x - Delta_0 on G, s u(z_x) > 0 on G, and s u(z_x) <= 0 at the other points of the support; the build
   s relu(s u(z)) + Delta_0 is one.
3. Every gate fold with objective L_G satisfies the conclusions 1 to 3 of Corollary T38.1 with region A = G and
   lambda_i = 0 on every kink point: its affine piece is the fit f_G on G, and its constant Delta_0 is N's average gap
   off G.
Proof. 0: gap_B and Delta_N are both functions of z_x, so each term of the objective is l(gap_B(x); Delta_N(x)) at the
point z_x with weight pi_x. 1: in a gate fold with sign s, unit theta and constant gamma, the gap on G is
phi(z) = s theta^T (z, 1) + gamma, an affine function, and off G it is gamma. So the objective is
sum_G pi l(phi; Delta_N) + sum over the other points of pi l(gamma; Delta_0). The first sum is at least L_G because
f_G minimises it over affine functions, and the second is at least 0 because l >= 0. 2: the first sum is a convex
function of the vector of values (phi(z_x)) on G, minimised over a linear space of value vectors. For D2 it is
strictly convex in the values, and for D_P its second derivative in each value is sigma(f)(1 - sigma(f)) > 0, so it is
strictly convex too, and its minimiser in the values is unique when it exists. It exists: for D2 by projection; for
D_P because 0 < sigma(Delta_N) < 1, so l(f; t) tends to infinity as f tends to plus or minus infinity. The second sum
is 0 if and only if gamma = Delta_0, because l(f; t) = 0 only at f = t and the other points carry weight. So equality
holds if and only if phi = F on G and gamma = Delta_0, that is s theta^T h~(x) = F_x - Delta_0 on G. The firing
condition of D32 is theta^T h~ > 0 on G and <= 0 off it. With u = s theta^T (z, 1) these are the stated conditions on
u; conversely the unit theta with theta^T (z, 1) = s u(z) gives the build s relu(s u(z)) + Delta_0. 3: by part 2 the
build equals the fit f_G on G and Delta_0 off G. Its kink points lie off G (it fires on all of G), and there the build
is Delta_0 = Delta_N, so the residual is 0 and the kink terms of T38.1 vanish for any lambda, in particular
lambda_i = 0. So the affine piece plus the constant is the least-squares (for D_P, logistic) fit on A = G (T38.1
conclusion 1); the constant is N's gap at every point off G, hence its average there (conclusion 2); and on the
boundary hyperplane the affine piece takes the value gamma (conclusion 3). QED.
Lean: none, by hand (two sums that decouple, and uniqueness of the minimiser of a strictly convex function of the
fitted values; this is general linear algebra over a finite point set, with no finite computation to check).
Comment: part 3 gives the conclusions of T38.1, not its premise: a gate fold need not be a least build (Theorem T40).

**Lemma T39a (when the fit is realisable) (under: two logits, a finite mix, first layer kept, H-front,
H-flatgate).** A gate fold with objective L_G exists if and only if F_x - Delta_0 is non-zero with one sign s at every
x in G. Then one is s relu(s u(z)) + Delta_0 with u(z) = f_G(z) - Delta_0 + s M (q - q_1), q the gate coordinate of z,
for any M with M q_1 > the largest value of s (f_G(z_x) - Delta_0) over the points off G.
Proof. If F_x - Delta_0 changes sign or is 0 on G, no u meets s u > 0 on G (T39 part 2). If it has one strict sign s,
take any minimiser f_G and u as stated. On G, q = q_1, so u = F - Delta_0 and s u > 0. Off G, q = 0, so
s u = s (f_G(z_x) - Delta_0) - M q_1 < 0 at each of the finitely many points off G. So u meets the conditions of T39
part 2 (with strict inequality off G, so the build has no kink points). QED.
Lean: none, by hand (a choice of one constant over a finite set).

**Corollary T39.1 (an exact width-1 build from N's weights when no member bends inside the gate) (under: two logits,
a finite mix, first layer kept, H-front, H-flatgate).** Call member i linear on G if its pre-activation
a_i^T z_x + b_i is >= 0 at every x in G (then n_i = a_i^T z + b_i on G) or <= 0 at every x in G (then n_i = 0 on G).
Suppose every member with c_i != 0 is linear on G, and let ON be the members of the first kind. Then on G, N's gap is
the affine function A(z) = sum over i in ON of c_i (a_i^T z + b_i) + c_0. Let u(z) = A(z) - Delta_0. If u has one weak
sign s on G (s u(z_x) >= 0 at every x in G; for example s = +1 when every c_i >= 0 and the members are silent off G,
so that Delta_0 = c_0), then the build
   B_G(x) = s relu(s u(z_x) + M (q(x) - q_1)) + Delta_0, with M q_1 >= the largest value of s u(z_x) over the points
   off G,
equals N at every point of the mix. So D2_P(B_G) = D_P(B_G) = 0, and B_G is a least build of width 1. Its weights are
N's own weights (the members in ON, their output weights, N's offset) plus the gate with the weight M. It is a gate
fold when s u > 0 at every point of G.
Proof. On G, q = q_1, so B_G = s relu(s u) + Delta_0 = u + Delta_0 = A = Delta_N, because s u >= 0 there. Off G,
q = 0, so the pre-activation is s u(z_x) - M q_1 <= 0, and B_G = Delta_0 = Delta_N by H-front. Both objectives are >= 0
and are 0 when the build equals N on the mix. QED.
Lean: none, by hand (direct evaluation at the two kinds of points; the instance I3 is checked in exact rationals by
`model/t40_gate_gap.py`).
Comment: "linear on G" is the ReLU form of the essay's picture "gate = region, value = distinction inside it"
(ESSAY-IDEAS I1): inside the gate each member is a straight-line value. Limit: in this case the least build pays no
cost at all (it equals N on the mix). So T39.1 does not answer the trunk's question, which is whether a rule finds a
least build when every build of the given widths pays a cost. The trunk's error is D(rule's build) - D(least build),
not D(least build). If T39a's sign condition holds, the gate fold reaches L_G, so the least width-1 value is at most
L_G; this bounds D(least build), not the rule's error. Without the sign condition no such bound is proved.

**Remark B.G.1 (the least build is not unique, and need not read the gate).** On I3, T39.1 applies with s = +1,
u = S + 20 q - 20 (equal to S on G) and M = 1. Any affine u equal to A - Delta_0 on G works, and the build
relu(S + (q - 1)) equals N on the mix (direct evaluation). The build 4 - relu(4 - S) also equals N on the mix: at
the eight points with S = 2 it gives 2, at the four corners (S = 4, a kink point) it gives 4, and at the origin
(S = 0) it gives 0. It never reads the gate, and it fires on nine points, not on G. So under T39.1 the gate gives one
least build, not the least build; the set of least builds has members whose regions are not the gate's. (Checked by
direct evaluation.)

**Theorem T40 (a perfectly clean gated instance where no gate fold is least) (under: none).** Take the network and
mix of I1. Then:
0. I1 meets every premise of Conjecture D34: two logits; a finite mix; layer 1 kept (the builds of the setting);
   H-front with Delta_0 = 0 (at the origin every member is relu(-6) = 0); H-flatgate with q_1 = 1; the mix is
   Gamma-invariant; Gamma fixes the gate; and N is perfectly clean for Gamma (Definition D20).
1. every width-1 gate fold has D2_P >= 1/26 = 7/182;
2. the build B*(x) = relu(19/14 (h_1 + h_3) + 1/2 (h_2 + h_4) - q - 1) + 2/7 has D2_P = 5/182.
So Conjecture D34 is false for D2_P. B* equals N at the two points (+-2, 0, 1) and at the four corners, and gives the
constant 2/7 at the other seven points: it breaks the rotation symmetry.
Proof. 0: The rotation (x_1, x_2, x_3) -> (-x_2, x_1, x_3) is orthogonal and sends the four value units of layer 1 to
each other in a 4-cycle (relu(x_1) -> relu(x_2) -> relu(-x_1) -> relu(-x_2)) and fixes relu(x_3); every non-identity
rotation moves relu(x_1), so the action on layer 1 is faithful. Layer 1 has rows e_1, e_2, -e_1, -e_2, e_3 of norm 1
and biases 0, so it is in reduced form. Layer 2 has rows (e_i + 5 e_5, -6) of norm sqrt(62); reduced form divides each
by sqrt(62) and multiplies its output weight 1 by sqrt(62), the same for all four members, so the members stay one
orbit and the readout stays symmetric (the logits (sum of members, 0) are fixed by every rotation, sigma = identity).
The member i reads only h_i and q, so the rotation that sends h_i to h_{i+1} sends member i to member i+1 and
W_2 pi_1(gamma) = pi_2(gamma) W_2 with equal biases. All units are read. The mix is a union of orbits plus the origin,
so it is Gamma-invariant. At x_3 = 1, q = 1 and member i is relu(h_i - 1); at x_3 = 0, q = 0 and member i is
relu(h_i - 6) = 0 since h_i = 0 at the origin. 1: by Lemma T39 part 1 every gate fold has D2_P >= L_G. On G the gate
is 1, so an affine fit is alpha + sum_i beta_i h_i. The loss on G is convex in (alpha, beta) and is unchanged when the
rotation permutes h_1, ..., h_4 cyclically (it permutes the points of G and fixes N's gap there), so the average of
the four rotated copies of a minimiser is a minimiser with all beta_i equal: alpha + beta S with
S = h_1 + h_2 + h_3 + h_4. S is 2 on the orbits of (2, 0) and (1, 1) (where N's gap is 1 and 0) and 4 on the corners
(gap 2). An affine function of S can take any two values at S = 2 and S = 4, so the least fit is 1/2 at S = 2 and 2 at
S = 4, with squared residual 1/4 at each of the 8 points with S = 2. L_G = (1/13) (8 / 4) / 4 = 1/26. 2: direct
evaluation. At (+-2, 0, 1): h_1 + h_3 = 2, h_2 + h_4 = 0, q = 1, the pre-activation is 19/7 - 2 = 5/7 and B* = 1 =
Delta_N. At (0, +-2, 1): 1 - 2 < 0, B* = 2/7, error 5/7. At the corners: 19/7 + 1 - 2 = 12/7, B* = 2 = Delta_N. At
(+-1, +-1, 1): 19/14 + 1/2 - 2 = -1/7 < 0, B* = 2/7, error 2/7. At the origin (q = 0): -1 < 0, B* = 2/7, error 2/7.
The sum of squared errors is 2 (25/49) + 5 (4/49) = 70/49, and D2_P = (1/13) (70/49) / 4 = 5/182 < 7/182. QED.
Lean: `t40_gate_floor` (part 1, the bound 2 on the residual sum of squares over all affine fits on G, without the
symmetry step) and `t40_bstar` (part 2), in `lean/coarse/Coarse/Gate.lean`. Part 0 is by hand.
Comment: the members here are relu(h_i - 1) inside the gate, so each one bends inside it (member 1 is off at (0, 2)
and on at (2, 0)). T39.1 does not apply. B* is shown to beat every gate fold; it is not shown here to be least.

## B.0 The write problem, from facts alone

**Setting of B.0.** Stack the readers of all branches (Fact F10) into one vector of r reader inputs, and index
positions by (branch, pooled position), written p. At input x and position p, the family sends W h(x, p) to the
readers, with h(x, p) in R^N the member outputs pooled by that branch's map M_b and W the matching r x N block
(zero outside the branch). A build with a fixed read sends B t(x, p), with t(x, p) in R^k the target signals pooled
by the same map and B an r x k matrix (the write). The error at the readers is e_x(p) = W h(x, p) - B t(x, p). The
metric is a positive semi-definite form G_x on the errors of one input, made of r x r blocks G_x(p, p') with
G_x(p', p) = G_x(p, p')^T. It may couple different branches. The objective is
Q(B) = 1/2 E_P sum_{p, p'} e_x(p)^T G_x(p, p') e_x(p').
For the frozen bench, G_x = D_x J_x^T Pi(y(x)) J_x D_x, with D_x the readers' gates and J_x the Jacobian of the
logits with respect to the readers' outputs. vec stacks columns.

**Lemma B0.1 (the second-order form is exact to second order) (under: none).** Suppose every layer above the
readers is piecewise linear (true for InceptionV1 above 3b), and that at the input x no reader pre-activation, later
pre-activation or pool tie sits exactly at a switching point. Then there is r_x > 0 such that, for every build whose
reader-input change e_x has |e_x| < r_x,
KL(softmax(y(x)) || softmax(y_B(x))) = 1/2 e_x^T G_x e_x + O(|e_x|^3).
Proof. Away from switching points each piecewise-linear layer is linear on a neighbourhood (Fact F1). So on a small
enough ball the logits change exactly by J_x D_x e_x. Fact F5 gives the expansion. QED.
Lean: none, the statement needs Taylor's theorem for the log-partition function.
Comment: the lemma is local. A build whose error flips reader gates on inputs of positive probability leaves the
second-order regime there.

**Theorem T0 (the write depends on the data through one moment object) (under: none).** In the setting of B.0, for
any law P and any fixed read:
1. Q(B) = 1/2 vec(B)^T S vec(B) - vec(B)^T R + c, with
   S = E_P sum_{p, p'} t(x, p) t(x, p')^T (x) G_x(p, p'),
   R = E_P sum_{p, p'} vec( G_x(p', p) W h(x, p) t(x, p')^T ),
   c = 1/2 E_P sum_{p, p'} h(x, p)^T W^T G_x(p, p') W h(x, p').
   Two laws with the same (S, R, c) give the same objective for every write.
2. If S is invertible, the optimal write is the unique solution of S vec(B) = R.
3. (Span.) Suppose G_x(p, p') = M K(p, p') with M (r x r) invertible and K a positive semi-definite kernel on
   positions, the same for every input, and Tbar = E_P sum K(p, p') t(x, p) t(x, p')^T invertible. Then the optimal
   write is B = W Lambda with Lambda = E_P[sum K(p, p') h(x, p) t(x, p')^T] Tbar^-1. It lies in the span of the
   family's columns and does not depend on M.
4. (Gates.) Suppose instead that G_x(p, p') = 0 for p != p' and G_x(p, p) = diag(g_{x,1}(p), ..., g_{x,r}(p)) with
   g >= 0 (each reader weighted by its own gate at each position). Then the objective splits over readers, and reader
   j's row of B is B_j = W_j Lambda_j with
   Lambda_j = E_P[sum_p g_{x,j}(p) h(x, p) t(x, p)^T] (E_P[sum_p g_{x,j}(p) t(x, p) t(x, p)^T])^-1 (when invertible).
   When the Lambda_j differ between readers, B need not lie in the span of the family's columns.
Proof. (1) e_x(p) is affine in B. For column vectors a, b and a matrix G, (B a)^T G (B b) = vec(B)^T (a b^T (x) G) vec(B)
(identity vec(G B b a^T) = (a b^T (x) G) vec(B)). Expanding e^T G e term by term and using G_x(p', p) = G_x(p, p')^T
to merge the two cross terms gives S, R and c. Expectations are linear. (2) Q is a convex quadratic with gradient
S vec(B) - R. (3) The gradient condition reads M (W Hbar - B Tbar) = 0 with Hbar = E sum K(p, p') h(x, p) t(x, p')^T.
M is invertible, so B Tbar = W Hbar, which gives the formula. M cancels. (4) With a diagonal, position-local metric
the objective is a sum over readers j of 1/2 E sum_p g_{x,j}(p) (W_j h(x, p) - B_j t(x, p))^2, a weighted least
squares problem in the row B_j alone. Its normal equations give B_j = W_j Lambda_j. Example of leaving the span: r = 3,
N = 2, k = 1, one position, t = h_1 + h_2, W with rows (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1). The law has two equally likely inputs:
x_1 with h = (1, 0) and x_2 with h = (0, 1), so t = 1 on both. Reader 1 is open only on x_1, reader 2 only on x_2,
reader 3 on both. Then Lambda_1 = (1, 0), Lambda_2 = (0, 1), Lambda_3 = (1/2, 1/2), and B = (1, 1, 1). The span of W's
columns is {(u, v, u + v)}, which requires B_3 = B_1 + B_2 = 2. So B is not in the span. QED.
Lean: `quad_moment_suff` (part 1 in its finite form: an objective that is a weighted sum of squares depends on the
law only through its weighted moment; e^T G e is a sum of squares after factoring G) and `exact_no_gain` (part 1's
consequence: two laws with the same statistic have the same optimum), `write_in_span` (part 3, for an invertible
metric, with the K-weighted moments in place of the plain ones), `gated_write_in_span` (part 4, applied to one reader
at a time with r = 1). These Lean statements assume the normal equations rather than deriving them from the
quadratic.

**Corollary T0.1 (the weights alone do not fix the generalist write) (under: H-stat).** Take P = P_train. If two
laws consistent with the same weights (in the sense of Fact F9) give optimal writes S_1^-1 R_1 != S_2^-1 R_2, then no
rule that reads only the weights gives the optimal generalist write for both.
Proof. A rule that reads only the weights returns the same write for both laws. It cannot equal two different optima.
QED.
Lean: none, the proof is one line of logic.
Comment: Fact F9 shows that such laws exist with different second moments. Whether their optimal writes differ is an
extra condition (the added Fisher matrix must change S^-1 R). So the corollary is conditional as stated.

## B.1 Symmetry fixes the shape of the coarse read and write

**Theorem T1a (circulant data give harmonic reads) (under: H-kron, H-pool).** Let the read be a same-position read
t = Lambda h, with Lambda a k x N matrix (by H-pool the pooled target is Lambda times the pooled members). Let C and M
be the factors of H-kron, and Phi = W^T M W. Premise: C and Phi are circulant (A_{i+1, j+1} = A_ij, indices mod N).
Write lambda_n = chat(n) phihat(n) for the product of their spectra at Fourier mode n (n and -n give the same value).
Write h0 for the summed read sum_i h_i (the constant mode) and call the cosine and sine reads at frequency 1 the
frequency-1 plane. Then:
1. For a read with row space V, the best write leaves the objective c - 1/2 tr(P_V C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2}), with P_V
   the orthogonal projection onto C^{1/2} V. The best k-dimensional read spaces are the spaces V such that C^{1/2} V
   is spanned by eigenvectors of C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} for k largest eigenvalues. When lambda at the k-th largest place
   is strictly larger than at the (k+1)-th, the best space is unique.
2. The Fourier modes in the member index are eigenvectors, with eigenvalue lambda_n, and C^{-1/2} maps each mode to
   itself. So a best read space can always be chosen as a span of Fourier modes. When two frequencies tie at the k-th
   place, combinations across them are also best.
3. (k = 1, data-free.) If the top eigenvalue of C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} is simple and its eigenvector has a non-zero
   entry sum, the best k = 1 read is the summed read t = sum_i h_i (up to scale), and its best write is the mean
   column B = (1/N) sum_i W_{., i}. Neither depends on C or M beyond the premise.
4. (k = 2d + 1, bumps.) If N >= 2d + 1 and min over |n| <= d of lambda_n > max over |n| > d of lambda_n, the best
   read space is unique and equals the trigonometric polynomials of degree <= d in the member angle
   theta_i = 2 pi i / N. It has a basis of non-negative reads: the 2d + 1 shifted Fejer kernels. For k = 3 these are
   the bumps lambda_{j, i} = 1 + cos(theta_i - phi_j), phi_j = 0, 2 pi / 3, 4 pi / 3.
5. (k = 2 is not unique.) If N >= 3 and lambda_0 > lambda_1 > max over |n| >= 2 of lambda_n, the best k = 2 read spaces are
   span(h0, v) for every unit vector v in the frequency-1 plane. They form a circle of optima.
Proof.
(1) With the read t = Lambda h and H-pool, e = (W - B Lambda) h, and by T0 part 1 with H-kron the objective is
1/2 tr((W - B Lambda)^T M (W - B Lambda) C). Put Y = M^{1/2} W C^{1/2} and Z = M^{1/2} B Lambda C^{1/2}, of rank <= k.
The objective is 1/2 |Y - Z|_F^2. For a fixed row space of Lambda, the best B makes Z the projection of Y onto the
row space C^{1/2} V, which leaves 1/2 |Y|^2 - 1/2 tr(P_V Y^T Y) and 1/2 |Y|^2 = c. By Eckart and Young the best Z is a
rank-k truncation of Y, whose row space is spanned by top right singular vectors of Y, which are top eigenvectors of
Y^T Y = C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2}. With a strict gap at place k the truncation is unique.
(2) A circulant matrix is a polynomial in the cyclic shift, so circulant matrices commute and share the Fourier
basis, and C^{1/2}, C^{-1/2} and C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} are circulant (Gray 2006). The eigenvalue of
C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} at mode n is chat(n)^{1/2} phihat(n) chat(n)^{1/2} = lambda_n. For real symmetric circulants
the spectrum is even in n.
(3) Let v be the top eigenvector. The cyclic shift sigma satisfies A_{sigma i, sigma j} = A_ij for
A = C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} (part 2). By `perm_fixes_simple_eigvec`, v is invariant under sigma, and by
`const_of_rotate_invariant` it is constant. C has constant row sums, so C^{-1/2} maps the constant vector to a
constant vector: the read is a multiple of sum_i h_i. For this read (Lambda = 1^T), the objective of part 1 is
1/2 tr((W - b 1^T)^T M (W - b 1^T) C) in the write column b. Its gradient condition is M (W C 1 - b 1^T C 1) = 0, so
b = W C 1 (1^T C 1)^-1 (M invertible, and 1^T C 1 > 0 because C is positive definite). The coefficient vector
C 1 (1^T C 1)^-1 is the constant 1/N by `k1_read_coeff`. So B = (1/N) W 1.
(4) Under the premise the 2d + 1 modes |n| <= d have the largest eigenvalues, strictly separated from the rest, so by
parts 1-2 the best space is unique and spanned by {1, cos n theta_i, sin n theta_i : 1 <= n <= d} (sampled at the N
member angles). A non-zero trigonometric polynomial of degree d has at most 2d zeros in a period, so sampling at
N >= 2d + 1 equally spaced angles is injective and the sampled space has dimension 2d + 1. The Fejer kernel F_d(t) = sum_{|n| <= d} (1 - |n| / (d + 1)) e^{i n t} equals
(1 / (d + 1)) (sin((d + 1) t / 2) / sin(t / 2))^2 >= 0. The coefficient matrix of its 2d + 1 shifts by
2 pi j / (2d + 1), in the basis e^{i n t} (|n| <= d), is the (2d + 1)-point Fourier matrix times
diag(1 - |n| / (d + 1)). Both factors are invertible, so the shifts are a basis. For d = 1 the shifts are the bumps
up to a constant factor (1 + 2 (1/2) cos t = 1 + cos t), which are non-negative by `bump_nonneg`.
(5) Modes n = 1 and n = -1 share lambda_1 (part 2). Every two-dimensional space containing the constant and one unit
vector of the frequency-1 plane captures lambda_0 + lambda_1, the maximum. QED.
Lean: `perm_fixes_simple_eigvec`, `const_of_rotate_invariant`, `k1_read_coeff`, `bump_nonneg` (`Coarse/Model.lean`).
Eckart and Young and the Fourier diagonalisation of circulant matrices are classical and not in Lean here.

**Lemma T1b (symmetry makes the data circulant) (under: H-clean, H-sym, H-read, H-kron).** In the plane model
(Definition D8), with H-clean exact, the matrices C and Phi of H-kron are circulant.
Proof. Write gamma for the rotation by 2 pi / N about the origin and tau_p for the shift by p. In the plane model,
H-clean with eps = 0 means h_i(x, p) = f_0((tau_p gamma^i)^-1 . x), where f_0 is the template unit at the origin. Then
h_{i+1}(gamma . x, gamma p) = f_0(gamma^-(i+1) tau_{-gamma p} gamma . x) = f_0(gamma^-(i+1) gamma tau_{-p} . x) =
h_i(x, p), because gamma tau_{-p} gamma^-1 = tau_{-gamma p}. The pooling commutes with gamma (D8), so the pooled outputs
satisfy the same identity. Let Pi be the cyclic shift on members. In
T = E sum_{p, p'} h(x, p) h(x, p')^T (x) G_x(p, p') (an integral over the plane in D8), substitute x = gamma . x' and
p = gamma q, p' = gamma q'. H-sym says gamma . x' has the law of x'. Rotation preserves the measure on the plane. H-read
gives G_{gamma x'}(gamma q, gamma q') = R G_{x'}(q, q') R^T. So (Pi (x) R) T (Pi (x) R)^T = T. With T = C (x) M this
reads (Pi C Pi^T) (x) (R M R^T) = C (x) M. A Kronecker product determines its factors up to a scalar a, and comparing
traces (tr Pi C Pi^T = tr C, and tr C > 0 because C is positive definite) gives a = 1. So Pi C Pi^T = C (C is circulant) and R M R^T = M. Finally, by H-read
W_{., i+1} = R W_{., i}, so Phi_{i+1, j+1} = W_i^T R^T M R W_j = Phi_ij. QED.
Lean: none for the plane substitution. The finite step (a Kronecker product determines its factors up to a scalar)
is a candidate for a later Lean port.

**Remark B1.1 (what the data still decides).** Under T1a the data enters the read only through the order of the
numbers lambda_n, n = 0, ..., floor(N/2): at most 6 numbers for N = 10, in place of the moment object of T0. For the
k = 1 write it enters not at all. Without H-kron, Lemma T1c says what remains.

**Lemma T1c (gated writes are shifts along reader orbits) (under: H-clean, H-sym, H-read).** In the plane model, take
the gated metric of T0 part 4 and the summed read t = sum_i h_i. Then the per-reader write vectors of T0 part 4 satisfy
Lambda_{R j} = Pi Lambda_j for every reader j. So the data enters this write through one N-vector per orbit of
readers. (Nothing here shows that the summed read is still the best k = 1 read under the gated metric. That is part of
the open object.)
Proof. Lambda_j = E sum_p g_{x,j}(p) h(x, p) t(x, p) / E sum_p g_{x,j}(p) t(x, p)^2. Substitute x = gamma . x' and
p = gamma q. By Lemma T1b's identity, h(gamma . x', gamma q) = Pi h(x', q), so t(gamma . x', gamma q) = t(x', q). By
H-read applied to the diagonal gated metric, g_{gamma . x', R j}(gamma q) = g_{x', j}(q). By H-sym and the invariance of
the measure on positions, Lambda_{R j} = Pi Lambda_j. QED.
Lean: none, the proof is the plane substitution of Lemma T1b. Checked on the exact plane-model instance
(`model/t1b_instance.py`, prediction P4).

**Remark B1.2 (premise of part 3).** By Perron and Frobenius, the premise of T1a part 3 holds when
C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} has positive entries. Without positivity the top mode may be the alternating mode n = N / 2
(which also has a one-dimensional real eigenspace), or a mode n >= 1 whose two-dimensional eigenspace makes the top
eigenvalue not simple.

**Remark B1.3 (T1a fixes a space, not a basis).** Part 4 fixes the best read space. Every basis of it gives the same
WHAT objective, because the write absorbs a change of basis (B Lambda = (B Q^-1)(Q Lambda) for invertible Q). The bumps
are one non-negative basis. Contiguous arcs of members are another candidate basis for an approximately equal space.
The choice matters only for the HOW (Proposition T1'), which T1a does not address.

**Remark B1.4 (the biases bench) (under: H-pool, with a constant metric G = M (x) K).** With free reader biases beta
(one per reader, the same at every position), the error is e(p) = E h(p) - beta with E = W - B Lambda. Write
kappa = sum_{p, p'} K(p, p') > 0 and m = E_P sum_{p, p'} K(p, p') h(x, p'). The objective is a convex quadratic in
beta. Its gradient condition is M (E m - kappa beta) = 0, so beta = E m / kappa (the K-weighted mean error).
Substituting gives the objective 1/2 tr(E^T M E Sigma) with Sigma = C - m m^T / kappa. So Sigma (the K-weighted
covariance) replaces C in T1a, which then needs Sigma positive definite (it is always positive semi-definite).
Lemma T1b's substitution applies to m (m_{i+1} = m_i), so Sigma is circulant under the same hypotheses. But Sigma need
not have positive entries, so the premise of T1a part 3 can fail (Remark B1.2) and the top mode may be n >= 1.

**Proposition T1' (a sum of members is one unit only when at most one hinge is crossed) (under: none).** Let U be an
open set of input fields of layer L. Let z_1, ..., z_m (m >= 2) be affine functions of the field whose zero sets are
pairwise different hyperplanes, and let lambda_1, ..., lambda_m > 0. Then t = sum_i lambda_i relu(z_i) equals relu(z')
on U for some affine z' only if at most one of the hyperplanes {z_i = 0} meets U.
Proof. On U, t is piecewise affine. Across the hyperplane {z_i = 0} its gradient jumps by lambda_i grad z_i, which is
not zero. Jumps across different hyperplanes sit on different sets, so they cannot cancel. Hence the set where t is not
differentiable is the union of the hyperplanes {z_i = 0} that meet U. relu(z') is not differentiable on at most one
hyperplane. QED.
Lean: none, the statement is about piecewise-affine geometry in several variables.
Consequence: on any open set of fields where two members' hinges are both crossed, the summed read of T1a part 3 is
not one unit. Then the WHAT of T1a is exact and the HOW is an approximation problem (Definition D6), the subject of T2.

## B.2 Contours fix the pairing of detectors

**Setting of B.2 (linearised contour laws).** Follow a curve from a tangent element at the origin with angle 0. In
the short-arc regime the curve is a graph y(s) over arc length s, with angle phi(s) = y'(s), and
y(s) = integral_0^s phi(u) du. Three laws:
| Law | Definition |
|---|---|
| circle | phi(s) = kappa_0 s |
| curvature process (H-contour, linearised) | phi(s) = kappa_0 s + sigma integral_0^s B(u) du, with kappa_0 ~ nu (finite variance) independent of the Brownian motion B |
| direction process | phi(s) = sigma B(s) |
The chord angle is alpha(s) = y(s) / s (linearised). The pairing slope, when E[phi | y] is linear in y, is
beta(s) = E[phi(s) | y(s)] / (y(s) / s).

**Lemma T3.0 (co-circularity is the tangent-chord rule) (under: none).** Two oriented tangent elements (v_1, phi_1)
and (v_2, phi_2) with v_1 != v_2 lie on one circle or line, traversed in their direction, if and only if
phi_1 + phi_2 = 2 alpha (mod 2 pi), with alpha the angle of v_2 - v_1. With phi_1 = 0 the partner angle is 2 alpha.
Proof. The tangent at each end of a chord makes equal angles with the chord, on opposite sides (tangent-chord angle
theorem): phi_1 - alpha = -(phi_2 - alpha). Conversely, given (v_1, phi_1) and v_2, exactly one circle (or line)
through v_1 with tangent phi_1 passes through v_2, and its tangent at v_2 is 2 alpha - phi_1. QED.
Lean: none, plane geometry. Checked symbolically on a parametrised circle in `model/t3_pairing.py`.

**Theorem T3 (pairing in the three contour laws) (under: none).** In the setting of B.2, with tau^2 = Var nu > 0:
1. (Sharpness, any nu.) Under the curvature process, phi(s) - 2 y(s) / s = sigma integral_0^s (s - w) (w / s) dB(w).
   It does not depend on kappa_0, has mean 0 and variance sigma^2 s^3 / 30. Since Var phi(s) = tau^2 s^2 + sigma^2 s^3 / 3,
   this error is the fraction rho s / (10 (rho s + 3)) of Var phi, with rho = sigma^2 / tau^2, which is O(rho s). So at
   short range the angle is 2 alpha (the co-circular rule) up to a small error, for every curvature law nu with
   tau > 0. For the circle (sigma = 0) the rule is exact. (If tau = 0 the rule fails: then phi itself is of order
   s^{3/2}, and the error is one tenth of Var phi at every s.)
2. (Slope, Gaussian nu.) If nu = N(0, tau^2), then E[phi | y] = beta(s) y / s with
   beta(s) = 2 (1 + rho s / 4) / (1 + rho s / 5), and Var(phi | y) = sigma^2 s^3 (rho s + 8) / (48 (rho s + 5)). The slope
   equals 2 in the limit s -> 0 and rises to 5/2 as rho s grows. The conditional variance tends to sigma^2 s^3 / 30.
3. (Direction process.) E[phi | y] = (3/2) y / s, and Var(phi | y) = sigma^2 s / 4, one quarter of
   Var phi = sigma^2 s. So the pairing is spread at every range. Also Var(phi - 2 y / s) = sigma^2 s / 3.
4. (Curvature-tuned detectors.) Under the curvature process, if the curvature is also fixed at both ends (kappa(0)
   and kappa(s), as for detectors tuned to curvature), then Var(phi - 2 y / s given kappa(0), kappa(s)) = sigma^2 s^3 / 180.
   The growth as s^3 is kept.
Proof. Write each term as a Wiener integral and use the Ito isometry.
(1) phi(s) = kappa_0 s + sigma integral (s - w) dB and y(s) = kappa_0 s^2 / 2 + sigma integral (s - w)^2 / 2 dB. In
phi - 2 y / s the kappa_0 terms cancel, and the kernel is (s - w) - (s - w)^2 / s = (s - w) w / s. Its square integrates
to s^3 / 30. Var phi adds tau^2 s^2 (independence) to sigma^2 integral (s - w)^2 = sigma^2 s^3 / 3.
(2) For Gaussian kappa_0 the pair (phi, y) is jointly Gaussian and centred, so E[phi | y] = (Cov / Var y) y and
Var(phi | y) = Var phi - Cov^2 / Var y, with Var y = tau^2 s^4 / 4 + sigma^2 s^5 / 20 and
Cov(phi, y) = tau^2 s^3 / 2 + sigma^2 s^4 / 8. Simplifying gives the stated forms.
(3) phi = sigma B(s) and y = sigma integral (s - w) dB: Var y = sigma^2 s^3 / 3, Cov = sigma^2 s^2 / 2. This gives the slope
3/2, the residual variance sigma^2 s - (sigma^2 s^2 / 2)^2 / (sigma^2 s^3 / 3) = sigma^2 s / 4, and
Var(phi - 2 y / s) = sigma^2 s - 4 (sigma^2 s^2 / 2) / s + 4 (sigma^2 s^3 / 3) / s^2 = sigma^2 s / 3.
(4) Fixing kappa(0) and kappa(s) fixes kappa_0 and B(s). The error eps = phi - 2 y / s has no kappa_0 term, and
Cov(eps, B(s)) = sigma integral_0^s (s - w) w / s dw = sigma s^2 / 6, with Var B(s) = s. Gaussian conditioning gives
sigma^2 s^3 / 30 - sigma^2 s^4 / (36 s) = sigma^2 s^3 / 180. QED.
Lean: none, the proof uses the Ito isometry. Every integral is checked symbolically in `model/t3_pairing.py`.
Comment: the linearisation (small angles) is exact for circles (Lemma T3.0). For the curvature process its error is
of higher order in the turning angle kappa s. A bound is an open lemma. Note that phi - 2 y / s is correlated with y
(covariance sigma^2 s^4 / 40), so part 1 is a statement about the joint law, not about phi given y.

**Corollary T3.1 (co-activity of ideal detectors on one curve) (under: none).** For ideal tangent-element detectors
(Definition D9) on one curve through (0, angle 0), the co-activity with the detectors at horizontal offset s is the joint
density of (y(s), phi(s)). Then:
1. (Any nu.) Under the linearised curvature process, the fraction of this co-activity with |phi - 2 y / s| > a is at
   most sigma^2 s^3 / (30 a^2): the co-activity concentrates on the co-circular line phi = 2 y / s.
2. (Gaussian nu.) At fixed offset y, the co-activity as a function of phi is a Gaussian with peak beta(s) y / s and
   variance sigma^2 s^3 (rho s + 8) / (48 (rho s + 5)).
3. (Direction process.) At fixed offset y it is a Gaussian with peak (3/2) y / s and variance sigma^2 s / 4.
Proof. (1) Chebyshev's inequality with T3 part 1. (2) and (3): the joint density is Gaussian, and its section at
fixed y is proportional to the conditional density of phi given y (T3 parts 2 and 3). QED.
Lean: none, it is a corollary of T3.
Comment: real detectors have finite tuning widths, which spread the co-activity further and move the peak toward the
regression slope of the smoothed law. Corollary T3.2 gives a test that does not need the widths.

**Corollary T3.2 (a width-robust test: how one statistic grows with distance) (under: none).** Let both detectors
carry independent Gaussian errors (Definition D9): across the curve with standard deviation w_y and in angle with
standard deviation w_phi. Measure the second element relative to the measured reference element: the offset
y' = (y + delta_1) - delta_0 - s eta_0 and the angle phi' = (phi + eta_1) - eta_0 (linearised frame rotation; the
deltas are position errors and the etas angle errors). Then, for the single statistic D(s) = Var(phi' - 2 y' / s):
1. under the linearised curvature process, D(s) = sigma^2 s^3 / 30 + 2 w_phi^2 + 8 w_y^2 / s^2;
2. under the direction process, D(s) = sigma^2 s / 3 + 2 w_phi^2 + 8 w_y^2 / s^2.
The width terms are the same under both laws and are constant or fall with s. The term that grows with s grows as s^3
under the curvature process and as s under the direction process. So the growth exponent of D decides between the two
laws without knowing the widths.
Proof. phi' - 2 y' / s = (phi - 2 y / s) + eta_1 + eta_0 - 2 (delta_1 - delta_0) / s (the reference angle error enters
twice: once in phi', and once through the frame rotation of y'). The four errors are independent of each other and of
the curve, so the variances add: 2 w_phi^2 + 8 w_y^2 / s^2. Theorem T3 parts 1 and 3 give the first terms. QED.
Lean: none, it is a sum of variances. Checked symbolically, with the four error variables carried explicitly, in
`model/t3_pairing.py`.

**Conjecture T2 (the k = 1 unit is a loop detector at the curvature centre) (under: H-clean, H-sym, H-read,
H-contour; CONJECTURE).** Let the read range over the members at all offsets inside the unit's window, so the group of
rotations about the unit's position acts on (member, offset) pairs, with rings as orbits. Then the best k = 1 read
puts its weight on the tangent rings (members placed on a circle around the unit's position, each tangent to it), and
the weight over radii peaks at r = 1 / kappa_template, the curvature the template detects. So the best k = 1 WHAT is a
circle detector centred at the unit's position: each member moved to its own centre of curvature.
Route: (i) T1a part 3 and Lemma T1b on the larger index set make the read constant on rings. (ii) Lemma T3.0: the
members of one ring are pairwise co-circular exactly when the ring is tangent. So under the circle law their
co-activity on that ring has rank one (all fire together when one circle of radius r around the position is present).
(iii) The co-activity C on the rings is the K-weighted pair occupation density of Definition D9, summed over the
ring pairs. The top eigenvector of the ring-invariant block must then be computed with both C and Phi on the rings. Its weight
over radii is set by the density of curvature 1 / r, the template's response to an arc of radius r, and the readers'
overlap Phi on the ring. (iv) Theorem T3 part 1 extends (ii) to the curvature process with an error of order
sigma s^{3/2}. (v) The HOW for this WHAT (Proposition T1') is the remaining step.
Lean: none, the route needs an infinite index set (offsets in the plane).

## B.2' Several families with a shared symmetry

**Setting of B.2'.** F families A_1, ..., A_F in layer L satisfying H-joint, in the plane model. Each
family is exactly clean under the same rotation gamma by 2 pi / N (h^{(f)}_{i+1}(gamma . x, gamma p) = h^{(f)}_i(x, p),
as derived in Lemma T1b). The readers satisfy H-read for every family with the same permutation R:
W^{(f)}_{., i+1} = R W^{(f)}_{., i}. The data object of all FN members factorises (H-kron): T = C (x) M, with C the
FN x FN joint co-activity matrix, made of N x N blocks C^{(fg)}. Phi = W^T M W has blocks Phi^{(fg)}.

**Theorem T5 (shared symmetry decouples the coarse problem by frequency) (under: H-clean, H-sym, H-read, H-kron,
H-pool, H-joint).** (H-pool is used in part 3, through T1a part 1.)
1. Every block C^{(fg)} and Phi^{(fg)} is circulant.
2. Let Chat(n) and Phihat(n) be the F x F Hermitian matrices of the blocks' Fourier coefficients at mode n. The Fourier
   transform in the member index (applied to every family at once) turns C and Phi into block-diagonal matrices with
   these F x F blocks, one per mode n.
3. A best k-dimensional joint read space (the best, when there is a strict gap at place k) is spanned by vectors of
   single frequency: for each mode n, take
   eigenvectors u of Chat(n)^{1/2} Phihat(n) Chat(n)^{1/2}, lift each to the members as u_f e^{i n theta_i} in family
   f, map by C^{-1/2}, and keep the k with the largest eigenvalues across all n (real reads from the pairs n, -n).
4. (Selection rule.) A best coarse unit can be chosen to read one frequency n only. The frequency-n parts of different
   families combine only with each other.
5. (Data count.) The co-activity C enters only through the floor(N/2) + 1 Hermitian F x F matrices Chat(n),
   n = 0, ..., floor(N/2) (Chat(-n) is the entrywise conjugate of Chat(n)), in place of an FN x FN matrix. The optimal
   value depends only on the eigenvalues of the products Chat(n)^{1/2} Phihat(n) Chat(n)^{1/2}. The best reads depend
   on Chat(n) itself (through the map Chat(n)^{-1/2}, which mixes families within frequency n), and the write also
   depends on M and W.
Proof. (1) The substitution of Lemma T1b, applied to a pair of families (f, g), gives
(Pi (x) R) T^{(fg)} (Pi (x) R)^T = T^{(fg)} for each block of T. With T = C (x) M, and M fixed by R (Lemma T1b on the
diagonal blocks), each C^{(fg)} commutes with the shift: Pi C^{(fg)} Pi^T = C^{(fg)}. The same for Phi by H-read.
(2) A matrix whose N x N blocks are all circulant is block-circulant in the member index. The unitary Fourier matrix U
on Z_N diagonalises every circulant block at once, so (I_F (x) U) C (I_F (x) U)^* is, after reordering the index to
(mode, family), block-diagonal with blocks Chat(n). (3) Matrix square roots, inverses and products preserve this block
structure, so C^{1/2} Phi C^{1/2} is block-diagonal with blocks Chat(n)^{1/2} Phihat(n) Chat(n)^{1/2}, and C^{-1/2}
is block-diagonal with blocks Chat(n)^{-1/2}. C is real, so its Fourier coefficient at -n is the conjugate of that at n. Its eigenvectors
can be chosen inside single blocks. The Eckart-Young argument of T1a part 1 then picks the k largest eigenvalues over
all blocks. (4) and (5) restate (3). QED.
Lean: none, the proof uses the Fourier diagonalisation of block-circulant matrices. Checked on an exact two-family
matrix instance in `model/t5_instance.py`.
Comment: T5 is the standard frequency split of a problem with a cyclic symmetry (block-circulant diagonalisation,
Schur's lemma). Its content is the selection rule and the data count, not new algebra. It is how symmetry lets the
theory scale from one family to a layer. Families that share a group do not
need to be coarsened one at a time. The joint problem splits by frequency into small problems, and the data enters
only through one small matrix per frequency.

## B.3 Where the data enters, and stability

**Conjecture T4 (symmetry reduces the data to a few numbers, and the build is stable) (under: H-clean, H-sym,
H-read, H-contour; CONJECTURE).**
1. Under the four hypotheses in the plane model, the per-reader-orbit write vector of Remark B1.1 depends on the law P
   only through the curvature law nu, the ratio sigma of H-contour and the background law.
2. If H-clean and H-sym hold up to eps_clean and eps_sym, the build made from the symmetric formulas has excess
   objective at most C_1 eps_clean + C_2 eps_sym over the optimum, with constants set by the spectral gap of T1a
   part 4 and by |S^-1| of Theorem T0.
Route: (1) Under H-sym the law of the family's activity is invariant under SE(2), so every gated moment is a function
of orbit invariants (relative angle and offset). H-contour fixes those functions through the Wiener integrals of
Theorem T3, up to nu, sigma and the background. (2) The optimum S^-1 R of T0 is a smooth function of (S, R) where S is
invertible: a perturbation of size eps moves it by at most |S^-1| (1 + |S^-1 R|) eps to first order. The link from
eps_clean to the size of (delta S, delta R): if each feature moves by at most eps |f_0|_P in L2(P) and |G_x| <= g,
then each entry of S and R is a bilinear form in the features and moves by at most (2 eps + eps^2) |f_0|_P^2 g times
the number of position pairs (Cauchy and Schwarz). The read space of
T1a part 4 moves by at most eps over the spectral gap (Davis and Kahan).
Lean: none, the route needs measure theory on SE(2). The finite-dimensional perturbation step is a candidate for a
later Lean port.

## B.4 The fold of a gated chain

This section closes the chain of Part D.1 inside one class of networks: gated chains (Definition D11, Hypothesis
H-gate). For them the fold is exact, covers every layer of the chain at once, and gives real units. Notation for the
whole section: u(x) = sum_p rho(p) G(x, p) a(x, p) in R^d with G = g_1 g_2 ... g_m (the product of the gates at one
position), uhat(x) = K^T u(x) in R^{N_1} (the gated, pooled pre-activations of the first family), A = H w_{m-1} ... w_1
(n_y x N_1, with A = H when m = 1), Chat = Cov_P(uhat) and Phi = A^T P_perp A (both N_1 x N_1). All moments are assumed
finite.

**Lemma T8 (a gated chain collapses to one linear map per input) (under: H-gate).** For every input x and every build
B of widths (k_1, ..., k_m), y_B(x) = Z_B u(x) + c' with Z_B = H' w'_{m-1} ... w'_1 K'^T. For the network itself,
y(x) = A K^T u(x) + c = A uhat(x) + c. The rank of Z_B is at most k = min_l k_l. Conversely, every n_y x d matrix of rank
at most k is Z_B for some build of widths (k_1, ..., k_m).
Proof. By induction on l, the l-th layer of the build is v'_l(x, p) = g_1 ... g_l (x, p) w'_{l-1} ... w'_1 K'^T a(x, p):
each gate is a scalar at (x, p), and a scalar commutes with a matrix. Summing the last layer over p with weights
rho(p) gives the formula. The product passes through a space of dimension k_l at every layer, so its rank is at most
k_l. For the converse, write Z = U V^T with U (n_y x r) and V (d x r), r = rank Z <= k. Take K' = [V, 0], every w'_l
equal to the identity on the first r units and zero elsewhere, and H' = [U, 0]. QED.
Lean: `gate_commute` (a gate commutes with an edge), `chain_rank_le` (the rank bound).
Comment: so the logit change y_B - y = (Z_B - A K^T) u(x) + (c' - c) is exactly linear in the build's map, with no
small-change condition. This is link 0 of Part D.1 inside the gated class, for the objective D2. The sum over
positions and the gates are absorbed into u(x), and the readout metric P_perp is the same for every input. So in
Theorem T9 the data enters through one covariance matrix. Inside the gated class, the role that H-kron plays in T1a
is played by this identity: H-gate implies it, and no further factorisation hypothesis is needed.

**Theorem T9 (the best coarse chain is a read of the first family) (under: H-gate).** Let mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ... >= 0 be
the eigenvalues of P_perp A Chat A^T P_perp (this is Cov_P(P_perp y), the covariance of the network's centred logits),
with orthonormal eigenvectors e_1, e_2, ..., and U_k = [e_1, ..., e_k]. Fix widths (k_1, ..., k_m) and let
k = min_l k_l.
