1. The minimum of D2_P over builds of widths (k_1, ..., k_m) is 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j. The non-zero mu_j are the
   non-zero eigenvalues of Chat^{1/2} Phi Chat^{1/2}.
2. One optimal build: the first layer reads the members with Lambda = U_k^T P_perp A (k x N_1), that is, coarse unit a
   is sum_i Lambda_{a i} v_{1,i}, with kernel K Lambda^T and gate g_1. Every edge is the identity, w'_l = I_k. The head
   is H' = U_k and c' = c + (A - U_k Lambda) E_P uhat.
3. If mu_k > mu_{k+1}, every optimal build has the same centred output. For P-almost every x it equals
   U_k U_k^T P_perp (y(x) - E_P y): the projection of the network's centred logits onto their top k principal
   components.
4. (Near-optimal builds compute nearly the optimal function.) If mu_k > mu_{k+1}, then every build B of widths
   (k_1, ..., k_m), with any bias, satisfies
   E_P |P_perp (y_B - E_P y_B) - P_perp (y_{B*} - E_P y_{B*})|^2 <= 2 (D2(B) - D2(B*)) (1 + sqrt(2 mu_1 / (mu_k - mu_{k+1})))^2,
   with B* the build of part 2. So any sequence of builds whose objective tends to the minimum (for example a training
   run that reaches the minimum value) has centred outputs that tend to those of B*.
So the data enters the fold only through Chat (an N_1 x N_1 matrix) and E_P uhat (for the bias).
Proof. By Lemma T8, D2 = 1/2 E |P_perp ((Z - A K^T) u + c' - c)|^2 over all Z of rank <= k and all c'. Write
Sigma = Cov_P(u). The term with E u is a constant vector, and c' is free, so the best c' makes it zero and leaves
1/2 E |P_perp (Z - A K^T)(u - E u)|^2 = 1/2 |P_perp Z Sigma^{1/2} - Y|_F^2 with Y = P_perp A K^T Sigma^{1/2}.
P_perp Z Sigma^{1/2} has rank <= k. By Eckart and Young the minimum over rank-k matrices is the sum of the squared
singular values of Y after the k-th, and it is reached at U_k U_k^T Y, with U_k the top left singular vectors of Y, which
are the top eigenvectors of Y Y^T = P_perp A K^T Sigma K A^T P_perp = P_perp A Chat A^T P_perp (since Chat = K^T Sigma K).
Z = U_k U_k^T P_perp A K^T reaches it: P_perp Z = Z because every e_j with mu_j > 0 lies in the range of P_perp (for
mu_j = 0 choose e_j in that range). This Z equals the Z_B of the build in part 2 (Lemma T8 with w'_l = I_k), and the
bias in part 2 is the best c'. The non-zero eigenvalues of Y Y^T and Y^T Y agree, and Y^T Y has the same non-zero
eigenvalues as Chat^{1/2} Phi Chat^{1/2} (both are (P_perp A Chat^{1/2}) times its transpose, in the two orders). (3) With
a strict gap the best rank-k approximation of Y is unique, so P_perp Z Sigma^{1/2} is unique, and the centred output
P_perp (y_B - E y_B) = P_perp Z (u - E u) is unique for P-almost every x. It equals U_k U_k^T P_perp A K^T (u - E u) =
U_k U_k^T P_perp (y - E y). (4) Changing the bias of B changes D2(B) but not its centred output, so it is enough to
take B with its best bias. Write Zhat = P_perp Z_B Sigma^{1/2}, of rank <= k, and let Q be the orthogonal projection onto
a k-dimensional space that contains the range of Zhat. Write f(Z) = |Y - Z|_F^2, so 2 (D2(B) - D2(B*)) = e with
e = f(Zhat) - f(Y_k), Y_k = U_k U_k^T Y. Since Zhat - Q Y lies in the range of Q and Y - Q Y is orthogonal to it,
f(Zhat) = |Zhat - Q Y|_F^2 + f(Q Y). Also f(Q Y) - f(Y_k) = tr(P M) - tr(Q M) with M = Y Y^T and P = U_k U_k^T. In the
eigenbasis of M, with q_j = e_j^T Q e_j in [0, 1] and sum_j q_j = k, this difference is at least
(mu_k - mu_{k+1}) (k - tr(P Q)) (`gap_trace`), and k - tr(P Q) = |P - Q|_F^2 / 2. Both terms are non-negative, so
|Zhat - Q Y|_F^2 <= e and |P - Q|_F^2 <= 2 e / (mu_k - mu_{k+1}). Then
|Zhat - Y_k|_F <= |Zhat - Q Y|_F + |(Q - P) Y|_F <= sqrt(e) + |Q - P|_F sqrt(mu_1), which gives the bound, because
|Zhat - Y_k|_F^2 is the left-hand side (both centred outputs are linear in u - E u, as in the proof of part 3). QED.
Lean: `gap_trace` for the gap step of part 4. None for the rest of the content (Eckart and Young is classical and not in Lean here). The rank bound it uses is
`chain_rank_le` (Lemma T8).
Comment: after the collapse the fold is reduced-rank regression (Anderson 1951; Izenman 1975) of the teacher's logits
on u. The content of the theorem is that the optimum is a read of the first family's members (a WHAT) and is built by
real units of the class (a HOW), with nothing to fit but Chat. It needs no symmetry. Theorem T10 adds the symmetry.

**Proposition T7 (with a shared gate, every WHAT is one unit) (under: H-gate).** For any read Lambda (k x N_1), the
targets t_a = sum_i Lambda_{a i} v_{1,i} are computed exactly by k units of the class: unit a has kernel K Lambda_a^T
and gate g_1. With Theorem T9 (whose optimum over all builds is such a read), the best WHAT is the best build (links
8 and 9 of Part D.1, inside the gated class).
Proof. sum_i Lambda_{a i} g_1 <K_i, a(x, p)> = g_1 <sum_i Lambda_{a i} K_i, a(x, p)>. QED.
Lean: `gated_sum`.
Comment: this is the step that fails for ReLU (Proposition T1'). There each member has its own gate, so a sum of members
has as many hinges as members.

**Theorem T6 (the optimal coarse chains form a fold ladder) (under: H-gate).** Take widths k < k' with strict gaps
mu_k > mu_{k+1} and mu_{k'} > mu_{k'+1}, and the optimal builds of Theorem T9 part 2 at k and at k'.
1. Nesting: the span of U_k lies in the span of U_{k'}.
2. Merge: Lambda_k = M Lambda_{k'} with M = U_k^T U_{k'} (k x k', orthonormal rows). So each coarse unit at width k is a
   fixed combination of the coarse units at width k', and by Proposition T7 it is one unit.
3. Fold of outputs: the centred output at width k is U_k U_k^T times the centred output at width k'.
4. Composition: for k < k' < k'' (strict gaps at all three), (U_k^T U_{k'}) (U_{k'}^T U_{k''}) = U_k^T U_{k''}.
So the optimal builds at the widths with a strict gap, with these merges, form a fold ladder (Definition D10). At a
width k with mu_k = mu_{k+1} the optimal build is not unique: every choice of e_k inside the tied eigenspace is
optimal, with the same value. The ladder is stated for the builds of T9 part 2. Other optimal builds have the same
centred outputs (T9 part 3) but may differ in directions that the law never excites, or recombine units inside a layer,
so for them the merge holds on centred outputs, not unit by unit.
Proof. (1) U_k and U_{k'} are top eigenvectors of one symmetric matrix, and with strict gaps the top-k and top-k'
eigenspaces are unique and nested. So U_{k'} U_{k'}^T U_k = U_k. (2) Lambda_k = U_k^T P_perp A
= (U_{k'} U_{k'}^T U_k)^T P_perp A = U_k^T U_{k'} U_{k'}^T P_perp A = M Lambda_{k'}. (3) U_k U_k^T U_{k'} U_{k'}^T = U_k U_k^T
by `nested_proj`, applied to Theorem T9 part 3. (4) is `merge_compose`. QED.
Lean: `nested_proj`, `merge_compose`.

**Theorem T10 (with symmetry, the fold keeps the same frequencies at every layer) (under: H-gate, H-eq, H-symN).**
Assume Chat is positive definite. Write Fourier mode n for the member index, and P_S for the orthogonal projection onto
the real span of the modes in a set S that is closed under n -> -n.
1. Chat and Phi are circulant, and E_P uhat is a constant vector.
2. The eigenvalues of Chat^{1/2} Phi Chat^{1/2} are lambda_n = chat(n) phihat(n) on mode n, with lambda_n = lambda_{-n}.
3. Let S hold the k modes with the largest lambda_n, with a strict gap (min over S > max outside S). Then the build
   "insert P_S after every layer" is optimal at width k. It is realised with an orthonormal real basis Q_S of the modes
   in S (Q_S Q_S^T = P_S): coarse units Q_S^T v_l at every layer, edges Q_S^T w_l Q_S, head H Q_S, and
   c' = c + A (I - P_S) E_P uhat. Its centred output is P_perp A P_S (uhat(x) - E_P uhat), and its objective is
   1/2 sum_{n not in S} lambda_n.
4. The optimal levels nest along the order of the lambda_n. The merge between two levels keeps a subset of the modes.
   A strict gap can sit only between whole mode pairs: a cut inside a pair (n, -n) with 0 < n < N / 2 gives a circle of
   optimal builds with equal value (T1a part 5 is a case).
5. Given the weights, the data enters the choice of S only through the floor(N / 2) + 1 numbers chat(n),
   n = 0, ..., floor(N / 2) (their values, since the order of lambda_n = chat(n) phihat(n) depends on them), and the bias
   through the constant E_P uhat.
Proof. (1) Substituting p = gamma q in the sum over positions, and using H-eq parts 1 and 2,
uhat_{i+1}(gamma . x) = sum_q rho(gamma q) G(gamma . x, gamma q) z_{i+1}(gamma . x, gamma q) = sum_q rho(q) G(x, q) z_i(x, q)
= uhat_i(x). So uhat(gamma . x) = Pi uhat(x). By H-symN, Chat = Cov(uhat(gamma . x)) = Pi Chat Pi^T and
E uhat = Pi E uhat (a constant vector, by `const_of_rotate_invariant`). By H-eq parts 3 and 4,
A Pi = H w_{m-1} ... w_1 Pi = H Pi w_{m-1} ... w_1 = R_y A, and P_perp commutes with every permutation, so
Pi^T Phi Pi = A^T R_y^T P_perp R_y A = Phi. (2) T1a part 2. (3) Put Y' = P_perp A Chat^{1/2}. Its right singular vectors
are the eigenvectors of Y'^T Y' = Chat^{1/2} Phi Chat^{1/2}, which by (2) and the gap span the range of P_S for the top
k. The projection onto the top-k left singular vectors satisfies U_k U_k^T Y' = Y' P_S (both are the rank-k
truncation of Y'). Multiplying on the right by Chat^{-1/2}, which commutes with P_S (both are circulant), gives
U_k U_k^T P_perp A = P_perp A P_S. By Theorem T9 part 3 the optimal centred output is P_perp A P_S (uhat - E uhat).
The build of part 3 computes it: every w_l commutes with P_S (circulant), so by `proj_commute_chain`
P_S w_{m-1} ... w_1 = w_{m-1} ... w_1 P_S, and Q_S^T w_l Q_S Q_S^T = Q_S^T w_l P_S = Q_S^T P_S w_l = Q_S^T w_l at every layer.
Its value is 1/2 tr((I - P_S) Chat^{1/2} Phi Chat^{1/2}) = 1/2 sum_{n not in S} lambda_n. (4) T6 and (2). (5) restates
(2) and (3). QED.
Lean: `proj_commute_chain` (truncating the first layer equals truncating every layer). The Fourier diagonalisation of
circulant matrices is classical (Gray 2006).

**Corollary T10.1 (a chain whose readout sees only the member sum folds to width one with no loss) (under: H-gate,
every edge w_l has equal column sums, and H = alpha' 1^T; H-eq with R_y = I implies the last two).** The width-1 build that reads the orbit sum sum_i v_{l,i} at every layer has D2 = 0 for every input
law: it gives the network's logits on every input.
Proof. Under H-eq (which includes N_l = N) with R_y = I, H Pi = H, so each row of H is invariant under the cyclic
shift, hence constant (`const_of_rotate_invariant`): H = alpha' 1^T. Each circulant w_l has equal column sums. In
general, write 1^T w_l = s_l 1^T. The sums
sigma_l(x, p) = 1^T v_l(x, p) then satisfy sigma_1 = g_1 1^T K^T a and sigma_{l+1} = g_{l+1} s_l sigma_l, and
y(x) = alpha' sum_p rho(p) sigma_m(x, p) + c. So the width-1 build with kernel K 1, edges s_l, head alpha' and bias c
computes y exactly on every input, and its units are the orbit sums. QED.
Lean: `const_of_rotate_invariant`.
Comment: so in a chain whose edges are pointwise in position and whose readout sees only the member sum, the non-zero
member frequencies carry nothing to the output. Ways out of this are edges that are not circulant, per-member gates, or
edges that mix positions between families (the last is Conjecture D3b).

**Corollary T10.2 (a guarantee for the distillation loss) (under: H-gate).** The optimal build of Theorem T9 at width k
has D_P (the KL objective of Definition D7) at most (1/4) sum_{j > k} mu_j.
Proof. Fact F11 at every input gives KL <= (1/4) |P_perp (y_B - y)|^2 = (1/2) times the integrand of D2. Take the
expectation and use Theorem T9 part 1. QED.
Lean: `softmax_var_le` (the variance lemma inside Fact F11).
Comment: the build is optimal for D2, not proved optimal for D_P. Corollary T10.2 bounds its D_P from above, and
Corollary T10.3 compares it with the best D_P.

**Corollary T10.3 (the D2-optimal build is within a fixed factor of the best range-bounded build for the distillation
loss) (under: H-gate).**
Suppose the network's logits have range max_i y_i(x) - min_i y_i(x) <= R for P-almost every x. Let B* be the optimal
build of Theorem T9 at widths (k_1, ..., k_m). Then for every build B of the same widths whose logits also have range
<= R almost surely, D_P(B*) <= (n_y e^R / 2) D_P(B).
Proof. Lower variance bound: for a probability vector q and any v, Var_q(v) = sum_i q_i (v_i - m_q)^2
>= (min_i q_i) sum_i (v_i - m_q)^2 >= (min_i q_i) |P_perp v|^2, because the plain mean minimises sum_i (v_i - c)^2
(`softmax_var_ge`). If
the range of y is at most R, then q_i = e^{y_i} / sum_j e^{y_j} >= e^{-R} / n_y. The range is a convex function of y,
so every point y + t delta (0 <= t <= 1) on the segment from y to y_B also has range <= R. In the Taylor formula of
Fact F11 this gives KL >= (e^{-R} / (2 n_y)) |P_perp delta|^2. So D2(B) <= n_y e^R D_P(B) for such B. With Fact F11,
D_P(B*) <= (1/2) D2(B*) <= (1/2) D2(B) <= (n_y e^R / 2) D_P(B). QED.
Lean: `softmax_var_ge` (the lower variance bound). The Taylor step is by hand.
Comment: the restriction to range-bounded builds cannot be dropped by this method: far from the network, KL grows
linearly in |delta| and D2 quadratically.
Comment: this is a global link from D2 to D_P (link 0 of Part D.1) inside the gated class. The factor n_y e^R is large
for confident networks, so the corollary says that the fold is the right object for D_P only up to that factor.

**Remark B4.1 (adjacent levels branch only at the first split) (under: H-gate, H-eq, H-symN, Chat positive definite).**
Take T10 with lambda_0 > lambda_{plus or minus 1} > lambda_{plus or minus 2} > every other lambda_n and N >= 5, so there
are strict gaps at widths 1, 3, 5 (the same width at every layer). Write V_1, V_3, V_5 for the read spaces (degree <= 0,
1, 2 in the member angle).
1. Levels 1 and 3 form a tree (Definition D10). The three bumps b_j(theta_i) = 1 + cos(theta_i - phi_j) are non-negative
   units and a basis of V_3 (T1a part 4), and the level-1 read is one third of their sum, because
   sum_j b_j(theta) = 3. The one parent has three children.
2. Levels 1 and 5 also form a tree: the five shifted Fejer kernels F_2(theta - 2 pi m / 5) are non-negative on the
   circle, hence non-negative units, they are a basis of V_5 (T1a part 4), and their sum is the constant 5.
3. Levels 3 and 5 do not form a tree, in any bases. Each of the 3 parents needs at least two children, with disjoint
   sets, so level 5 would need at least 6 units. The same count shows that adjacent levels whose widths are 2d + 1 and
   2d + 3 (when the order of the lambda_n gives strict gaps there and N >= 2d + 3) are never a tree for d >= 1.
4. A different statement, on the circle, with children allowed to overlap. View reads as trigonometric polynomials on
   the circle and ask for non-negativity on the WHOLE circle (the limit of many members). No basis of the degree-2 space
   made of five EQUALLY SPACED rotated copies p(t - 2 pi m / 5) of one p that is non-negative on the circle contains the
   bump 1 + cos t in its non-negative cone. Two warnings. (a) For reads on N members only, non-negativity at N points is
   weaker, and the statement can fail: at N = 5, V_5 is the whole space, the five single members are equally spaced
   copies of one non-negative read, and the bump read is a non-negative combination of them. (b) With unequal spacing
   the statement is false: p(t) = 1 + sqrt(2) cos t + (1/2) cos 2t is non-negative, and
   (1/2) p(t - pi/4) + (1/2) p(t + pi/4) = 1 + cos t; adding any three further distinct shifts of p gives a basis (the
   five shifts have an invertible Vandermonde-type coefficient matrix, as p has non-zero coefficients at 0, 1 and 2).
Proof of 4. Normalise p(t) = 1 + 2 Re(alpha e^{i t}) + 2 Re(beta e^{2 i t}) (constant term 1, which a non-negative p
that is not zero allows). If beta = 0 the five copies span only degree <= 1, so they are not a basis. If alpha = 0, the
coefficient at mode 1 of any combination of copies is zero, but the bump's is 1/2, so the bump is not in their span.
Otherwise, suppose 1 + cos t = sum_m a_m p(t - psi_m), psi_m = 2 pi m / 5. Matching the Fourier coefficients at 0, 1 and
2 gives sum_m a_m = 1, sum_m a_m e^{-i psi_m} = 1 / (2 alpha) and sum_m a_m e^{-2 i psi_m} = 0. Inverting the 5-point
Fourier transform, a_m = (1/5) (1 + cos(psi_m - arg alpha) / |alpha|). For all a_m >= 0 we need
|alpha| >= max_m (-cos(psi_m - arg alpha)), and the smallest value of this maximum over arg alpha is cos(pi / 5). But a
trigonometric polynomial 1 + 2 Re(sum_{k=1}^{d} c_k e^{i k t}) of degree d that is non-negative on the circle has
|c_1| <= cos(pi / (d + 2)) (Fejer; Egervary and Szasz), so here |alpha| <= cos(pi / 4) < cos(pi / 5). QED.
Lean: none, the proofs are a count and Fourier analysis on the circle.
So between adjacent levels beyond level 3 the merges need shared children, signed weights or a parent with a single
child. Under H-gate this does not limit what can be built (Proposition T7). It limits only whether "children add up to
their parent" with non-negative weights and without sharing.

## B.5 Self-contained folds, and a lower bound for maps with a width-k affine head

Part B.4 folds the value path and keeps the gate path at full size. This section removes the gate path: the gates are
computed from the value path through fixed reads (H-selfgate), and a build computes its own gates. Notation as in B.4:
u, uhat, A, Chat, Sigma = Cov_P(u), P_perp, and mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ... the eigenvalues of Cov_P(P_perp y). For a
self-gated chain, R_0 is an N_1 x r matrix whose columns are a basis of the forced read space R (Definition D12),
f(x) = R_0^T uhat(x) in R^r are the **forced features**, C_f = Cov_P(f) = R_0^T Chat R_0 and
C_yf = Cov_P(P_perp y, f) = P_perp A Chat R_0. When C_f is invertible, the **residual** of the centred logits is
e(x) = P_perp (y(x) - E_P y) - C_yf C_f^{-1} (f(x) - E_P f),
the part of the centred logits that the forced features do not explain linearly. Write nu_1 >= nu_2 >= ... for the
eigenvalues of Cov_P(e), with orthonormal eigenvectors e'_1, e'_2, ... in the range of P_perp, in one fixed order.

**Theorem T12 (no map whose logits are affine in k numbers beats the top k principal directions) (under: none).** Let
y have finite second moments under P. Let B be any map from inputs to logits of the form y_B(x) = H' phi_B(x) + c', with
phi_B: X -> R^k measurable, H' an n_y x k matrix and c' in R^{n_y}. This covers any network whose last k units feed a
linear head, whatever comes below them (ReLU, max-pool, any depth). Then D2_P(B) >= 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j.
Proof. If D2_P(B) is infinite there is nothing to prove. Otherwise put delta(x) = P_perp (y_B(x) - y(x)), which has a
finite second moment, so P_perp H' phi_B = delta + P_perp (y - c') has one too. A second moment is at least the
variance, so D2_P(B) = 1/2 E |delta|^2 >= 1/2 E |delta - E delta|^2 = 1/2 E |b - ytilde|^2, with
b(x) = P_perp H' phi_B(x) - E P_perp H' phi_B and ytilde(x) = P_perp (y(x) - E y). Every b(x) lies in the range V of P_perp H', of dimension at most k. Let Q be the
orthogonal projection onto V. Then |b - ytilde|^2 = |b - Q ytilde|^2 + |(I - Q) ytilde|^2 >= |(I - Q) ytilde|^2, and
E |(I - Q) ytilde|^2 = tr C - tr(Q C) with C = Cov_P(P_perp y). In an orthonormal eigenbasis of C, tr(Q C) =
sum_j mu_j q_j with q_j = e_j^T Q e_j in [0, 1] and sum_j q_j = rank Q <= k. So tr(Q C) <= sum_{j <= k} mu_j (Ky Fan;
the coordinate step is `kyfan_coord`, with the threshold mu_k >= 0 because C is positive semi-definite). Hence
D2_P(B) >= 1/2 (sum_j mu_j - sum_{j <= k} mu_j). QED.
Lean: `kyfan_coord` (the coordinate step). The diagonal of a projection is in [0, 1] with sum equal to its rank: by hand.
Comment: this is the first statement of the paper that needs no hypothesis about the network. It is a statement about
the objective D2 and about logits that are affine in one k-vector. Theorem T9 (narrowest layer of width k), Theorem T10,
Corollary T11.1 and Theorem T13 reach the bound, so in those classes it is the exact optimum. For the distillation loss
D_P, Fact F11 and the range argument of Corollary T10.3 give a lower bound up to the factor of that corollary, for
range-bounded builds only.

**Lemma T11a (a read-faithful build computes the network's gates) (under: H-selfgate).** For a read-faithful
self-contained build (Definition D12), g'_l(x, p) = g_l(x, p) for every l, every input x and every position p. So, for
this build, the gates are fixed functions of (x, p), which is the only property of the gates that the proof of Lemma T8
uses, and its conclusion holds: y_B(x) = H' W'_m K'^T u(x) + c'.
Proof. By induction on l. Gate 1: S'_1^T K'^T a = (K' S'_1)^T a = (K S_1)^T a = S_1^T z, so g'_1 = g_1. Suppose
g'_j = g_j for j <= l, and write G_l = g_1 ... g_l. By the induction of Lemma T8 (a scalar gate commutes with an edge),
v'_l = G_l W'_l K'^T a and v_l = G_l W_l K^T a. Then S'_{l+1}^T v'_l = G_l (K' W'_l^T S'_{l+1})^T a =
G_l (K W_l^T S_{l+1})^T a = S_{l+1}^T v_l, so g'_{l+1} = g_{l+1}. QED.
Lean: `faithful_read` (the step from equal effective read kernels to equal reads), `gate_commute`.

**Theorem T11 (the best read-faithful build keeps the forced reads, then folds the residual) (under: H-selfgate).**
Assume C_f is positive definite. Take a uniform width k >= r (k_l = k for every l). If k - r exceeds the number of
non-zero nu_j, the extra eigenvectors may be any vectors: their units carry zero.
1. Every read-faithful self-contained build of uniform width k has D2_P >= 1/2 sum_{j > k - r} nu_j.
2. One build reaches it. Its first layer reads Lambda = [R_0^T ; Lambda'] (k x N_1), with
   Lambda' = U'^T (P_perp A - C_yf C_f^{-1} R_0^T) and U' = [e'_1, ..., e'_{k-r}]: coarse unit a is
   sum_i Lambda_{a i} v_{1,i}, with kernel K Lambda^T. Every edge is the identity. The read matrices are
   S'_1 = M_1 and S'_{l+1} = M_{l+1}, with M_1 (k x r_1) and M_{l+1} (k x r_{l+1}) the unique matrices that are zero below the first r rows
   and satisfy Lambda^T M_1 = S_1 and Lambda^T M_{l+1} = W_l^T S_{l+1}. The head is H' = [C_yf C_f^{-1}, U'] and the bias
   is c' = c + (A - H' Lambda) E_P uhat.
3. Its centred output is C_yf C_f^{-1} (f(x) - E f) + U' U'^T e(x): the forced features' linear prediction of the
   centred logits, plus the projection of the residual onto its top k - r principal directions.
4. (Instant switching.) For all widths k >= r, the builds of part 2 are prefixes of one stored build: the read at width
   k is the first k rows of the read at any larger width, every edge is the identity, and the head at width k is the
   first k columns of the larger head. Only the bias c' depends on k in another way (one vector per width). No gap
   condition is needed for this, only one fixed order of the eigenvectors e'_j.
5. (Smallest width.) No read-faithful build has k_1 < r, and at k = r the build of part 2 is the forced reads alone,
   with value 1/2 sum_j nu_j = 1/2 tr Cov_P(e).
Proof. (1) Let B be read-faithful. By Lemma T11a and Lemma T8, y_B = Z_B u + c' with Z_B = H' E'_m^T, where
E'_l = K' W'_l^T (d x k). The column spaces are nested: col(E'_{l+1}) = col(K' W'_l^T w'_l^T) is in col(E'_l), so all
lie in V = col(E'_1) = col(K'), of dimension at most k. Read-faithfulness says that K S_1 = E'_1 S'_1 and
K W_l^T S_{l+1} = E'_l S'_{l+1} lie in V, so V contains K R. The rows of Z_B lie in col(E'_m), which is in V.
As in the proof of Theorem T9, with the best bias, D2_P(B) = 1/2 |Y - P_perp Z_B Sigma^{1/2}|_F^2 with
Y = P_perp A K^T Sigma^{1/2}, and any other bias only adds. The rows of P_perp Z_B Sigma^{1/2} lie in
W = Sigma^{1/2} V, a subspace of dimension at most k. For any matrix X whose rows lie in W,
|Y - X|_F^2 >= |Y - Y Pi_W|_F^2 = |Y|_F^2 - tr(Y Pi_W Y^T), with Pi_W the orthogonal projection onto W.
W contains Ftilde = Sigma^{1/2} K R, and dim Ftilde = r: if Sigma^{1/2} K R_0 c = 0 then
c^T C_f c = |Sigma^{1/2} K R_0 c|^2 = 0 (since C_f = R_0^T K^T Sigma K R_0), so c = 0. Write W = Ftilde + W' with
W' = W intersected with the orthogonal complement of Ftilde, of dimension at most k - r. Then Pi_W = Pi_F + Pi_W', the sum of
two projections that annihilate each other (`proj_add_orth`), and Pi_W' = (I - Pi_F) Pi_W' (I - Pi_F). So
tr(Y Pi_W Y^T) = tr(Y Pi_F Y^T) + tr(Pi_W' M') with M' = (I - Pi_F) Y^T Y (I - Pi_F). By Ky Fan (`kyfan_coord`, as in
Theorem T12), tr(Pi_W' M') is at most the sum of the k - r largest eigenvalues of M'. The non-zero eigenvalues of M'
are those of Y (I - Pi_F) Y^T (the two orders of one product). Now compute: Y Y^T = P_perp A K^T Sigma K A^T P_perp =
P_perp A Chat A^T P_perp = Cov(P_perp y); Y Sigma^{1/2} K R_0 = P_perp A Chat R_0 = C_yf; and
(Sigma^{1/2} K R_0)^T (Sigma^{1/2} K R_0) = C_f. So Y Pi_F Y^T = C_yf C_f^{-1} C_yf^T and
Y (I - Pi_F) Y^T = Cov(P_perp y) - C_yf C_f^{-1} C_yf^T = Cov_P(e) (the covariance of a least-squares residual). Hence
D2_P(B) >= 1/2 (tr Cov(P_perp y) - tr(C_yf C_f^{-1} C_yf^T) - sum_{j <= k - r} nu_j) = 1/2 sum_{j > k - r} nu_j, because
tr Cov_P(e) = tr Cov(P_perp y) - tr(C_yf C_f^{-1} C_yf^T).
(2) and (3) The matrices M exist: the columns of S_1 and of W_l^T S_{l+1} lie in R, which is the column space of R_0, and
the first r rows of Lambda are R_0^T. With identity edges W'_l = I, so K' W'_l^T S'_{l+1} = K Lambda^T M_{l+1} =
K W_l^T S_{l+1}, and K' S'_1 = K S_1: the build is read-faithful. By Lemma T11a, y_B = H' Lambda K^T u + c' =
H' Lambda uhat + c', and the bias gives E y_B = E y. The units' centred values are f - E f (first r) and
Lambda' (uhat - E uhat) = U'^T e (the rest), because P_perp (y - E y) = P_perp A (uhat - E uhat). So the centred output
is C_yf C_f^{-1} (f - E f) + U' U'^T e, as in part 3. It lies in the range of P_perp. Its error against the centred
logits is -(I - U' U'^T) e, so D2_P(B) = 1/2 tr((I - U' U'^T) Cov(e)) = 1/2 sum_{j > k - r} nu_j.
(4) By construction: R_0^T comes first and the eigenvectors are taken in one fixed order, so the reads and the heads at
smaller widths are prefixes (`prefix_span_mono` for the spans). (5) In the proof of part 1, V contains K R, which has
dimension r, and dim V <= k_1. At k = r, U' is empty. QED.
Lean: `faithful_read`, `kyfan_coord` (the coordinate step), `proj_add_orth` (only that the sum of the two projections is
idempotent; that it is the projection onto W is by hand), `prefix_span_mono` (only the nesting of spans). The rest is
linear algebra by hand.
Comment: the proof of part 1 uses only dim col(K') <= k_1, not uniform widths or invertible edges. So every read-faithful
build with k_1 >= r has D2_P >= 1/2 sum_{j > k_1 - r} nu_j, and by Theorem T9 also D2_P >= 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j with k the
narrowest width.
Comment: this is reduced-rank regression with r predictors kept at full rank (literature table, A.4). The content is
that the forced predictors are the gates' own reads, and that the result is a build with no separate gate path.
Comment: the theorem compares read-faithful builds only. A self-contained build that reads different values for its
gates computes different gates, and its output is no longer linear in the build. Theorem T12 still bounds it from below
(when its D2 is finite), by 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j, which is at most the value of part 1. Where the best such build lies is
open (Theorem T15 shows that it can lie strictly between; Conjecture D7 asks whether it can be computed
efficiently).

**Corollary T11.1 (r extra units below the top remove the cost) (under: H-selfgate, depth m >= 2).** Take widths
k_l = k + r for l < m and k_m = k. Let Lambda_9 = U_k^T P_perp A be the read of Theorem T9 part 2. The self-contained build
with first-layer read [R_0^T ; Lambda_9], identity edges up to layer m - 1, last edge w'_{m-1} = [0, I_k] (it drops the
forced units), head U_k, the bias of Theorem T9 part 2, and read matrices as in Theorem T11 part 2, is read-faithful, and
D2_P = 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j. So it is optimal among all builds of the gated chain with the network's gates whose
narrowest layer has width k (Theorem T9), and among all maps with a width-k linear head (Theorem T12).
Proof. The gates read z and the layers 1, ..., m - 1 only, and those layers carry the forced units R_0^T v_1 with
W'_l = I, so the read matrices of Theorem T11 part 2 make the build read-faithful. By Lemma T11a the gates are the
network's. Layer m is v'_m = G [0, I_k] [R_0^T ; Lambda_9] K^T a = G Lambda_9 K^T a, so y_B = U_k Lambda_9 uhat + c', the
build of Theorem T9 part 2. Its value is 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j. QED.
Lean: `faithful_read`, `chain_rank_le` (through Theorem T9).
Comment: so a network with no gate path folds to any top width k, down to k = 1, at its exact optimum, if the layers
below the top keep r extra units for the gates' reads. The extra units sit in a prefix too (forced reads first).

**Corollary T11.2 (with symmetry and invariant single-column reads, the only forced read is the orbit sum) (under:
H-selfgate, the conditions of H-eq for a self-gated chain: N_l = N, the map gamma, and parts 1, 3 and 4; every read
matrix S_l a single column s_l 1 (an invariant read), rho invariant, H-symN, Chat positive definite).**
1. R lies in the span of the all-ones vector, so r <= 1. The gates are invariant (H-eq part 2 holds), so parts 1 and 2
   of Theorem T10 apply (their proofs use H-eq parts 1, 3 and 4, invariant gates, rho invariance, circulant pointwise
   edges and H-symN).
2. If r = 1, the forced feature is the orbit sum f = 1^T uhat, and the non-zero nu_j are the non-zero lambda_n of
   Theorem T10 for n != 0, each with its multiplicity. (If r = 0, every gate is constant.)
3. If r = 1: at uniform width k >= 1, a best read-faithful build reads mode 0 and the k - 1 modes n != 0 with the largest
   lambda_n. Its value is 1/2 times the sum of lambda_n over the other modes. When the cut after k - 1 modes falls inside
   a pair (n, -n), every choice inside the pair is optimal. At k = 1 it is the orbit-sum unit alone at every layer,
   computing its own gates. Reads beyond the non-zero lambda_n carry zero.
4. If r = 1: against the bound of Theorem T12, which here is 1/2 the sum of the lambda_n outside the k largest (T9 part 1
   and T10 part 2), the cost is
   (1/2) [(the sum of the k largest lambda_n over all n) - (lambda_0 + the sum of the k - 1 largest lambda_n over
   n != 0)]. The cost is non-negative, and it is zero when lambda_0 is among the k largest. When the depth m >= 2,
   Corollary T11.1 removes it with one extra unit below the top.
Proof. (1) A circulant edge has equal column sums (`circulant_colsum`), so 1^T w_l = sigma_l 1^T and
W_l^T 1 = sigma_1 ... sigma_{l-1} 1. So every pulled-back read is a multiple of 1. Invariance of the gates, by induction:
H-eq part 1 says z(gamma . x, gamma p) = Pi z(x, p), and 1^T Pi = 1^T, so g_1 is invariant. If
v_l(gamma . x, gamma p) = Pi v_l(x, p), then g_{l+1}, which reads s_{l+1} 1^T v_l, is invariant, and
v_{l+1}(gamma . x, gamma p) = g_{l+1} w_l Pi v_l = Pi v_{l+1} by H-eq part 3. (2) From the proof of Theorem T11,
Cov(e) = Y' (I - Pi') Y'^T with Y' = P_perp A Chat^{1/2} and Pi' = Chat^{1/2} R_0 C_f^{-1} R_0^T Chat^{1/2}. With R_0 = 1
and Chat circulant (T10 part 1), Chat^{1/2} 1 = chat(0)^{1/2} 1, so Pi' = (1/N) 1 1^T = P_0, the projection onto mode 0.
The non-zero eigenvalues of Y' (I - P_0) Y'^T are those of (I - P_0) Chat^{1/2} Phi Chat^{1/2} (I - P_0), a circulant
matrix with eigenvalue lambda_n on mode n != 0 and 0 on mode 0 (T10 part 2). (3) The value is Theorem T11 parts 1 and 2
with r = 1. The reads: with R_0 = 1, C_f = 1^T Chat 1 = N chat(0), which is positive because Chat is positive definite, and C_yf = P_perp A Chat 1 = chat(0) P_perp A 1, so
C_yf C_f^{-1} 1^T = P_perp A P_0 and Lambda' = U'^T P_perp A (I - P_0) = U'^T Y' (I - P_0) Chat^{-1/2}, because the
circulant matrices Chat^{-1/2} and P_0 commute. The columns of U' are top left singular vectors of Y' (I - P_0), whose
right singular vectors are eigenvectors of the circulant matrix of (2); choose them as real Fourier modes (inside a tied
pair any choice is optimal). Then each row of U'^T Y' (I - P_0) is a multiple of one real Fourier mode n != 0, and
Chat^{-1/2} keeps each mode. So the reads are mode 0 (the forced read) and the k - 1 top modes n != 0. (4) Subtract the
two values. QED.
Lean: `circulant_colsum` (the column sums, for a matrix given in the form c(i - j); that a matrix commuting with Pi has
this form is by hand). Parts 1 and 2 of T10 are used through their own Lean lines.
Comment: so under symmetry with invariant single-column reads the whole network, gates included, folds to one unit per
layer: the orbit sum. This matches Corollary T10.1 (an invariant readout needs only the orbit sum). Symmetry alone does
not force single-column reads: a norm gate |S^T v| with S the cosine and sine reads of one mode n is invariant and has
r = 2 (the shape of Worrall et al. 2017). The result is the exact optimum only among builds that keep the gates' reads.

**Theorem T13 (a chain with spatial edges folds to its visible widths at the optimum for its top width) (under:
H-sgate).** Let y have finite second moments under P. Let mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ... be the eigenvalues of Cov_P(P_perp y),
with one fixed orthonormal eigenbasis e_1, e_2, ... (used at every width), k at most the number of positive mu_j, and
U_k = [e_1, ..., e_k]. Let
O_l, Rch_l and d_l be as in Definition D13 for U_k. Choose at each layer a d_l x N_l matrix B_l whose rows lie in O_l and
whose rows, restricted to Rch_l, are a basis of O_l restricted to Rch_l. At the top choose the rows of B_m to be
e_j^T P_perp H, j = 1, ..., k.
1. The build with widths (d_1, ..., d_m), first-layer kernel K' = K B_1^T, edges w'_l(q) the unique d_{l+1} x d_l
   matrices with B_{l+1} w_l(q) x = w'_l(q) B_l x for every x in Rch_l, head H' = U_k, bias
   c' = c + (I - U_k U_k^T P_perp) (E_P y - c) and, when self-gated, read matrices M_l with S_l^T x = M_l^T B_{l-1} x for
   every x in Rch_{l-1} (B_0 = B_1 and Rch_0 = Rch_1, for the first gate), computes v'_l(x, p) = B_l v_l(x, p) at every
   layer and position, for P-almost every x, and its gates are the network's there.
2. Its centred output is U_k U_k^T P_perp (y(x) - E_P y), and D2_P = 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j. By Theorem T12 no map whose
   logits are affine in k numbers does better. The lower widths d_l are not claimed minimal, and they may equal N_l: the
   optimality is for the top width only.
3. (Nesting and instant switching.) For k < k' (k' also at most the number of positive mu_j), O_l(k) lies in O_l(k') at
   every layer. Choose the bases so that B_l(k)
   is the first d_l(k) rows of B_l(k') (extend a basis of the restricted smaller space to one of the restricted larger
   space; at the top this holds for the rows e_j^T P_perp H). Then the stored edge w'_l(q; k') has w'_l(q; k) as its
   top-left block and zeros to its right, the stored reads have M_l(k) on top and zeros below, and the head at width k
   is the first k columns of U_{k'}. So the folds at all widths are prefixes of one stored build, with prefix length
   d_l(k) at layer l and a bias per width.
4. (Pointwise edges.) If Q = {0} and the chain is self-gated with forced read space R of dimension r (Definition D12),
   then d_l <= k + r at every layer.
5. (Pointwise edges, lower bound.) If Q = {0}, then d_l >= k at every layer. With a gate path, d_l = k at every layer,
   which by Theorem T9 is the least width that reaches the value of part 2.
Proof. (1) Existence and uniqueness: for a row r^T of B_{l+1} and an offset q, r^T w_l(q) lies in O_l, so its restriction
to Rch_l is a unique combination of the restricted rows of B_l, which are independent. The same holds for M_l (the
columns of S_l lie in O_{l-1}, and O_1 contains the columns of S_1). At the top, the rows e_j^T P_perp H restricted to
Rch_m are independent: if sum_j c_j e_j^T P_perp H vanishes on Rch_m, then, since v_m(x, p) lies in Rch_m for every p
and P-almost every x, sum_j c_j e_j^T P_perp (y(x) - c) = 0 for P-almost every x, so the variance sum_j c_j^2 mu_j is zero,
and c = 0 because every mu_j > 0. Since U_k^T P_perp H is B_m
itself, the head U_k reads it directly. Induction on l: v'_1 = g_1 K'^T a = g_1 B_1 z = B_1 v_1. If v'_l = B_l v_l at every
position and the gates agree, then, since every v_l(x, p + q) lies in Rch_l (or is zero by padding),
v'_{l+1}(x, p) = g_{l+1} sum_q w'_l(q) B_l v_l(x, p + q) = B_{l+1} (g_{l+1} sum_q w_l(q) v_l(x, p + q)) = B_{l+1} v_{l+1}(x, p)
(`visible_step`). With a gate path the gates agree by definition. Self-gated: M_{l+1}^T v'_l = M_{l+1}^T B_l v_l =
S_{l+1}^T v_l because v_l lies in Rch_l, so the gates agree, which closes the induction.
(2) y_B = U_k B_m sum_p rho v_m + c' = U_k U_k^T P_perp H sum_p rho v_m + c' = U_k U_k^T P_perp (y - c) + c'. Its centred
value is U_k U_k^T P_perp (y - E y), the optimum of Theorem T12, and the bias makes the means agree. So
D2_P = 1/2 E |(I - U_k U_k^T) P_perp (y - E y)|^2 = 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j.
(3) O_m(k) is the row space of U_k^T P_perp H, which lies in that of U_{k'}^T P_perp H, and the map from O_{l+1} to O_l
in Definition D13 preserves inclusion (the gate reads it adds do not depend on k). For a row of B_{l+1}(k), the
restriction of r^T w_l(q) lies in the restriction of O_l(k), which is spanned by the first d_l(k) restricted rows of
B_l(k'). By uniqueness of the coefficients in the larger basis, the coefficients on the later rows are zero, and the
coefficients on the first rows are those of w'_l(q; k). The same argument applies to M_l.
(4) With pointwise edges, v_l = G_l W_l z, so Rch_l lies in W_l Rch_1. Map a read r in O_l to the restriction of W_l^T r
to Rch_1. If that restriction is zero, r vanishes on W_l Rch_1, hence on Rch_l. So d_l is at most the dimension of the
image. Unrolling Definition D13, O_l is spanned by the reads r^T w_{m-1} ... w_l with r in O_m and the reads
S_{j+1}^T w_{j-1} ... w_l (j >= l; the empty product at j = l is the identity), plus S_1 at l = 1. Their pull-backs W_l^T are the rows of U_k^T P_perp H W_m (at most k
of them) and reads whose columns lie in R. So the image has dimension at most k + r.
(5) O_l contains the reads e_j^T P_perp H w_{m-1} ... w_l, j <= k. If a combination sum_j c_j of them vanishes on Rch_l, it
vanishes on v_l(x, p), hence sum_j c_j e_j^T P_perp H v_m(x, p) = 0, because v_m = g_m ... g_{l+1} w_{m-1} ... w_l v_l with
scalar gates; then sum_j c_j e_j^T P_perp (y - c) = 0 for P-almost every x and c = 0 as in (1). So d_l >= k. With a gate
path, O_l holds only these reads, so d_l <= k. A build with a layer narrower than k has value at least
1/2 sum_{j > k - 1} mu_j > 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j by Theorem T9 (the collapse of Lemma T8 holds with the network's gates). QED.
Lean: `visible_step` (the induction step, with the edge identity on the reachable subspace only), `prefix_span_mono`
(only the nesting of spans). The uniqueness arguments of parts 1 and 3 and the counts of parts 4 and 5 are linear
algebra by hand.
Comment: this folds every layer between the raw input and the readout, including the layers below the first family,
with no gate path when the chain is self-gated. The price is the visible width: with pointwise edges it is between k and
k + r (parts 4 and 5; at most the widths of Corollary T11.1), and with spatial windows it can grow toward the input. The
reachable spaces depend on the law P. Smaller widths are open: for spatial windows this is Conjecture D3b, and for
pointwise self-gated chains it is the question of Theorem T15 and Conjecture D7.


## B.6 Where the exact fold stops

Parts B.4 and B.5 give the exact optimum in closed form, with every width a prefix of one stored build, in three
settings: the narrowest layer of a pointwise gated chain (T9), read-faithful self-contained builds (T11, T11.1), and
spatial chains at their visible widths (T13). This section shows that the next step in each of the two open directions
leaves that regime. For spatial edges, deciding the optimal value at width (1, 1) is as hard as a tensor problem that
is NP-hard. For self-contained builds whose gates may change, the read-faithful fold need not be the optimum, and the
optimum need not reach the floor.

**Theorem T14 (at width (1, 1), deciding the optimal value of a spatial fold is NP-hard) (under: none; the chains
built satisfy H-sgate; hardness relative to Hillar and Lim 2013: the theorem that deciding the spectral norm is NP-hard
and the theorem that best rank-1 approximation is NP-hard, see the literature table for their numbers).** Write the tensor
dimensions as n_1, n_2, n_3, to keep a, c and the biases free. For every 3-tensor T in R^{n_1 x n_2 x n_3} with rational
entries there is a spatial gated chain of depth 2, with constant gates from a gate path, and a law P uniform on a finite
set of rational points, both of size polynomial in n_1 n_2 n_3 and in the bit length of T, such that the minimum of D2_P
over builds of widths (1, 1) equals |T|_F^2 - ||T||_sigma^2, where ||T||_sigma is the maximum of
sum_{i,j,q} T_{ijq} h_i kappa_j omega_q over unit vectors h, kappa, omega (the spectral norm).
1. (Decision.) For a fixed nonzero rational sigma, deciding for such instances whether the optimal value at width
   (1, 1) equals the rational |T|_F^2 - sigma^2 is NP-hard. So, unless P = NP, no algorithm that runs in time polynomial
   in the size of the chain and the law decides, for every spatial gated chain, every finite rational law and every
   rational r, whether the optimal value at width (1, 1) equals r.
2. (Builds.) From an optimal build, a best rank-1 approximation of T is obtained by a polynomial map, so computing an
   optimal build is at least as hard as best rank-1 approximation of a 3-tensor, in the sense of Hillar and Lim's
   best rank-1 theorem.
Proof. Construction. Positions Pos = {0, ..., n_3 - 1}, a subset of the group Z, window Q = {0, ..., n_3 - 1},
rho(0) = 1 and rho(p) = 0 otherwise (so only p = 0 is read, and 0 + q lies in Pos for every q: padding is never used),
gates g_1 = g_2 = 1. Input field a(x, p) in R^{n_2}, first family K = I (N_1 = n_2), edge w_1(q) = T_q, the
n_1 x n_2 slice of T at q (N_2 = n_1), head H = [I ; -I] (n_y = 2 n_1), bias 0. Then y(x) = H sum_q T_q a(x, q). Stack
u(x) = (a(x, 0), ..., a(x, n_3 - 1)) in R^{n_2 n_3}. Let M be the least power of two strictly greater than n_2 n_3
(so M <= 2 n_2 n_3), take n_2 n_3 columns of the Sylvester Hadamard matrix of order M other than the all-ones column, and
let P be uniform on its M rows. Each such column sums to zero and the columns are orthogonal with squared norm M, so
E_P u = 0 and Cov_P(u) = I.
Value. A build of widths (1, 1) has kernel kappa in R^{n_2}, edge scalars omega_q, head eta in R^{2 n_1} and bias c',
so y_B(x) = eta sum_q omega_q kappa^T a(x, q) + c'. The columns of H sum to zero, so P_perp H = H, and H^T H = 2 I.
Write P_perp eta = H h + eta_perp with H^T eta_perp = 0 (then h = (1/2) H^T eta, since H^T P_perp = H^T). With E u = 0
and Cov u = I, D2_P(B) = 1/2 sum_q |H (omega_q h kappa^T - T_q) + omega_q eta_perp kappa^T|_F^2 + 1/2 |P_perp c'|^2
= sum_q |omega_q h kappa^T - T_q|_F^2 + 1/2 |eta_perp|^2 |omega|^2 |kappa|^2 + 1/2 |P_perp c'|^2
(`orth_head_split`, column by column). If T = 0 the minimum is 0. Otherwise kappa and omega are non-zero at an optimum,
so eta_perp = 0 and P_perp c' = 0 there, and sum_q |omega_q h kappa^T - T_q|_F^2 = |T - h (x) kappa (x) omega|_F^2. So
the minimum over builds is the best rank-1 approximation error of T; an optimal build gives the best rank-1
approximation h (x) kappa (x) omega with h = (1/2) H^T eta, and every best rank-1 approximation g (x) k (x) o gives an
optimal build (kappa = k, omega = o, eta = H g, c' = 0). For a unit vector x of R^{n_1 n_2 n_3} and a scale lambda,
|T - lambda x|^2 >= |T|^2 - <T, x>^2 with equality at lambda = <T, x> (`rank1_fit`, `rank1_fit_eq`). The maximum of
<T, x>^2 over unit rank-1 x is ||T||_sigma^2, attained (the unit spheres are compact). So the minimum is
|T|_F^2 - ||T||_sigma^2.
Hardness. |T|_F^2 is a rational computed from T in polynomial time. So ||T||_sigma = |sigma| if and only if the optimal
value equals |T|_F^2 - sigma^2, and the map (T, sigma) -> (chain, law, |T|_F^2 - sigma^2) is a polynomial-time
reduction from the problem of Hillar and Lim's spectral-norm theorem (over the reals, for 3-tensors) to the decision problem of
part 1. Part 2: h = (1/2) H^T eta and the products are polynomial. QED.
Lean: `orth_head_split` (the head split), `rank1_fit` and `rank1_fit_eq` (the rank-1 step). The construction and the
reduction are by hand; the hardness is cited.
Comment: in these instances the top width is 1. Theorem T13 reaches the floor 1/2 sum_{j>1} mu_j with widths (d_1, 1),
where d_1 is the visible width of layer 1 (the dimension of the span of the reads e_1^T H T_q, q in Q, restricted to the
reachable space), which can be as large as min(n_2, n_3). When d_1 = 1, T13 already gives the width-(1, 1) optimum in
closed form, so the hard instances are those with d_1 >= 2, where width (1, 1) lies below the visible widths. At the
visible widths the optimal value is the sum of the smaller eigenvalues of an explicit matrix (T12, T13). At width (1, 1)
the decision problem is NP-hard in general. T14 says nothing about symmetric chains (its instances are not H-eq
chains), which is where Conjecture D3b remains open.

**Theorem T15 (builds that change their gates can beat the read-faithful fold, and need not reach the floor)
(under: H-selfgate).** There is a self-gated chain of depth 1 with N_1 = 2 members, n_y = 2 logits, one position, the
step gate phi_1(t) = 1[t > 0] reading one column s, and a law P uniform on 4 points of R^2 (z = a, K = I), such that at
the uniform width k = r = 1:
0 = 1/2 sum_{j > 1} mu_j < min over self-contained builds of D2_P <= 1/32 < 1/16 = the value of Theorem T11.
The minimum is attained. (Remark: an exact enumeration gives the minimum as 1/32; the proof below does not need it.)
Proof. With n_y = 2, P_perp y is one number times a fixed vector: write tau(x) = (y_1(x) - y_2(x)) / sqrt 2, so
|P_perp delta|^2 = (delta_1 - delta_2)^2 / 2 for every delta, and D2_P(B) = 1/2 E (tau_B - tau)^2 with
tau_B = (y_{B,1} - y_{B,2}) / sqrt 2. Cov_P(P_perp y) has rank at most 1, so mu_2 = 0 and the floor at k = 1 is 0.
A self-contained build of width 1 has unit lambda^T z, gate 1[sigma lambda^T z > 0] for a read scalar sigma, and
output tau_B = eta 1[sigma lambda^T z > 0] lambda^T z + b. For sigma > 0 the unit is relu(lambda^T z), for sigma < 0 it
is -relu(-lambda^T z), and for sigma = 0 it is zero. So the outputs are exactly the functions
tau_B = t relu(mu^T z) + b with t real, mu in R^2, b real (equivalently (beta^T z) 1[mu^T z > 0] + b with beta = t mu). On the 4
points, the pattern A(mu) = {i : mu^T z_i > 0} is constant on each open sector between consecutive directions in
{+-R z_i} (R the rotation by a right angle), and for mu in the closed sector S the output vector is
(beta^T z_i 1[i in A_S])_i + b 1 with beta in S or in -S (the boundary rays give the same outputs as the neighbouring
pattern, because the changed coordinate is zero). So the set of output vectors is the union, over the 8 closed
sectors S and the two signs, of the linear images of the closed polyhedral cones (+-S) x R. Each image is closed, so the
union is closed and the minimum of D2_P over builds is attained; it is zero only if tau itself (up to a constant) lies in
the union. The read-faithful build at k = r = 1 is the forced read alone: tau_B = eta relu(s^T z) + b, a least-squares
fit on one feature.
The instance: z_1 = (-1, 0), z_2 = (1, 1), z_3 = (0, 1), z_4 = (-1, 1) (no two on a line through the origin, so the 8
directions +-R z_i are distinct), s = (-1, 0), and the teacher's logits y = (tau / sqrt 2, -tau / sqrt 2) with
tau = 1[s^T z > 0] alpha^T z, alpha = (-1, 1). Then s^T z = (1, -1, 0, 1), the gate is on at z_1 and z_4, and
tau = (1, 0, 0, 2).
Read-faithful value. The feature relu(s^T z) = (1, 0, 0, 1). Centred, tau is (1/4, -3/4, -3/4, 5/4) and the feature is
(1/2, -1/2, -1/2, 1/2); the least-squares slope is 3/2, the residual (-1/2, 0, 0, 1/2), and the value
1/2 x 1/4 x 1/2 = 1/16.
A better build. mu = (-3/2, 1/2) gives mu^T z = (3/2, -1, 1/2, 2), so the self-contained unit relu(mu^T z) (read
sigma = 1, head 1) outputs (3/2, 0, 1/2, 2). The error against tau is (-1/2, 0, -1/2, 0); centred, (-1/4, 1/4, -1/4, 1/4),
with value 1/2 x 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/32 < 1/16.
No exact fit. Write m_i = mu^T z_i, so m_1 = -mu_1, m_2 = mu_1 + mu_2, m_3 = mu_2, m_4 = m_1 + m_3, m_2 = m_3 - m_1. An
exact fit tau_B = tau needs tau_i = b on the off set {i : m_i <= 0} and t m_i + b = tau_i on the on set. Since
tau = (1, 0, 0, 2), the off set is one on which tau is constant: empty, a single point, or {2, 3}. Empty: t m_2 = t m_3
= -b gives t m_1 = 0, so t = 0 (m_1 > 0), so b = 0 and tau_1 = 0, false. Off {2, 3}: b = 0, t m_1 = 1, t m_4 = 2, so
t m_3 = 1; t > 0 gives m_3 > 0, against 3 being off; t < 0 gives m_1 < 0, against 1 being on. Off {1}: b = 1 and
t m_i = (-1, -1, 1) on {2, 3, 4} with every m_i > 0, impossible since the signs differ. Off {2}: b = 0, t m_3 = 0 with
m_3 > 0 gives t = 0, against t m_1 = 1. Off {3}: b = 0, t m_2 = 0 with m_2 > 0 gives t = 0, against t m_1 = 1. Off
{4}: b = 2, t m_1 = -1, t m_2 = t m_3 = -2, so t m_1 = t (m_3 - m_2) = 0, false. So tau is not in the closed union, and
the attained minimum is positive. With the build above, 0 < min <= 1/32 < 1/16. The read-faithful build is legitimate
for Theorem T11: C_f = Var(relu(s^T z)) = Var(1, 0, 0, 1) = 1/4 > 0. QED.
Lean: none, the proof is a finite case check by hand (above). The exact minimum 1/32 of the Remark is computed in
`model/t15_instance.py` (rational arithmetic on tau, Python fractions).
Comment: Theorem T15 resolves the existence question that was Conjecture D6. Theorem T16 below says where the gain comes from
and reduces the optimum to a search over the gates' reads. Whether that search can be done efficiently in general is
Conjecture D7.

**Theorem T16 (the infimum over self-contained builds equals an infimum over the gates' effective reads, with a closed
form inside) (under: H-selfgate; finite second moments of y and of u_R for every R, as defined in part 1).** Take a
self-gated chain (Definition D12) and a self-contained build of uniform width k, with W'_1 = I and
W'_l = w'_{l-1} ... w'_1. Its **effective reads** are the d x r_l matrices R_1 = K' S'_1 and
R_{l+1} = K' W'_l^T S'_{l+1} (l = 1, ..., m - 1); write R = (R_1, ..., R_m) and r'(R) = the dimension of the span of all
their columns.
1. (Gates.) The build's gates depend on the build only through R: g'_1(x, p) = phi_1(R_1^T a(x, p)) and
   g'_{l+1}(x, p) = phi_{l+1}(G'_l(x, p) R_{l+1}^T a(x, p)), with G'_l = g'_1 ... g'_l. Write G_R for the product of all
   of them and u_R(x) = sum_p rho(p) G_R(x, p) a(x, p).
2. (Collapse.) y_B(x) = Z u_R(x) + c' with Z = H' W'_m K'^T, and the columns of every R_l and the rows of Z lie in
   V = col(K'), a space of dimension at most k. So r'(R) <= k.
3. (Inner problem.) For R with r'(R) <= k let J_k(R) be the infimum of 1/2 E |P_perp (Z u_R + c' - y)|^2 over c' and
   over Z whose rows lie in some subspace V of dimension at most k that contains the columns of R. It is attained. If
   Sigma_R = Cov_P(u_R) is positive definite, then with Y_R = Cov_P(P_perp y, u_R) Sigma_R^{-1/2}, F the span of
   Sigma_R^{1/2} R and nu_1(R) >= nu_2(R) >= ... the eigenvalues of Y_R (I - Pi_F) Y_R^T,
   J_k(R) = 1/2 [tr Cov_P(P_perp y) - tr(Y_R Pi_F Y_R^T) - sum_{j <= k - r'(R)} nu_j(R)].
4. (Exactness.) Every self-contained build B of uniform width k has D2_P(B) >= J_k(R_B). Conversely, for every R with
   r'(R) <= k there is a self-contained build of uniform width k with identity edges whose effective reads are R and
   whose D2_P equals J_k(R). So the infimum of D2_P over self-contained builds of uniform width k equals the infimum of
   J_k(R) over R with r'(R) <= k.
5. (The formula as one point.) Assume Cov_P(u) is positive definite (u the network's own gated features), C_f positive
   definite and k >= r (the premises of Theorem T11). At the network's own reads R* (R*_1 = K S_1,
   R*_{l+1} = K W_l^T S_{l+1}) the gates are the network's, r'(R*) = r, and J_k(R*) is the value of Theorem T11. So T11 is
   optimal over all self-contained builds exactly when R* attains the infimum of J_k. And J_k(R) >= 1/2 sum_{j > k} mu_j
   for every R (Theorem T12).
6. (Two parts of the loss.) If Sigma_R is positive definite, J_k(R) = E_gate(R) + E_width(R) with
   E_gate(R) = 1/2 [tr Cov(P_perp y) - |Y_R|_F^2] >= 0 and
   E_width(R) = 1/2 [|Y_R|_F^2 - tr(Y_R Pi_F Y_R^T) - sum_{j <= k - r'} nu_j] >= 0. E_gate is the part of the centred logits
   that no linear map of the gated features u_R explains; under the premises of part 5 it is zero at R*.
Proof. (1) By induction on l, v'_l = G'_l W'_l K'^T a, because each gate is a scalar at (x, p) (Lemma T8). So the read of
gate l + 1 is S'_{l+1}^T v'_l = G'_l (K' W'_l^T S'_{l+1})^T a = G'_l R_{l+1}^T a (`effective_read`), and the read of gate 1
is S'_1^T K'^T a = R_1^T a. (2) Then v'_m = G_R W'_m K'^T a, and summing over positions gives y_B = H' W'_m K'^T u_R + c'.
The columns of R_1 = K' S'_1 and of R_l = K' (W'_{l-1}^T S'_l) for l >= 2, and the rows of Z = (H' W'_m) K'^T, lie in
col(K'). (3) Attainment: for each V the infimum over Z and c' is a least-squares problem, attained; V ranges over a compact
set of subspaces (a closed subset of a Grassmannian, for each dimension) on which the least-squares value is lower
semicontinuous, so the infimum over V is attained. The closed form: write u = u_R, Sigma = Sigma_R and C = Cov(P_perp y, u).
For M = P_perp Z, E |P_perp (y - E y) - M (u - E u)|^2 = tr Cov(P_perp y) - 2 tr(M C^T) + tr(M Sigma M^T) =
tr Cov(P_perp y) - |Y_R|_F^2 + |Y_R - M Sigma^{1/2}|_F^2, by completing the square; the best c' removes the mean. The rows
of M Sigma^{1/2} lie in W = Sigma^{1/2} V (the rows of P_perp Z are combinations of rows of Z), and W contains F, with
dim F = r' because Sigma is positive definite. From here the proof of Theorem T11 part 1 applies with Y_R in place of Y
(`proj_add_orth`, `kyfan_coord`): the minimum over W of dimension at most k containing F of |Y_R - Y_R Pi_W|_F^2 is
|Y_R|_F^2 - tr(Y_R Pi_F Y_R^T) - sum_{j <= k - r'} nu_j, at W = F plus the top k - r' eigenvectors of
(I - Pi_F) Y_R^T Y_R (I - Pi_F), chosen orthogonal to F. It is attained by Z = Y_R Pi_W Sigma^{-1/2}, whose rows lie in
V = Sigma^{-1/2} W and which satisfies P_perp Z = Z (the rows of Y_R are in the range of P_perp). (4) The first claim is
(2) and the definition of J_k. For the converse, take an optimal V from (3), padded to dimension k (any directions; if
k > d, take a d x k matrix K' whose columns span V), identity edges (W'_l = I), read matrices S'_l with K' S'_l = R_l (they
exist because the columns of R_l lie in V), the optimal Z written as H' K'^T (possible because its rows lie in V), and the
optimal c'. With identity edges its effective reads are K' S'_l = R_l, so by (1) its gates are those of R, and by (2) its
value is J_k(R). (5) At R*, a read-faithful build has the network's gates (Lemma T11a), so u_{R*} = u. The span of the
columns of R* is K R, of dimension r because C_f is positive definite (proof of T11 part 1), so r'(R*) = r. Then y = A K^T u
+ c is affine in u, Y_{R*} = P_perp A K^T Sigma^{1/2}, and (3) is the formula of T11 part 1 (the same matrices, with
Chat = K^T Sigma K). The bound is Theorem T12 applied to the build of (4). (6) Add and subtract |Y_R|_F^2; E_gate is the
residual of an unconstrained linear regression of P_perp y on u_R, and E_width >= 0 by (3). At R* the regression is exact
because y is affine in u. QED.
Lean: `effective_read` (the read step of part 1; the induction is by hand), `proj_add_orth` and `kyfan_coord` (part 3,
through the proof of T11). The completion of the square and the attainment are by hand.

**Corollary T16.1 (at uniform width an optimal self-contained build needs only one input subspace) (under: as Theorem
T16).** For every self-contained build of uniform width k there is one with identity edges, the same effective reads and
a D2_P no larger. Such a build is described by a subspace V of R^d of dimension at most k (its kernels), gates whose reads
lie in V, and a head. So, at uniform width, depth adds nothing to what the value path can carry; it changes only which
gates the reads produce.
Proof. Theorem T16 part 4 applied to R_B gives a build with identity edges, effective reads R_B and value J_k(R_B), and
part 4 also gives D2_P(B) >= J_k(R_B). QED.
Lean: none beyond Theorem T16.

Comment: the infimum over the weights of a self-contained build equals an infimum over the effective reads R, at most
m x d x max r_l numbers, with the rest in closed form (variable projection, literature table). The reduced problem is still
non-convex in R and can be discontinuous where r'(R) changes. How the loss divides: the formula of T11 sets E_gate to zero
and pays E_width with r slots spent on the reads; a different R may accept some E_gate to lower E_width, for example by
reading through the gates a direction that also carries output. Two special cases. (a) Step gates, depth 1, one read
column (r_1 = 1): the gate depends on R_1 only through the sign pattern of R_1^T a(x, p), constant on each open chamber of
the arrangement of the hyperplanes a(x, p)^perp. On a law with finite support there are finitely many chambers (at most
polynomially many in the number of points for a fixed input dimension; Cover 1965, Zaslavsky 1975), and the infimum is
a minimum over chambers of the infimum of J_k over the chamber, where u_R is fixed but J_k still depends on R through F.
For k = 1 and n_y = 2 each chamber gives two convex problems (the proof of T15); for larger n_y the chamber problem is a
ratio of quadratic forms over a cone, which is not convex in general. (b) Differentiable gates: if Cov(u) is positive
definite, the columns of R* are independent, phi_l is differentiable, the law has finite support, the gap
nu_{k-r}(R*) > nu_{k-r+1}(R*) holds, and the gradient of J_k at R* is not zero, then some R near R* has J_k(R) < J_k(R*), and
the build of part 4 for that R beats the T11 build: the T11 build is then not optimal over self-contained builds.

## B.7 Formulas for the gates' reads: exact for affine gates under a Gaussian field, with a price for curved gates

Theorem T11 copies the network's gate reads into the build. Theorem T16 shows that the best self-contained build is a
search over the reads, and Theorem T15 shows that the copy can lose. This section gives formulas for the reads
themselves. The tool is one fact: a build sees the input only through its first-layer units, so the best it can do is
the network's logits averaged over what those units do not see (Lemma T17a). For a Gaussian input field (H-gauss) that
average has a closed form. With affine gates and a linear-seen kept space it is exactly a build, whose gate reads the
network's gate argument regressed onto the kept units (Theorem T17). With curved gates the same build is off by an explicit term that vanishes
with the unseen part of the gate argument (Proposition T17.1). At width 1 the best kept unit lies on one explicit curve,
from the network's read toward the strong directions of the logits, and it is one of finitely many roots of one
polynomial (Theorem T17.2). At larger widths the best kept space solves a self-consistent eigenproblem (Proposition
T17.3), which reduces to a search over one vector (part 4). For any law, a finite family of builds, each with the
formula of Theorem T16 part 3, is never worse than the copy, because the copy is one of them (Proposition T18). The
exact results assume affine gates, so the network is a quadratic in a Gaussian input and no gate switches; for gates
that switch, this section gives the seen mean (T17.1, Lipschitz gates and the step gate), a price for Lipschitz gates
only (T17.1 part 3) and a candidate list (T18), not an optimum.

Notation. A self-gated chain (Definition D12) of depth m = 1 with one read column: g_1(x, p) = phi(s_1^T z(x, p)),
s_1 in R^{N_1}. Write s = K s_1 in R^d (the network's effective read, R*_1 of Theorem T16) and M = H K^T (n_y x d), so
y(x) = sum_p rho(p) phi(s^T a(x, p)) M a(x, p) + c. A build of width k has kernel K' (d x k), read column q' in R^k,
head H' and bias c'. Its kept features are w(x, p) = K'^T a(x, p) (Definition D14), its effective read is K' q', and
y_B(x) = sum_p rho(p) phi(q'^T w(x, p)) H' w(x, p) + c'. Write rho_1 = sum_p rho(p) and rho_2 = sum_p rho(p)^2. Under
H-gauss, a(x, p) ~ N(m_a, Sigma) for p in Pos+. For a kernel K' put M2 = E a a^T = Sigma + m_a m_a^T and
Gamma = M2 K' (K'^T M2 K')^+ (d x k; ^+ is the pseudo-inverse).
Four facts used below; (i) and (ii) are for a linear-seen kernel (Definition D14). (i) E[a | w] = Gamma w almost surely: if
E[a | w] = Gamma_0 w, then M2 K' = E a w^T = Gamma_0 K'^T M2 K', so Gamma w = Gamma_0 (K'^T M2 K')(K'^T M2 K')^+ w, and
this is Gamma_0 w because w lies almost surely in the range of its second moment K'^T M2 K'. (ii) The unseen part
e = a - Gamma w is Gaussian with mean zero and independent of w, with covariance C_e = E e e^T: (e, w) is a linear image of
a, hence jointly Gaussian; E[e | w] = 0 gives E e = 0 and E e w^T = 0; uncorrelated jointly Gaussian vectors are
independent. (iii) Gaussian conditioning, singular case included: put L = Sigma K' (K'^T Sigma K')^+. If
K'^T Sigma K' v = 0 then |Sigma^{1/2} K' v|^2 = 0, so Sigma K' v = 0; hence Sigma K' (K'^T Sigma K')^+ (K'^T Sigma K')
= Sigma K' (the product with the pseudo-inverse is the projection onto the orthogonal complement of the kernel).
So a - m_a - L (w - K'^T m_a) is uncorrelated with w, hence independent of it, and E[a | w] = L w + b_0 with
b_0 = m_a - L K'^T m_a. (iv) Exact criterion: let supp(w) = K'^T m_a + range(K'^T Sigma K'). It is the support of w,
because w - K'^T m_a = (K'^T Sigma K')^{1/2} xi with xi standard normal. K' is linear-seen if and only if b_0 = 0 or 0 is
not in supp(w). Proof: if L w + b_0 = Gamma_0 w almost surely, the set where the two affine maps agree is closed and has
probability 1, so it contains supp(w); if 0 is in supp(w), w = 0 gives b_0 = 0. If 0 is not in supp(w), there is ell
with ell^T w = 1 on supp(w), and Gamma_0 = L + b_0 ell^T works. Special cases: m_a = 0; or one kept unit reads a
non-zero constant entry of a alone (then 0 is not in supp(w)). Cost of a bias entry: if a has a constant entry equal to
1 (the bias convention of D11), that row of Sigma is zero, so the same row of L is zero and that entry of b_0 is 1. So
b_0 != 0 for every kernel, and K' is linear-seen if and only if some combination of its units is 1 almost surely. Then
Cov(w) has rank at most k - 1: one dimension of V is spent on the constant.

**Lemma T17a (a build is a function of what it keeps, and the seen mean is its floor) (under: none; finite second
moments of y).** Let B be a self-contained build (Definition D12, any depth and widths) with first-layer kernel K', kept
features W and V = col(K'). If D2_P(B) is finite, then
D2_P(B) = F(V) + 1/2 E_P |P_perp (y_B - m_V)|^2,
with m_V and F(V) as in Definition D14, provided every phi_l is Borel measurable (assumed throughout B.7). The same
holds for y_B = h(W) with any measurable h. The kept features of a kernel whose column space lies in V are functions of
W, so no build whose first-layer kernel has column space in V has D2_P below F(V), and F(V) <= F(V'') when V'' lies in
V. A build reaches F(V) exactly when P_perp y_B = P_perp m_V almost surely.
Proof. Every unit of B at position p is a function of w(x, p): by the proof of Theorem T16 part 1,
v'_l(x, p) = G'_l(x, p) W'_l w(x, p), and gate l + 1 is phi_{l+1}(G'_l(x, p) S'_{l+1}^T W'_l w(x, p)) (gate 1 is
phi_1(S'_1^T w(x, p))), so by induction every gate and unit at p is a function of w(x, p). So y_B = H' sum_p rho(p) v'_m(x, p) + c' is a function of W. A kernel K'' with the same column space
is K' T for some matrix T, and K' = K'' T', so its kept features are linear functions of W and the reverse: m_V depends on
V only. Put delta = P_perp (y_B - y). It is square integrable because D2_P(B) is finite, so P_perp y_B = delta + P_perp y
is square integrable, and so is P_perp m_V = E[P_perp y | W] (conditional expectation is a contraction in L2). Write
P_perp (y_B - y) = P_perp (y_B - m_V) + P_perp (m_V - y). The first term is W-measurable and square integrable, and
E[P_perp (m_V - y) | W] = 0, so by the tower property the cross term has expectation zero. Taking 1/2 E |.|^2 gives the
identity. QED.
Lean: `fiber_split` (the finite form: on a law with finitely many points, on each value of W the weighted mean is the
best constant, with the exact split of the error; the sum over the values of W is by hand).
Comment: this is a second floor beside Theorem T12. T12 bounds every map whose logits are affine in k numbers; F(V)
bounds every map of the kept features, nonlinear ones included. A build satisfies both.

**Theorem T17 (affine gates: a best build reads the network's gate argument regressed onto the kept units) (under:
H-selfgate, H-gauss; depth m = 1, one read column, phi(t) = alpha t + beta).** Let K' (d x k) be linear-seen, with
Gamma and C_e as in the notation. Let B_V be the build with kernel K', read q' = Gamma^T s, head H' = M Gamma and bias
c' = c + alpha rho_1 M C_e s.
1. B_V computes the seen mean: y_B = m_V almost surely. So D2_P(B_V) = F(V), and no measurable function of W does
   better, so no build whose first-layer kernel has column space in V does better (Lemma T17a). The read need not be
   unique (for example, every read is optimal if P_perp M Gamma = 0).
2. Its read is the least-squares predictor of the network's gate argument from the kept features: q' = Gamma^T s
   minimises E (s^T a - q^T w)^2 over q in R^k. When M2 is positive definite, the effective read K' Gamma^T s is the
   projection of s onto V that is orthogonal in the inner product (x, x') -> x^T M2 x'.
3. If s lies in V (the copy of Theorem T11 is possible), then the build's gate argument equals the network's almost
   surely, C_e s = 0 and c' = c. So the copy is the case in which the kept units see the whole gate argument.
Proof. (1) By H-gauss, (a(x, p), w(x, p)) is independent of (w(x, p'))_{p' != p}, so E[f(a(x, p)) | W] =
E[f(a(x, p)) | w(x, p)] for every integrable f. At one position write a = Gamma w + e (fact (ii)). Then
(alpha s^T a + beta) M a = (alpha s^T Gamma w + beta) M Gamma w + (alpha s^T Gamma w + beta) M e
+ alpha (s^T e) M Gamma w + alpha (s^T e) M e (`gate_expand`, coordinate by coordinate). Given w, the second and third
terms have mean zero (e has mean zero and is independent of w), and the last has mean alpha M C_e s. With q' = Gamma^T s
and H' = M Gamma, E[(alpha s^T a + beta) M a | w] = (alpha q'^T w + beta) H' w + alpha M C_e s. Summing over positions
with the weights rho, m_V = sum_p rho(p) phi(q'^T w(x, p)) H' w(x, p) + c + alpha rho_1 M C_e s = y_B. Gaussian moments
of every order are finite, so D2_P(B_V) is finite, and Lemma T17a gives the rest. (2) The normal equations for q are
K'^T M2 K' q = K'^T M2 s, and q = (K'^T M2 K')^+ K'^T M2 s = Gamma^T s solves them (the pseudo-inverse of a symmetric
matrix is symmetric, and K'^T M2 s lies in the range of K'^T M2 K' because M2 is positive semi-definite). When M2 is
positive definite, K' Gamma^T s is the M2-orthogonal projection onto col(K') by the same equations. (3) If s = K' q_0,
then s^T a = q_0^T w, so s^T e = s^T a - E[s^T a | w] = 0 almost surely; then C_e s = E[e (s^T e)] = 0, and the least
squares fit of part 2 is exact, so q'^T w = s^T a almost surely. QED.
Lean: `gate_expand` (the expansion). Facts (i) to (iii) are proved in the notation paragraph; the algebra is checked in
`model/t17_sympy.py`.
Comment: so with affine gates the switch is not copied. It reads the best linear guess of the network's switch argument
that the kept units can form, and the bias absorbs the average effect of the part they cannot see. For every linear-seen
kept space V this solves the inner search of Theorem T16 over the reads with no search. What remains is the choice of V
(Theorem T17.2, Proposition T17.3). T17 does not cover depth 2 or more.

**Proposition T17.1 (curved gates: the same build, with an explicit price for what the kept units cannot see) (under:
H-selfgate, H-gauss; depth 1, one read column, a linear-seen kernel K'; parts 1 to 4: phi absolutely continuous with
|phi'| <= L almost everywhere; part 5: phi(t) = 1[t > 0] and sigma > 0).** Let sigma^2 = s^T C_e s (the variance of the part of the gate argument that the kept units do not
see), xi a standard normal variable, phi_sigma(t) = E phi(t + sigma xi), psi_sigma(t) = E phi'(t + sigma xi), and
t(x, p) = s^T Gamma w(x, p).
1. m_V(x) = sum_p rho(p) [phi_sigma(t(x, p)) M Gamma w(x, p) + psi_sigma(t(x, p)) M C_e s] + c (when sigma = 0 the
   second term is zero, because C_e s = 0, whatever psi_0 is).
2. The build of Theorem T17 (read Gamma^T s, head M Gamma), with its best bias, has
   D2_P = F(V) + 1/2 tr Cov_P(P_perp Delta), with
   Delta(x) = sum_p rho(p) [(phi - phi_sigma)(t(x, p)) M Gamma w(x, p) - psi_sigma(t(x, p)) M C_e s].
3. For the build of part 2 with its best bias (written B_V here), D2_P(B_V) - F(V) <= rho_2 L^2 sigma^2 [(2 / pi) E |P_perp M Gamma w|^2 + ||P_perp M C_e^{1/2}||^2]
   <= rho_2 L^2 sigma^2 (1 + 2 / pi) tr(P_perp M M2 M^T P_perp), with w = w(x, p) at one position and ||.|| the operator
   norm. The last bound does not depend on V, so the price tends to zero with sigma uniformly over linear-seen V, and it
   is zero at sigma = 0.
4. If phi is affine, Delta is constant and the build reaches F(V) (Theorem T17).
5. (Step gate.) If instead phi(t) = 1[t > 0] and sigma > 0, parts 1 and 2 hold with psi_sigma(t) = phi_N(t / sigma) / sigma,
   phi_N the standard normal density. Part 3 does not apply.
Proof. (1) Fix one position and put u = s^T e, which is normal with mean zero and variance sigma^2 and is independent of
w. If sigma = 0, then u = 0 almost surely, C_e s = E[e u] = 0, and E[phi(t + u) M (Gamma w + e) | w] = phi(t) M Gamma w
(e has mean zero and is independent of w), which is the formula. If sigma > 0, write M e = (M C_e s / sigma^2) u + eta.
Then eta and u are jointly Gaussian and uncorrelated (E eta u = M C_e s - M C_e s = 0), so eta is independent of u, and
both are independent of w, with E eta = 0. So E[phi(t + u) M (Gamma w + e) | w] = phi_sigma(t) M Gamma w
+ (M C_e s / sigma^2) E[phi(t + u) u], with t fixed by w. Stein's identity for u ~ N(0, sigma^2),
E[f(u) u] = sigma^2 E f'(u) for absolutely continuous f with E |f'(u)| finite (here |f'| <= L), gives
E[phi(t + u) u] = sigma^2 psi_sigma(t). Positions combine as in Theorem T17. Since |phi(t)| <= |phi(0)| + L |t|, every
term has finite second moments. (2) y_B - m_V = Delta + (c' - c), and Lemma T17a gives
D2_P = F(V) + 1/2 E |P_perp (Delta + c' - c)|^2; the best c' leaves 1/2 tr Cov(P_perp Delta). (3) Delta is a sum over
positions of rho(p) Delta_p, with Delta_p a function of a(x, p) alone, and the positions are independent with one law,
so tr Cov(P_perp Delta) = rho_2 tr Cov(P_perp Delta_p) <= rho_2 E |P_perp Delta_p|^2. Also |phi(t) - phi_sigma(t)| <= L E |sigma xi|
= L sigma sqrt(2 / pi), |psi_sigma| <= L, and |P_perp M C_e s| = |P_perp M C_e^{1/2} C_e^{1/2} s| <=
||P_perp M C_e^{1/2}|| sigma, because |C_e^{1/2} s|^2 = sigma^2. With |x + x'|^2 <= 2 |x|^2 + 2 |x'|^2,
E |P_perp Delta_p|^2 <= 2 L^2 sigma^2 [(2 / pi) E |P_perp M Gamma w|^2 + ||P_perp M C_e^{1/2}||^2]. Multiply by 1/2.
For the uniform bound: Gamma w = E[a | w], so E |P_perp M Gamma w|^2 <= E |P_perp M a|^2 = tr(P_perp M M2 M^T P_perp)
(conditional expectation is a contraction in L2); and M2 = E (Gamma w)(Gamma w)^T + C_e, so C_e <= M2 in the Loewner
order and ||P_perp M C_e^{1/2}||^2 = ||P_perp M C_e M^T P_perp|| <= tr(P_perp M M2 M^T P_perp).
(4) For phi(t) = alpha t + beta, phi_sigma = phi and psi_sigma = alpha, so Delta = -alpha rho_1 M C_e s, a constant.
(5) The proof of part 1 uses phi only through E[phi(t + u) u]. For the step gate,
E[1[t + u > 0] u] = sigma integral_{-t / sigma}^{infinity} z phi_N(z) dz = sigma phi_N(t / sigma) = sigma^2 psi_sigma(t). All
moments are finite, so part 2 follows as before. QED.
Lean: none. The proof is Gaussian independence and Stein's identity (classical; Stein 1981, literature table).
Comment: this makes the split of Theorem T16 part 6 explicit. The copy of Theorem T11 sets sigma = 0 by spending units on
the reads (no gate error). The projected read keeps those units for the output and pays the price of part 3, which grows
with sigma^2. Which is better depends on V; Proposition T18 compares the two on any law. B_V is not claimed optimal for
curved gates: the seen mean has the smoothed gate phi_sigma, which a build with the function phi cannot compute exactly,
and another read or head may come closer.

**Theorem T17.2 (width 1: the best kept unit lies on the resolvent curve of the network's read) (under: H-selfgate,
H-gauss with m_a = 0 and Sigma positive definite; depth 1, one read column, phi(t) = alpha t + beta with alpha != 0;
k = 1).** Write stilde = Sigma^{1/2} s and Q = Sigma^{1/2} M^T P_perp M Sigma^{1/2} (positive semi-definite), with
distinct eigenvalues lambda_1 > ... > lambda_n, eigenprojections P_j and r_j = |P_j stilde|^2. For a unit vector u put
f(u) = (2 alpha^2 (stilde^T u)^2 + beta^2) u^T Q u, and f_tot = alpha^2 (|stilde|^2 tr Q + stilde^T Q stilde) + beta^2 tr Q.
1. (Value.) For the single kept unit kappa = Sigma^{-1/2} u, the build of Theorem T17 is optimal among all builds whose
   first-layer kernel lies in span(kappa), with D2_P = (rho_2 / 2) (f_tot - f(u)). So the best width-1 build is the build
   of Theorem T17 at a maximiser u* of f on the unit sphere, which exists. Its gate reads its own unit:
   g' = phi(q* kappa*^T a), with q* = s^T Sigma kappa* / (kappa*^T Sigma kappa*).
2. (The curve.) Assume Q != 0 and r_j > 0 for every j (stilde has a component in every eigenspace of Q). Then every
   maximiser has stilde^T u* != 0, and u* = x(mu) / |x(mu)| or its negative, with x(mu) = (mu I - Q)^{-1} stilde for a
   real mu that is not an eigenvalue of Q. In the original coordinates the best kernel is proportional to
   (mu I - M^T P_perp M Sigma)^{-1} s.
3. (Finitely many candidates.) Under the assumption of part 2, that mu solves g(mu) = 2 alpha^2 A (A - B) + beta^2 D = 0, with A = sum_j r_j / (mu - lambda_j),
   D = sum_j r_j / (mu - lambda_j)^2 and B = sum_j lambda_j r_j / (mu - lambda_j)^2. Multiplied by prod_j (mu - lambda_j)^3
   this is a polynomial of degree exactly 3n - 2 (if beta = 0: the equation sum_j r_j (mu - 2 lambda_j) / (mu - lambda_j)^2 = 0,
   of degree exactly 2n - 1 after multiplying by prod_j (mu - lambda_j)^2). Only the real roots that are not eigenvalues
   of Q are candidates (the polynomial can vanish at mu = 0 when Q is singular, which is the usual case, since Q has rank
   at most n_y - 1). The two unit vectors plus or minus x(mu) / |x(mu)| give the same build up to the sign of the
   kernel. So the best width-1 build is the best of at most 3n - 2 explicit candidates (at most 2n - 1 if beta = 0).
4. (The two ends.) Under the assumption of part 2: as mu -> plus or minus infinity, x(mu) / |x(mu)| tends to plus or minus stilde / |stilde|: the copy of
   the network's read. As mu -> lambda_j, it tends (up to sign) to P_j stilde / |P_j stilde|, a direction inside one
   eigenspace of Q, the whitened Gram matrix of the value map P_perp M. If n >= 2, neither the copy nor any unit vector
   inside one eigenspace of Q is a maximiser.
Proof. (1) m_a = 0 makes every kernel linear-seen. Scale kappa so that kappa^T Sigma kappa = 1 (|u| = 1); then the kept
feature w = kappa^T a is standard normal, Gamma = Sigma kappa, s^T Gamma w = a_0 w with a_0 = stilde^T u, and
P_perp M Gamma w = w B u with B = P_perp M Sigma^{1/2}. At one position, P_perp m_V = (alpha a_0 w + beta) w B u plus a
constant, so its covariance has trace (E[(alpha a_0 w + beta)^2 w^2] - (E[(alpha a_0 w + beta) w])^2) |B u|^2
= (3 alpha^2 a_0^2 + beta^2 - alpha^2 a_0^2) u^T Q u = f(u). For y, write a = Sigma^{1/2} g with g standard normal in
R^d: P_perp y = (alpha stilde^T g + beta) B g plus a constant. By the Gaussian fourth moments (Isserlis),
E[(stilde^T g)^2 |B g|^2] = |stilde|^2 tr Q + 2 stilde^T Q stilde, the odd moments vanish, and E[(alpha stilde^T g + beta) B g]
= alpha B stilde, so the trace of its covariance is f_tot. The positions are independent with one law, so both traces are
rho_2 times these. Since m_V is the seen mean, E m_V = E y and Cov(P_perp (y - m_V), P_perp m_V) = 0, so
F = 1/2 (tr Cov P_perp y - tr Cov P_perp m_V) = (rho_2 / 2) (f_tot - f(u)). By Theorem T17 the build B_V reaches F, and
by Lemma T17a nothing with kernel in span(kappa) does better. A build with zero kernel has the value (rho_2 / 2) f_tot,
which is not smaller. f is continuous on the compact sphere. The gate: q' = Gamma^T s = s^T Sigma kappa (with
kappa^T Sigma kappa = 1), and phi(q' w) = phi(q' kappa^T a), which is the formula after rescaling kappa.
(2) Put a_0 = stilde^T u, q = u^T Q u and c = 2 alpha^2 a_0^2 + beta^2. At a maximiser on the sphere there is a multiplier
omega with grad f = 2 omega u, that is, c Q u + 2 alpha^2 a_0 q stilde = omega u; the inner product with u gives
omega = q (c + 2 alpha^2 a_0^2). First, a_0 != 0: otherwise f(u) = beta^2 q <= beta^2 lambda_1, while the unit vector
u_1 = P_1 stilde / |P_1 stilde| has q = lambda_1 > 0 (Q != 0 is positive semi-definite) and a_0 = |P_1 stilde| > 0, so
f(u_1) = (2 alpha^2 r_1 + beta^2) lambda_1 > beta^2 lambda_1 >= f(u). So c > 0 and, with mu = omega / c,
(mu I - Q) u = (2 alpha^2 a_0 q / c) stilde. If mu were an eigenvalue lambda_j, applying P_j gives
0 = (2 alpha^2 a_0 q / c) P_j stilde with P_j stilde != 0, so q = 0, Q u = 0 and f(u) = 0 < f(u_1), a contradiction. So
mu is not an eigenvalue, q > 0, and u is a non-zero multiple of x(mu); |u| = 1 fixes it up to sign. In the original
coordinates kappa = Sigma^{-1/2} u is proportional to Sigma^{-1/2} (mu I - Sigma^{1/2} N Sigma^{1/2})^{-1} Sigma^{1/2} s
= (mu I - N Sigma)^{-1} s with N = M^T P_perp M, because Sigma^{-1/2} (mu I - Sigma^{1/2} N Sigma^{1/2}) Sigma^{1/2} = mu I - N Sigma.
(3) In an orthonormal eigenbasis of Q, |x(mu)|^2 = D, stilde^T x(mu) = A and x(mu)^T Q x(mu) = B, so a_0^2 = A^2 / D and
q = B / D. Termwise, mu r_j / (mu - lambda_j)^2 - lambda_j r_j / (mu - lambda_j)^2 = r_j / (mu - lambda_j)
(`resolvent_shift`), so mu D - B = A. The relation mu = omega / c = q (4 alpha^2 a_0^2 + beta^2) / (2 alpha^2 a_0^2 + beta^2)
becomes mu D (2 alpha^2 A^2 + beta^2 D) = B (4 alpha^2 A^2 + beta^2 D). Replacing mu D by A + B and cancelling gives
2 alpha^2 A^3 + beta^2 A D - 2 alpha^2 A^2 B = 0, that is, A g(mu) = 0, and A = |x(mu)| a_0 != 0. Degree: as
mu -> infinity, mu^2 g(mu) -> 2 alpha^2 R^2 + beta^2 R with R = sum_j r_j = |stilde|^2 > 0, so g(mu) prod_j (mu - lambda_j)^3
is a polynomial of degree exactly 3n - 2. If beta = 0, g = 0 with A != 0 means A = B, and
A - B = sum_j r_j (mu - 2 lambda_j) / (mu - lambda_j)^2; times prod_j (mu - lambda_j)^2 its leading term is R mu^{2n-1}. Each
real root gives two unit vectors plus or minus x / |x| with the same value of f (f is even), and every maximiser is among
them by (2). (4) mu x(mu) -> stilde as mu -> plus or minus infinity, and (mu - lambda_j) x(mu) -> P_j stilde as mu -> lambda_j.
Let n >= 2. If u is a multiple of stilde and a maximiser, then by (2) a_0 != 0 and c > 0, and the stationarity equation
gives Q stilde in span(stilde), so stilde lies in one eigenspace and r_j = 0 for the others, a contradiction. If Q u = lambda_j u
and u is a maximiser, then (omega - c lambda_j) u = 2 alpha^2 a_0 q stilde with a_0 q != 0 by (2), so stilde is a multiple
of u and lies in one eigenspace: the same contradiction. QED.
Lean: `resolvent_shift` (the termwise identity behind mu D - B = A). The Lagrange condition on the sphere and the
